Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Forget warp speed, why is it so hard to get to even 1% of the speed of light with modern (or even near future tech) whether manned or unmanned? Is it that hard to come up with a new fuel source better than rocket fuel?
Answer: Ultimately, there is no practical reason to go faster given its cost. 1% the speed of light is about 7 million miles an hour. That’s unfathomably fast. 100x faster then the fastest rocket that takes enormous boosters to get to that speed. We’ve gotten pretty close going 400,000 miles an hour with a gravitational assist from the sun. That takes time though, but 1% the speed of light seems achievable. There are various ideas that could get us that fast, but when you need billions of dollars to go relatively slow, the real thing that makes going faster hard is why? With time we can get to every planet in our solar system and have done just that well within a human lifetime. Getting there faster would certainly help, but getting a budget is more of a problem then waiting decades for the result. The best use of limited money is to do more science slower rather then less faster. Speed wouldn’t really help our currently feasible missions given the cost. Now of course the reason to go really really fast is to get to places we haven’t been to. The problem is even going to speed of light isn’t terribly helpful. Space to just too damn big. We are 12 years away from the closest interesting extra solar planet at the speed of light. That’s 1200 years away at 1% the speed of light. Its also likely not any more interesting then Venus, which we have barely explored. That’s the closest, the top 100 list of interesting planets ends at thousands of light years away. Quite simply even if we could go the speed of light, it would still take an extraordinary amount of luck to find some place more interesting then the planets we have in our own solar system. In other words, until we discover new laws of physics that would let us change the maximum speed at which matter can travel, well beyond the speed of light, going faster doesn’t matter, practically speaking, the speed of light is just too damn slow to be worth a damn in the vastness of space.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If you're in San Francisco, would you take up an offer to own a three-bedroom property worth $1.8 million for just $488,000, but you can't move in until 2053?
Answer: Including adjusting for inflation $488,000 would be worth $3,319,983 in today’s dollars if invested in the S&P500 and the average return holds over the next 30 years. The average home in San Francisco also costs far more than the average resident can afford, meaning, it’s over priced for the current residents. It has managed to keep rising due to an influx of new residents who get paid ever increasing amounts. Currently just the top 6% of San Francisco residents could actually afford to buy a home there. To match the S&P 500 returns over the next 30 years, the price of a house would have to double relative to median income levels in today’s dollars. That means only the top 1% of households to afford to buy a home there. The pessimist in me says that’s entirely plausible, but seems a far riskier bet and likely far less upside then an index fund. It’s a pretty bad deal. Keep looking.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Which is the world's most dangerous disease? Why?
Answer: My son died of adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) when he was 8. He was born perfectly normal and had a seemingly perfectly healthy life up until half way through kindergarten. Our first clue came when one of his teachers called us in for a conference to tell us our son, who was for all of his life before that point, exceptionally well behaved, was acting out in school. Nothing particularly mean or even really relatable. He basically just seemed like he was no longer aware of good manners. He would do things like pee outside the urinal or behave erratically at inappropriate times. We had him diagnosed by experts who promptly diagnosed our son with mild autism and ADHD. A bit weird considering he was highly social, reading above level, and prior to this had no real signs of either. We start ABA therapy and do all the things you need to do for a child with special needs. He makes progress he learns to do things better after weeks of intense therapy, but then a few more weeks go by and he gets worse in every way. We didn’t know it then, but he was just relearning to do things with different parts of his brain, not getting better. He starts forgetting things. He’s talking less. He’s climbing furniture and doing immature things he never even did when he was younger. The psychologists imply it’s our fault. We must not be sticking to the therapy. We try harder. Nothing is working. He tells us he has brain freezes and asks us if he’s dying. We tell him of course not, everything is fine, we will work through this and you will get better. Regressions go on for several months. We start to doubt the diagnosis, but there’s nothing we can do except complain to our psychologist who tells us he was misdiagnosed. He actually has severe autism! We ask for a referral to a neurologist to rule out other possibilities. The psychologist refuses, letting us know it’s us. We need to work harder. This goes on for months and we keep on begging for a referral. By the time he is close to non-verbal we finally have another appointment and show the psychologist a video of our son singing and dancing when he was a year younger. It’s a stark contrast to the child we now have who can no longer even attend a regular school. That’s not how autism works. We finally get a referral to a real doctor. We get an MRI and it’s lit up like a Christmas tree. An incredibly intense week of more testing follows. We test for hundreds of different diseases. Finally a genetic test for Adrenoleukodystrophy comes back positive. There’s no doubt. It fits. It’s also a death sentence. There’s no known cure once symptoms start. Over the next year we watch our son forget who we were. Lose the ability to hear, see, smell, taste, and walk. He went through epileptic seizures and eventually became a walking zombie, not really cognizant of the world around him, but still able to perform basic life sustaining tasks like feeding himself. After he ate something he should not have, we had to take him to the ER. The anesthesia, messed with what was left of his brain and he never quite came back. He never walked again after that and could no longer feed himself or really do anything as he lost all of his senses. Once symptoms start, every single person who has ever had this disease dies within a few years at most. Some people have prolonged it by using machines to keep their children alive, but their brains are totally gone except for the autonomic functions. No one has ever reversed the brain damage. The only thing worse then watching your son die is knowing he’s absolutely going to die, knowing he has nothing to live for except more pain and suffering, and the only way to stop the suffering is to starve him to death. We had a team of doctors at that point. Not helping our son. There was nothing they could do for him and his body was actually quite healthy. He was just in a semi vegetative state. Awake, but not cognizant of the world around him. His soul was actually the first thing to go. His behaviors changed and for all intents and purposes, the disease took our son’s identity and dignity before any of the more physical ailments. There was no hope he was still in there. No question he was gone for over a year. This team of doctors was there for us, his parents, to guide us through his death. They were his palliative care team. We were at Stanford and they were some of the most qualified, compassionate, and intelligent doctors I have encountered. Near the end, I wanted to punch every one of them. It wasn’t their fault. They are messengers in a broken system, but they all knew our son was dying. They all knew his brain function was gone. They all knew he was never coming back. The adrenoleukodystrophy expert actually told us down to the month when our son would lose each of his functions. He was incredibly accurate. The last few meetings we had were all about how removing nutrition and hydration isn’t so bad, hes past where he is aware of most things. The body “knows” it’s dying and just peacefully gives up. It all felt made up. They said they will control the pain with morphine. Fuck! I know what morphine does. My first question is what is the point of prolonging his life. Theres no answers of hope coming back, no answers of he might still be there. Just the elephant in the room no one explicitly brings up. Society says this is the only path. “It’s fine.” But it wasn’t fine. My next question was how much morphine will stop all the pain immediately forever. They wouldn’t answer that one. My son died when he was 8 after 3 weeks without food or water. Adrenoleukodystrophy is a rare genetic disease. It can be cured if it's caught with a test before symptoms start with a simple genetic test at birth. The federal government recommended this test before my son was born to be included with all newborn screenings. No state at the time he was born adopted the test as part of newborn screening despite that it pays for itself. When he died only 5 states did, today 44 do. If you have a son that was born with the gene for ALD, 1/3rd develop adrenoleukodystrophy most of the rest develop a related disorder that has very serious symptoms that start in the 20s or 30s. 10% have just minor adrenal gland issues that are treatable. This is a photo of the last time I was able to get Griffin to laugh. He was otherwise non-verbal at this point, and struggling with a lot of his senses, but often you would barely know it if you saw us out. Physically his body was healthy. He was mobile nearly to the end. The one saving grace about the progression of his disease is that he seemed to lose the ability to comprehend death and other abstract concepts early. We wasted so much precious time with the misdiagnosis. Nothing will ever make up for that, but I’m glad we tried. Happy Father's Day!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can you provide insight on the cost of housing in the San Francisco Bay area compared to other expensive cities like NYC or LA? What has been your experience with buying or renting in the Bay area?
Answer: The San Francisco Bay Area has some of the country’s most expensive properties. Just as expensive as NYC. Unlike NYC, some of the most expensive places tend to be in suburbs where many of the biggest companies also are. That means a couple of things. The majority of housing is single family homes and there is no place cheaper to commute from. Everywhere is expensive. If you work in Manhattan, you can live is several places within an hour commute that are substantially cheaper. In the Bay Area, you have to drive 2 plus hours one way to find something affordable. Even the ghettos are crazy expensive. There’s almost nothing you can afford to buy on the median income for the area. You have to be in the 1% of earners to buy a house there. The weird thing is rent tends to be substantially cheaper as it is priced closer to what median incomes can afford. The place I lived in rented for 3 times cheaper then what the mortgage would be! Most other places it’s the other way around where a typical conforming loan is slightly more expensive then rent. The place I moved from was within an hour commute from both Baltimore and Washington DC as my place in the Bay Area was from San Francisco. It was a nice house. 3 times larger then what I had in the Bay Area. It sold for less then just what a 20% down payment would be for the place in the Bay Area. The same is true in LA too. It has massive sprawl and a lack of big tall buildings where people want to live. Just to a lesser degree then the Bay Area. Costs are significantly lower, but still very expensive. California is special because it has NIMBYISM enshrined in its laws to an extraordinary degree. Local towns highly restrict zoning. I lived in a single story single family home that was right next to a train station as well as many businesses. The entire area was zoned that way. In an area that would be comparable to a place like Hoboken New Jersey where places are also expensive since it’s close to the train to New York, but they are mostly massive buildings and you can afford a tiny place on the median income. If that weren’t enough, California also doesn’t adjust property taxes unless you sell the home. That means people stay where they are. The place I rented would be about $30k a year in property taxes at its current valuation. The owner was paying just a few thousand a year though as he inherited it from his parents. He owned multiple homes. He didn’t need this one, but there is no income restriction on the property tax limits so the state effectively subsidized a rental home for a one percenter and effectively put a huge penalty for selling. Any home improvements to say build a duplex or something else that could bring in more tenants or rent would also reset the tax base so the Bay Area just remains mired in housing that is very poorly suited for the area’s density. It’s nice though. The existing residents who already own like living in a suburb that’s right next to their work. Just don’t be middle class or poorer and try to move there!

Question: Why can't Donald Trump pay off the $464 million civil fraud case judgement since he's a billionaire?
Answer: If you read the judgement, the amount Trump has to pay is just the amount he and his company profited off the I’ll gotten loans he was given plus fees and interest. All his properties in question have risen since he bought them, some drastically so. That’s why the judgement seems so high, but really just wiped out his gains. He will effectively only be a little worse off then when he bought the properties. In any case, he easily has the assets to cover the judgement. The problem is all that money appears tied up in real estate and other not easily liquidable. Large properties in expensive markets like his have very limited number of buyers that can afford that transaction. That makes for a hard sale for just one property even if it’s on Trump’s own terms. It’s not. He is under a time crunch and every buyer will know it and he’s got several properties he will likely need to liquidate or find some other very substantial source of cash. Trump’s position in DWAC. The company set to merge with Truth Social and which Trump has a majority stake in has a market cap of $1.31 billion. If he can figure out how to cash out without tanking the stock price, he can easily cover his judgement. Unfortunately he will be under a 6 month lock out period after the merge, but as the majority owner he can simply change that rule. In any case, Trump actually has several sub optimal ways in which he can raise the cash.

Question: Democrats that are pushing electric cars can't explain how the electric grid will handle it. What is going to happen when we have a million plus new EVs on the grid?
Answer: 36% of households had Air conditioners in the 70s. It’s nearly 90% today. A central air conditioner uses about 3 kw per hour. That is equivalent to about 6 miles of charge per hour. In other words we have done this before. In fact, we have been dramatically increasing electricity usage since the 60s. We actually slowed in the 2000s as we started paying attention to efficiency, but the fact remains, we know how to increase electricity capacity. All it takes is money. What is going to happen when we add a million more EVs to the grid? We will simply build more capacity.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If Donald Trump did inflate the values of his properties when applying for loans (as Letitia James contends), who was hurt? I would genuinely like to know what specific person or business was harmed by this.
Answer: Lookup Lehman Brothers. They were one of the primary agents of the subprime mortgage default crisis of 2008. It took out the entire US economy. Almost every American was hurt. Vast sums of wealth were lost and a majority of Americans who had investments at that time are still at least a little less wealthy now because of it. Some people lost their entire savings. They lost homes, jobs, and income they will never be able to recover. They did it by inflating the value of garbage assets and certifying to investors they were actually great when they knew otherwise. The thing about the Lehman Brother’s crime and other financial crimes like it is that it only hurts the general population if the market turns in a certain direction and it is at a certain stage due to the equally bad actions of others. That’s exactly what happened and without laws that curtail such activity before it takes place and sending a strong message to those who violate it, the US economy can’t survive. The premise of your question is wrong. First of all, the judge has already ruled, based on overwhelmingly clear evidence, that Trump inflated the value of his assets. The trial is just focusing on the details to determine his exact culpability. It’s not a question of if. He did, we are just determining how greedy he was and how much he should be punished. The crime Trump committed is more akin to negligence building a bridge where a critical defect is caught before it can collapse. There isn’t a specific person that was harmed, but Trump created the circumstances for significant harm to a great number of people through dishonest acts. Donald Trump put the entire US economy at risk. Still the attorney general isn’t trying to put him in jail, just make him a lot poorer. Fitting for someone who ignored the risk of doing the same to all of us just to enrich himself.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do you think will happen to Cruise and General Motors following the revocation of their permits to test and operate fully driverless vehicles on California roads?
Answer: They will temporarily add drivers back to their cars, fix the issues that got their permits revoked, reapply and at some point next year be back to status quo. Driving is one of the most time consuming, dangerous, and inefficient things we do. Practically everyone from CEOs to minimum wage workers lose precious time and money driving. Some of us lose our lives to it. Large percentages of our most expensive real estate is taken up for parking. Automated vehicles have the promise to revolutionize all that. There is absolutely nothing that will stop that from happening. It’s too important and too valuable. I’ve ridden in driverless Waymo vehicles. They are absolutely amazing and show it’s possible. Arguably we don’t even have an automation issue anymore, we have an infrastructure issue that allows people to be on roads and do unpredictable things that confuse even very robust driverless systems. Put some restrictions on humans being on roads and regulations around construction and emergency events and current technology is good enough to work way better then humans already.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Who is worse, and why, Israel or Hamas?
Answer: Israel is a democratic country. They have multiple political parties that range from far left to far right and switch back and forth between right leaning or left leaning. About half the population wants to expel all Israeli Arabs who make up 18% of the population. The rest want to find a path to peaceful coexistence. Those are not static numbers. They change over time coinciding with events or a lack of them. Palestine is run by the Palestinian Authority. An authoritarian regime that has not held elections in over 15 years. Hamas is one of two major political parties of the PLA and rules the Gaza Strip with an iron fist. They are often labeled a terroristic organization and have brutal crackdowns against any dissenters. Some sources put support for Hamas at 40% of the population, but given public dissent of Hamas within Gaza comes with severe punishment, it’s really hard to know just how authentic Palestenian support for Hamas is. In any case, your question is really like comparing apples to oranges, but it’s not hard to answer. Hamas is way worse for society then Israel. That being said, there are certainly factions in Israel that, if given a chance, would be just as callous with human suffering as Hamas and I don’t have a hard time imagining scenarios where Israel could be led by a group similar to Hamas. Netanyahu, in fact, has been eroding the democratic institutions and moving Israel to the right and more authoritarian despite being relatively retrained in the past with attacks on Hamas. At the end of the day, the question is nonsensical. There can be no moral winner to this war and Israel is responsible for killing way more civilians then Hamas and makes some pretty poor decisions that escalate situations in ways that ultimately lead to more collateral damage that may have been avoidable. There is still a huge and unambiguous moral difference to passively killing civilians who shelter terrorists, knowingly or unknowingly, versus directly targeting them as a strategy to instill fear in the population. It’s a race to the bottom though. Hamas is just going to hell first.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What would happen if type 2 or type 3 civilization declared war on humanity?
Answer: The fact they declared war on us bodes very well. That means they want a dialog and don’t want to just kill us all. It should be really trivial to make a biological weapon that would kill just humans in short order and leave the rest of earth largely intact. It would also absolutely be trivial to make earth inhospitable to all life instantly if they didn’t care about the collateral damage. That says to me they probably want something from us. To take the time to declare war means traveling incredible distances and learning our language and how to communicate with us. That gives us negotiating power to set some terms of our slavery. They would also presumably want us to be as productive as possible and likely endow us with amazing technology to do it. War, climate change, the problems created by man would have to stop. They still might want us to compete with each other to find the best way to fulfill whatever they are looking for. They also might only need only certain people and could kill 99% of the population. They could also likely give us labotomies or change our brains to not have so much independent thought. In any case, one way or another we would be slaves to this civilization for as long as the wanted us to be.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can an average person legally not pay any income tax without cheating or breaking any law whatsoever?
Answer: 40% of US households pay no individual income tax. Most of those do not pay because they simply do not meet the income thresholds combined with typical deductions to qualify or are simply independently wealthy. That’s not very interesting though. The real question is how does someone working a 9 to 5 job who makes enough to have to pay a lot in income taxes take advantage of loopholes in the system to minimize their tax burden to next to nothing? I live in the United States. I work a high paying job 40+ hours a week that gets me in the upper brackets of income tax thresholds. Despite that, for the past few years I paid around 5% in income taxes when my statutory rate between federal and state taxes was in the mid 40s! I did it by moving to Puerto Rico and taking advantage of Act 60. Almost anyone living in the states can qualify for the program, but for you to take advantage of the tax savings you will have to work under a certain set of circumstances. First of all, you have to move to Puerto Rico full time and live here at least 6 months out of the year. The second big thing is you have to have your own company and you have to work remotely for customers in the states. If you are a salaried employee now, you would have to start your own consulting business and contract your services out. You can also start a business or move an existing one here. As long as your customers are in the states and you perform the work in PR, you can get the tax savings. There are some details to how it works that will vary from person to person, but you can assume you will probably have an effective rate from 4–8%. The more you make, the lower your effective rate will likely be. There are a bunch of fixed expenses and without getting into too many details, you need at least $100k in income to just make it break even and likely you would want $150k+ in ordinary income to really make it worth while. If that’s you, I can say, it’s definitely real, it’s perfectly legal, and you don’t need to be independently wealthy or game the system to take advantage. It’s obviously not for everyone, but for high income white collar workers, who can work remotely it’s huge. I came to Puerto Rico from the Bay Area in California. It’s a very big cultural and environmental switch, but aside from the tax savings, my cost of living is relatively low. I own a veritable mansion overlooking the Atlantic Ocean in an upscale gated community all for less then the cost of 700 sq/ft apartment in San Francisco. There are some downsides to moving to a small island whose economy has been basically terrible for its entire existence, but that’s why the tax savings are trying to lure some of the better talent in the US to come live here. Overall though, it’s one of the best places I have ever lived!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I was taught intro in C++ in Computer Science last semester and now I want to dive deeper into it but people keep telling me it’s old and companies don’t use them anymore. Should I quit?
Answer: C++ is old and it’s a niche language that is only used by certain companies for specific projects. If you want to build embedded systems, compilers, or operating systems, it may make sense for you to become a C++ expert, but even those things have higher level alternatives now. I gave C++ up about 15 years ago and now more or less program exclusively in JavaScript. The funny thing is, despite that it’s a scripting language that is way higher level then C++, it’s lack of inherent strong typing actually makes it able to do a lot of things in ways that few other modern languages can, but you could do in C++ with pointers. I have a lot of really powerful knowledge that most of my web development peers don’t have the grasp of and it’s because of C++. In any case, I think it’s good you learned about C++ even though you may not use it directly in your future career, it is closer to the metal in a computer and using it gets you a more fundamental understanding of how computers work. Other language tend to abstract a lot of the memory management and other details that makes it easy to use, but hides details about how things actually work that is critical for performance tuning. Diving deeper into it would also be great for your education, but don’t expect to use it at your job directly. You will most likely have to learn higher level and more modern languages. You should have decades to do that and I have been paid to pick up several languages throughout my career. Once you know one language it’s pretty easy to learn a new one. College is where you should concentrate on learning theory and how computers work on a fundamental level. You will likely never get another opportunity to focus on theory then you have now. C++ is one of the best languages for learning computer science. Go for it, but realize when to move on and go with the flow. The best thing it will do is make you realize how much easier other languages make common coding tasks.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does artificial intelligence begin to show signs of human-like creativity?
Answer: No. AI excels so much at creativity, it has far surpassed human levels of it. Ask Dale-E to draw any abstract idea and it will relatively quickly generate tons of variations, many with only very tangential relationships to the original query. It can keep going iterating on a concept ad Infinitum. It operates on a scale no human is capable of being creative at. It still has major flaws and biases, most of which are simply reflections of society’s inherent biases made public on the internet, but for all intents and purposes, it is literally a creativity machine.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Received higher salary job offer. Current employer trying hard to make me stay. They speak negatively about other company and sent note to them claiming offer is unfair to the industry. What do I do?
Answer: The fact your employer knows of your other offer means you told them about it. That tells me there probably isn’t something fundamentally wrong with your current company that would compel you to quit as soon as your career needs are met elsewhere. I’m assuming you are just seeing greener grass on the other side. If your current employer made it worthwhile to stay. Stay with the devil you know especially if your primary gripe was just compensation. If it wasn’t, offer solutions for your other issues and let them know if they work with you on them, there is so much about the company you love. If it doesn’t work out, you can always shop around again. As to a company speaking negatively of a competitor, well that’s just natural at a lot of places. You shouldn’t think too much about it. It’s no worse and likely no more true then your company thinking you are a bad employee because you explored your options. That’s just how capitalism works. It’s not unfair. Don’t hate the player, hate the game.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I am 18 and was wondering if a career in computer science is still worth it because everybody is going to college to be one? Will all the jobs be gone by the time I graduate university?
Answer: A lot of people may go to college for computer science, but about a quarter of those never finish their degrees. Many more start in the field, but find themselves quickly overwhelmed or disinterested. Of those that remain, a lot aren’t great at it. The programming part of computer programming is actually quite easy. That’s what they teach the most at university. Writing a small application from scratch is not hard. Scaling it is way more difficult. That being said, I have spent decades doing software development and I would say the vast majority of my time is not really spent on programming, it’s spent on problem solving. That means using critical thinking skills more so then just knowing how to make a computer do a certain thing, but it will often fit a more generic pattern and identifying those is critical to solving problems quickly. I also use all the tools I can and try to stay as up to date as possible on the newest trends and techniques, including, most recently, using AI. Despite all that, computer programming is still a very specialized skill, it’s also one of the most consistently highest paying jobs around. That says to me, demand is far from being met and my personal experience tells that the more programmers a company can manage effectively, the more they will hire. In other words, demand has remained high for my entire career as a programmer and I don’t remotely see that changing any time soon. The difficulty of scaling applications means even as AI gets much stronger and better at solving problems, computer programming will be one of the last white collar careers to go. It does mean that your skill level will have to get higher as lower level programmers will be replaced with more productive higher level ones who will leverage tools more effectively to get the simple tasks junior level programmers do done quicker then they can be explained to them. Not only is a career in computer science still worth it, but you should double down even more on the academics as the demand for highly qualified programmers will likely get even stronger in the future. If you stay ahead of the curve, the jobs will definitely be there.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it possible to get through four years of computer science without taking any breaks or vacations from the subject?
Answer: Of course. This probably only applies to a minority of students, but It’s actually much easier then what many people will do once they graduate and get a job. Add in kids, a spouse, aging parents, and a house and lots of other stuff to maintain and well college, even without breaks will still feel like you had tons of time to get through your school work. That doesn’t mean school is not stressful, but for a typical college student from a well to do family, the workload isn’t that bad. They breaks don’t really help with that either. It’s just procrastinating. That being said a lot of people aren’t that fortunate and are working while attending schools. That’s a person who can really appreciate what a break is. Anyway, I enjoyed my computer science courses more then even the easy A ones, like intro to floral design. Enjoy learning about what you are passionate about and you won’t need a vacation.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it possible to run a house off solar panels or wind turbines alone, without having to buy electricity from your utility company? If so, how would you go about doing this technically speaking?
Answer: Of course. I live in Puerto Rico. My understanding is our electrical grid was designed by a few bros after a taking tour of the Bacardi plant. Anyway, I digress. Our power grid is by far the worst in the US. I experience several blackouts a month. My home has 11 kW of solar panels and 23.5 kWh of battery capacity to deal with it. My home averages about 50 kWh of usage per day and my home solar is designed to cover exactly that. In a good year I will produce about 120% of my usage. Bad years have been about 70%. During hurricanes and prolonged outages of the grid I cut back to just the essentials and can easily run indefinitely off grid as long as the sun is out at least every other day. That can get tough sometimes, but the essentials, like my fridge always stay on. I still have access to grid power for when my solar doesn’t deliver enough and I use net metering to export extra energy I generate during the day to the grid and take it out at night to preserve my batteries. If I wanted to go fully off grid, I would likely need to double my battery capacity and add maybe 25% - 50% more panels to live as comfortably as I do now, but the system would be basically the same. It would be a little simpler as you wouldn’t need an auto transfer switch to deal with being on grid or off as the power goes out, but there’s really nothing special about off grid solar. Any solar company could install such a system simply as long as you have the roof space.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Do people use solar panels on their houses? If so, why? If not, why not, especially in California where there's so much sun almost all year long?
Answer: California is actually not a great place to install home solar as the cost of electricity is relatively low compared to the costs associated with installing your own solar and the break even point can be well past the average time a person will own a home for. pG&E also offers the option of sourcing your electricity from green providers so there may not be any significant advantage to installing it. A significant part of the costs for residential solar is for installation and other build of system materials that get way cheaper the more you scale. Utility solar can easily be built for less then half the cost per watt then residential. I live in Puerto Rico now. The power company is not well run and has declared bankruptcy. Power is .33 cents a kWh. The grid here is also extremely dirty and finicky and we have blackouts multiple times a month virtually every month. I installed solar and powerwalls. Over the life of the equipment, my costs break down to about 5 cents a kWh for generation and another 5 cents for storage. Any way you slice it, the economic case for installing solar here is a no brainer. The fact that it also is way more reliable, especially after storms is just icing on the cake. so to answer your question, people install home solar because it will be cheaper, more reliable, and / or cleaner. That will vary greatly by location though and it tends to have way more to do with how your utility is run then with how much sun your particular location gets.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why did the Titanic submarine not have a steel rope connected with the boat on the surface?
Answer: Miles of rope are heavy. They get tangled. A steel rope would provide almost no utility for the sub and greatly hinder its movements underwater and be another thing that could get caught or fail. In this case it wouldn’t of helped either. The sub was lost due to catastrophic failure. Even if it wasn’t, there are very few scenarios where a rope would help over the existing mechanisms. The sub has redundant ballast mechanisms, any of which would have gotten the sub to the surface even with multiple failures. The only way the sub gets stuck at the bottom is if it gets caught on something, which a steel rope likely wouldn’t be much help with. if the sub makes it to the surface it had multiple beacons on it that could be used to find it that would be extraordinarily unlikely to all fail at once. The exhaustive surface search that was conducted was built on the dreams of unicorns and the smallest sliver of hope. One of the first reports I heard soon after the sub was lost said the fact that multiple communication mechanisms failed at the same time when the sub was entering the deepest part of the dive made any scenario other then catastrophic failure extraordinarily unlikely and that’s exactly what seems to have happened.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How many lines of code do professional programmers write per hour?
Answer: For the application I wrote for a startup I founded I wrote about a million lines of code over 4 or so years. Or around 100 lines an hour. When I worked for a government contractor on an application where safety was the top priority and people would die if there was a serious bug in production, the government target was 7 lines of code a day and quite frankly it was difficult to average much higher then that. Of course I would usually be quite prolific on some days then do almost nothing for several more as things were designed, reviewed and reviewed again. So to answer your question, I would say it’s perfectly acceptable to write anywhere between 1 and 100 lines of code an hour. Context matters, but even then, at the end of the day, it’s not a metric that matters much. On some refactoring projects, I can often delete more code then I add while optimizing the things I actually care about. What you should care about is how well the end product works, how long it took to get there, and how well it scales over time. The best practical metrics I would say make you a good professional programmer would be do you consistently hit the release dates you set for yourself and does it get easier to do more challenging things over time. If both those things are true, don’t overanalyze it, just keep doing what you are doing no matter how many lines it takes!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why doesn't ChatGPT and other AI programs have Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics in its programming?
Answer: While the Three Laws of Robotics are a popular concept in science fiction, they are not currently feasible to implement in AI systems. The laws are based on the assumption that robots are sentient and possess consciousness, which current AI technology has not yet achieved. Furthermore, the laws themselves have been subject to critique and debate in the field of robotics and AI, as they may not be practical or appropriate for all situations. The laws were intended to protect humans from potential harm caused by robots, but in practice, they could restrict the ability of robots to carry out certain tasks that may benefit humans. Therefore, while the Three Laws of Robotics have captured the imagination of science fiction enthusiasts, they are not currently part of the programming of real-world AI systems. Instead, AI systems are designed and programmed to follow a set of rules and guidelines set by their creators and developers to ensure they operate safely and ethically.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Which salary is more between pilots and software engineer?
Answer: Pilots are basically glorified bus drivers. They have a lot of responsibility and are paid well for it, but at the end of the day, no one cares about having an excellent pilot, you just want any pilot that gets you from A to B safely and consistently. The upside is limited. The median salary is more then a software engineer, but that can be deceiving. You aren’t just going to start flying a 747 after you pass a flying test, you need lots of training and certifications. That takes time and money. On the other hand, if you can code, companies will pay you handsomely regardless of your qualifications. Even more to the point, there is a great disparity between an average coder and a great software engineer. The right design for an application can make it 10x easier to scale and maintain your code base. Companies can and will pay an order of magnitude more for a software engineer they can trust to securely architect an application as it will save them lots in the long run. Software engineers also out number commercial pilots 40:1 in the US and I would be willing to bet the top 140,000 software engineers largely all make significantly more then all 140,000 commercial pilots with maybe a few exceptions.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is chatGPT going to be really scary to software engineer?
Answer: Assuming that ChatGPT or its AI derivatives are transformative to software development, within the next few years, they will enable remotely competent software developers to be several times more productive, leading to a significant reduction in software development costs. Although this will likely reduce team sizes, it will have an even greater impact on making previously unviable projects feasible due to cost constraints. This is especially true for prototype projects that need to prove a concept and do not require specific high-quality output, which is still a challenge for AI. The ability to prove a concept at a fraction of the cost will create more opportunities for software developers than it will take away. In fact, for every halving of costs, there will likely be a fourfold increase in the number of projects. AI is just another tool in software development, similar to high-level programming languages and other development tools that have dramatically improved developer productivity over the past few decades. AI may have a more abrupt impact on developer productivity, but the lesson remains the same: lower development costs and easier development will enable more projects and create more work for software engineers. The second assumption is that individuals without technical ability will not be able to create high-quality software beyond a certain size using AI tools. It still requires significant skill to architect, debug, and fine-tune the output of AI tools. Based on experience using AI tools for development, this is evident and is likely to remain true until general AI is capable of replacing any human job. As a software engineer, this writer sees AI as only an opportunity, at least for the immediate future. Although there may come a time when the nature of work and the role of humans play doing it may have to be carefully reconsidered, this day is not yet here, and it is impossible to predict when it will arrive from what we currently see with AI, whether it's in years, decades, or centuries.

Question: What is the difference between a UI developer, web developer, and front end developer?
Answer: At one time you may have been able to differentiate these based on the languages and skills one would have to know to say create a desktop application versus a website. These days very few things are not created using web technologies no matter what they do. Question: As a senior software engineer with 12 years of experience, does it make sense to accept an L4 offer from Google? The salary is slightly better than the other senior engineer offers that I have at the moment.

Question: How do you become a full-time Web designer if you have no prior experience in this field?

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Unfortunately, Elon Musk cancelled all remote work because work from home does not work. Does that mean as a propeller of artificial intelligence, he is unrealistic?
Answer: I am a software architect. I have worked at startups both inside and outside of Silicon Valley . I have been one of the highest level of employees at a Fortune 500 tech company that still had a direct part in making the sausage. I have spent over a decade being in an office and almost as much time working remotely. I have founded a startup that grew from nothing to millions in revenue in a couple of years. I have been the lead software developer on projects that have grown from nothing to 100 million dollar businesses. More importantly, I have failed spectacularly in a multitude of ways and experienced first hand what doesn’t work. I have also rescued multiple projects that were driven into the ground that would have been cancelled otherwise and turned them into revenue producing beasts. I am now a consultant and my work comes mostly from that reputation. I work remotely and the project I have been on most recently for a number of years now may be the most productive for revenue per engineering hour spent. Suffice it to say, I can tell you working remotely, not only works, it works better for certain roles on certain projects. Like everything else, the details matter and there are some projects better suited to remote work then others. Musk’s remote work policy is a bit naive as a general rule of thumb and sounds basically like a plan for grossly control chaos. It is a recipe for success at startups where most of your employees have to wear multiple hats and do whatever needs to get done to make something work and more importantly, it matters much less if you piss off your existing customer base by releasing a feature that will revolutionize it. Working remotely is the best for detailed oriented work where the business model is well known and precise engineering is required. It’s less valuable when your business plan hinges on blindly throwing darts at a board and finding the one that sticks. The latter usually means you are doing some crazy implementation and ignoring some general rules to get something novel out quickly. Being in person becomes more helpful to maintain speed and let your teammates know not just the technical direction you are going, but to better appreciate how your mind works so they can quickly compliment it at that point in time even though no one truly understands the full implications yet. That type of work less successful at large enterprises where revenue growth tends to be driven more by wowing existing customers by mostly keeping the wheels on and spinning at 100mph. Those customers love new features that compliment their existing workflows, but absolutely hate it when features change that they have built their business around. Musk saw that hate firsthand when he came into Twitter and shook things up. That being said, it might not actually be a bad move. It’s definitely risky and kudos to Musk for putting his own money and resources on the line to fix a really tricky problem. Twitter seemingly more or less saturated it’s market and was stuck at where it was and hemorrhaging cash. Not to mention Twitter was becoming a target and more and more hated by the general public on both sides of the political aisle just for doing its job. An explosive shake up and a return to a startup mentality may be the only thing that can get the company back to growth so its hard to really call Musk out at Twitter for his tactics. They have been immediately negative, no doubt, but I can see long term success if he plays his cards right. Tesla, on the other hand, is now a finely tuned enterprise that has vey successful products and a robust roadmap that should keep them growing hugely well into the future. They seem to be struggling with execution just as completion from the big auto companies is heating up in their segment. They need to focus on simply delivering value to their existing customers. They need incremental change now. Tesla’s engineering employees would do well to relax, work smarter, not harder and focus on the detailed oriented work of simply making existing processes work better. They should be focused on the hard facts. They should largely know the path they just have to execute it well without a lot of noise. That’s they core value for remote work. It is the home of the mundane where you can be comfortable working long hours on relatively boring stuff that has to get done. A remote worker doesn’t have a physical presence in front of their boss and coworkers to prove they are working, they just have their output. It has to work and be done well otherwise your excuses sound only like excuses. In any case, this is the real world, there is both a place for remote work and in office work. Musk is both a brilliant CEO and flawed human. He’s taking huge risks that may or may not pay off and he makes mistakes. I actually think he would be best served by empowering a new CEO at Tesla to take the reigns and do the boring things to grow the company that Musk is very Ill suited for. He should drop his public highly partisan political statements, but otherwise shake the bird till it either dies or flies at Twitter. As to your actual question, let me just state the obvious… the reality of artificial intelligence is that no one knows what it takes to get to a general all around human-like level of intelligence. We have spent enough time growing the technology to know that just knowing what good enough looks like in an AI is in itself a very hard problem. We will know it when we see it and live with it and it’s flaws for a while. That type of thing is totally unpredictable and yes Musk or anyone else saying they know a timeline for AI performing at acceptable levels for currently impossible task for computers is unknowable. It also has nothing to do with Musk’s stance on remote work.

Question: What if Trump wins in 2024 and at the end of his term gas is at 99 cents per gallon? What would your reaction be?
