Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What if I do UX/UI internship and get a job there now and DROP-OUT of my bachelors in finance which I don't like?
Answer: I have a master’s degree in usability engineering (UX). I have been a UI architect at multiple Fortune 500 companies and have done formal UX testing as well as UI design and development. I have interviewed an innumerable number of candidates for different UI related fields. First off, UI and UX are completely different things. They take a completely different skill set. Formerly UX is an analysis career. In a nutshell you will create a hypothesis about what a good user experience could be or take an existing UI and test it, analyze the data, and report on what makes a good user experience so a more usable UI can be designed and iterated upon. You do not need to be able to code or to be artistic to be a good UX engineer, although those things may help and often UX engineers do UI design, especially wire frame design, or at least work very closely with a design team. You do need to understand statistics and testing processes to do formal UX and all the actual jobs in it are going to be at large enterprises with multimillion dollar projects that can afford not only to make a working application, but spend significant amounts of money on incremental improvements to usability that may only be impactful when spread across millions of users. If you just have an eye for design and focus on making things usable in that design, that’s great, but it’s not UX. UX is just about validating or improving what you have built with some formal analysis. You will struggle to get an actual UX job without a degree and usually a master’s degree. Arguably an undergrad degree in psychology or finance would prepare you better then a design or code centric one as true UX is more about analysis then making pretty things. That being said recruiters and the entire industry often group UX and UI together, but in the majority of those cases, it really is just UI. I realize I am being pendantic here, but education requirements for UX and very different then those for UI. Where UX is science, UI is art. There are a couple order of magnitudes more designers then usability engineers. UI design is a creative pursuit where style and making things look cool trumps almost everything else including usability. If you can manage to design things that users both love to look at and love to use, you will be a top designer and it’s much more possible to obtain that with little formal training as good art in the UI world tends to be very trendy. If you just want to design UIs especially at small to medium size companies, dropping out of finance and pursuing the right internship may be for you. Getting a job in UI design is more about your portfolio then anything else and building a portfolio with a real world company can be a path to a fruitful career. You will struggle to get another job in UX even with some relevant experience if you can’t pass a highly technical interview and likely won’t even get in the door with a resume that doesn’t include some formal training. If you actually do want to go into UX, a finance degree wouldn’t be a bad place to start. The fact you don’t like finance may mean UX is not for you, but school is hard and often not emblematic of your experience at a job. It’s also 10 times harder to go back to school then to leave it. If you have the grades to graduate, my general recommendation would be to get a degree. It will get you in the door at way more places and create open opportunities you can’t otherwise access. Without a degree you will have to rely solely on your network to get good jobs, that’s great if you have it, but having a fallback position opens way more opportunities. Many of those opportunities will be higher paying too. UI design is also easy to do on the side. Projects can be exceptionally small and easy to find, particularly if you are more interested in experience then pay right now. Maybe switch majors, but if you are thinking about UI, start building your portfolio on the side with personal projects or with anyone who will give you a flexible opportunity. If you have that portfolio already, enjoyed creating it, and people are willing to pay you market rate salaries just to get you to do it for them, dropping out may be good move, but I would only recommend that if the opportunity is truly a once in a lifetime one that you might not be able to replicate in a few years with a degree. If you are thinking about leaving for an unpaid or underpaid position. Forget about it. That’s not a good career path. It may have some value, but it’s more then likely far less valuable to your future then having a college degree.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What's stopping a car manufacturer from making an ultra cheap electric car with lead-acid batteries that only runs for like, 60 miles and can be recharged with a solar cell?
Answer: There are a ton of ultra cheap electric vehicles made every year with lead acid batteries. I own two of them. One is a club car golf cart the other is a Neighborhood electric vehicle called a GEM shown below. The GEM is completely street legal in every state, unlike golf carts. By federal law it has to be capable of more then 20 mph and less then 25 mph and can drive on any street 35 mph or under. It came stock with lead acid batteries, but I changed them out to lithium. Lead acid batteries are currently the worst choice of battery you could possibly choose for any vehicle. With the recent precipitous decline of the price of lithium batteries over the last decade or so, lead acid batteries aren’t even a good value anymore. They are simply cheap. Compared to lithium they are 3 times as heavy, which is not a good characteristic for a car. Worse they only last 3 to 5 years and if they are flooded lead acid, the cheapest of the cheap, you will need to perform maintenance on them at least monthly to ensure the water levels are the right level. On my GEM, that means 6 batteries, each with 4 compartments that must be opened checked and possibly filled with distilled water. That’s 24 caps to unscrew and rescrew and that’s the better part of 30 minutes you have spend every month if you want your batteries last at most 5 years. Flooded lead acid batteries for my GEM cost $1200 or so. Going a step up to AGM or gel batteries will get rid of the periodic maintenance, but are 50% more expensive and still have all the other downsides as they are still lead acid batteries. Longevity is hardly the only downside lead acid batteries have. Their power curve is horrendous compared to lithium. As you discharge your battery, the voltage drops significantly. The less voltage, the slower your vehicle will go! With lead acid batteries, with the batteries still half full, you might not be able to make it up hills any more due to the voltage drop. Decide to try to use your battery anyway with it below 50% capacity and you may damage it such that it will never be able to hold the same charge again. Worse still, the more amps you try to draw at once, the more the voltage will drop! Mash the accelerator and ask for more power to get up a hill and the more you press the accelerator, the less efficient the battery performs! These characteristics all become worse as the battery ages too and the more you push the batteries, the more you will degrade them. They are basically batteries that seem designed to fail. You might not notice much when the batteries are brand new, but within a couple of months, you’ll be thinking electric vehicles just suck, when really, its just your battery is not up to par with the high performance even a cheap electric motor can deliver. Lithium has almost none of those issues. They still cost quite a bit more out right, but they are maintenance free. The 2x to 3x premium you will pay for them more than makes up for itself as they last 3 to 5 times as long. Major car manufacturers like Tesla are now getting pretty close to making them cost the same as lead acid too. They crush hills and the voltage drop isn’t much so you can draw them down all the way to 5% without worrying. It’s not even a choice. Imagine if every 3 years your car would stop making it up a hill to your house on your way home and to fix it you had to replace a literal ton of batteries. As to solar, even my relatively light weight club car would only get 1 to 2 miles of range a day if I covered the entire roof with solar and it had ideal conditions. It’s way more practical to install solar on a fixed roof that won’t be subject to the shade of buildings and trees at street level. You simply don’t have the surface area on a car to make solar practical. Certainly not for a super heavy car weighed down by massive batteries. It’s also likely cheaper to buy a slightly bigger battery with several more miles of range as well as solar panels for your garage then custom, high efficiency panels for your car. Suffice it to say, car manufacturers don’t use lead acid batteries because they aren’t practical for vehicles that need to go highway speeds. GM tried and failed to use lead acid with the EV1. Tesla succeeded soon thereafter not so much because they made a better car, they did, but really the primary reason they were successful where others have failed was because lithium made it practical to make a no compromise, fun to drive car.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is everyone ignoring the fact that there is no efficient way to recycle batteries used in electric cars?
Answer: We are fucked! As a species we have built our society and expanded for a world ideally warmed and cooled to sustain us. For virtually all of human existence we have lived in easy times. On a geologic timescale, the earth is really not hospitable for humans and tends to kill off almost all life periodically. By some estimates we were looking at at least another 100,000 years of a great human friendly climate. Not anymore. We have just started to see the effects of the industrial revolution and they are massive. Yet we still have questions like why we should ignore other forms of pollution. Species are dying off. Regions of the world are becoming to hot to live in. Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent. It’s only going to get worse. However, we can control how much worse it gets. Lithium batteries is one of those ways. The cost is high in absolute terms. They take way more power to build then ICE vehicles. They aren’t easily recyclable and the difficulty will mean we will probably fuck it up for decades with disastrous effects on small regions of the planet before we learn to do it more sustainably. Still, they are the only currently practical path to reducing our vehicles carbon footprint. That makes the cost trivial. They will still be be toxic to our environment in many ways. None of that compares to the ramifications of climate change. Not even remotely. It’s like comparing something that kills your goldfish to something that kills your kid. I love that goldfish. I wish I could save that goldfish, but I’ll kill every goldfish in the world if it had just a chance to save my kid from dying. I don’t want to ignore any form of pollution and we don’t have to, but if the choice is between ruining a few things I like and ruining the entire planet for our kids and everyone else, well that’s not even a choice. Call it ignorance if you must, but we have to do this.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Some voter fraud from the 2020 election was Republicans voting for a dead relative. Given that we have reached 700,000 COVID-19 deaths, is the Democratic Party going to be auditing the 2022 election for votes from the dead?
Answer: Of course! US voting is some of the safest and most regulated in the world. A vote from someone who died of Covid will actually be very easy to catch as the deaths tend to happen in hospitals where they will be registered. 700,000 may seem like a lot, but it’s not enough to swing a federal election, unless it’s for a very tight race. It’s also incredibly hard to do on that type of scale, but if the presidential race is within a million votes, I can guarantee you the audits will be numerous and almost certainly turn up such a trivial hack as a dead person voting. Regardless, it’s much cheaper to just buy a vote with money that funds deceptive campaigns or heck, you just gerrymander all the votes you don’t want counted into a single county you were going to lose anyway.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would you rather hire a software engineer who is excellent in data structures and algorithms but mediocre in full stack development or, would you hire someone who is great at full stack development but mediocre in data structures and algorithms? Why?
Answer: You can be great at data structures and algorithms, but only focus on one part of the stack. You absolutely cannot be a great full stack developer with out also being great at data structures and algorithms. I would never hire that full stack developer. I would only hire the data structures specialist if that developer simply had no need to work outside the box that he was working in, if it was obvious that person was unwilling to go outside that box when needed they should also not be hired, but otherwise being an excellent specialist is a feature.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would taxes paid by the rich actually increase if the current "progressive" tax rates with deductions were replaced by a flat 20% tax with no deductions?
Answer: Loopholes the ultra wealthy take advantage of are not so straightforward. For example, 401ks have been used by some ultrasavy startup investors such that a preIPO company will sell some shares for whatever value the company says they are worth, like $5k. A 401k has very strict limits on how much you can put in a year, but if a CEO uses his personal 401k to purchase those shares, there is no law that stops a $5k investment from growing to billions. Thus the tax free account can be used to store ones wealth if you have control of a preIPO company. Others will simply take advantage of the fact the tax basis of investments resets when you die to whoever inherits it. So rather then paying capital gains on a highly appreciated investment, they will simply take a loan out against it, never cashing out to trigger a taxable event and simply watching the money grow and grow. none of these loopholes are remotely accessible to someone with just a million dollars, nor remotely imaginable to the writers of the laws. They aren’t direct and the laws are written pretty clearly to discourage this type of behavior. Have enough money to afford your own full time tax attorney and it doesn’t really matter, all it takes is time and money to find ways around the most well written and best intentioned laws. The solution isn’t a simpler tax code, there will always be a need to make sure certain things aren’t taxed and that means there will always be loopholes. What is needed is constant attention. Updating the laws every time it becomes clear they aren’t working as intended for certain individuals. So to answer your question, yes taxes would probably increase for some ultra wealthy individuals. It would just be short lived for those rich enough to have full time staff dedicated to reducing their taxes, for the majority of everyone poorer, taxes would just go up.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are some good ways to avoid or drastically reduce your capital gains tax?
Answer: Move to Puerto Rico and reduce your Capital Gains tax to zero by applying for Act 60. There are few requirements other then having to live in Puerto Rico. There is a fixed $15k in mandatory donations and fees due yearly so unless you have 7 figures plus in investment or significant short term capital gains, it probably won’t be financially advantageous, but otherwise, there is no cap to how much you can save.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I just moved to a new state and lost my drivers license can I get a new license in my new state?
Answer: Laws vary by state, but you will most likely have to either retake the driving tests required as if you didn’t have a license or request a copy of your driver’s license from your old state. The later option is likely more difficult then it sounds as they will want to ship the copy to the address you have on file with the state and I’m not sure if the post office will forward an official document to a new address.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why doesn't California pass a YIMBY-Style Law with massive zoning deregulation in order to help address the housing crisis; sure, it might get worse in the interim but after a substantial supply increase, wouldn't housing prices stabilize?
Answer: YIMBY laws don’t work at the local level where zoning laws are legislated as homeowners vote. Quite simply your supposition that voting residents want to see home values drop is completely untrue. Those homeowners have seen their most valuable asset rise at they same time they experienced the problems that growth surpassing housing supply have brought. While one can easily argue building more housing is a solution to the problems that plague an area on a macro level, a high rise going up across the street from a single family house is seen as only a problem to that resident. So in other words, even the most left liberal is going to ardently fight legislation that has the potential to cost them a substantial amount of their net worth and change the character of the neighborhood they live in. California should stop all restrictions that limit density and rather just have zoning that simply ensures quality of life no matter how dense the neighborhood gets. It is a direct path to bring home prices in line with median incomes. It is a well understood practical solution. It’s also politically impossible.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why would anyone bother with solar panels when they cost an average of 30k per home and it takes 10 years to pay for themselves at least and probably will have to be replaced by then?
Answer: I live in Puerto Rico. I installed solar in 2020 for $1.90 per watt with a guaranteed life of 25 years. It cost $21k for an 11kw system that averages 50kWh over the year. Round up to to $24k for 25 years of supplemental insurance for acts of nature. Net metering in PR allows me to store any excess power I generate during the day and pull it out for free at night. Do a little math and that works out to an installed cost for 5.2 cents per kWh of guaranteed power for the next 25 years. Electricity from the grid is super expensive in PR for a number of reasons and is most often generated by natural gas. The price fluctuates with the price of natural gas, which was cheap in 2020, but still resulted in an average price around 20 cents per kWh. That means my solar system will pay for itself in around 6 years and pay dividends for the next 19 years after that. Economically, if you own a roof, that makes it a no brainer to install solar here. On top of that though, PREPA, Puerto Rico’s one and only power provider is notoriously bad. Aside from being some of the most expensive power in the United States, it is also one of the worst in terms of reliability. I lose grid power upwards of 20 times a month in the summer. Most outages are short, others can stretch into days, but in any case, as long it’s sunny, I have enough capacity to live in comfort indefinitely and still for less then what I would pay PREPA. The cost of solar is going to vary greatly by where you live and it might not always be such a windfall, but for me it’s both substantially cheaper and much higher quality.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do rich people avoid paying taxes legally?
Answer: The complexity of the US tax code means there are no shortage of ways to not pay taxes. My favorite would be moving to Puerto Rico. Unlike other tax havens you are still living in the US and on an island with a population greater then most states. That means there are costcos and other brand names commonly found in the US unlike the Cayman Islands or the Virgin Islands that have a 10th of the population and is much more like living in a bubble with a monoculture. Puerto Rico is diverse from the California like vibe on the west side in Ricon, to city living in San Juan, the ultra luxury of Dorado Beach, the close knit family friendly community of Palmas Del Mar, or the small island feel of Vieques. You can find beautiful places to live right next to the beach for next to nothing in secluded areas or spend several million to be in exclusive gated community that caters mostly to Gringos. Puerto Rico gives anyone who moves to the Island and successfully applies for Act 60 a 0% tax rate on capitol gains and a 4% tax rate for corporations and 0% tax rate on dividends issued. It’s not just for the rich, but you do need substantial income of at least $100k to break even and more typically closer to $250k to see a significant financial windfall. There are also some rules you have to follow, like you actually have to spend the majority of your time living on the island and you need to pay a fixed $15k a year in various fees as well a reasonable PR salary if you open a business , but those who do typically bring their effective tax rates down to 1% to 10% total and it’s highly regressive, so the more you make the better it gets. Also, be prepared to live in summer year round, next to the beach, learn to speak Spanish, and slow yourself down to be on island time!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does academic study in software engineering (computer science) help us learn the tech (senior web/software developer) better and deeper?
Answer: Academic study gives us patterns to use with the hodgepodge of software frameworks. It’s certainly possible to build a successful app without that, it’s just nearly impossible to scale it. If you want other developers to understand your code. Heck, if you want to be able to miantain your code for more then a year after you wrote it, you need a plan to organize and build it. Thinking about how to build your software for the long term in a way that allows it to be built into anything anyone may think of in the future is extraordinarily difficult. Knowing how to classify the efficiency of your algorithms abstractly lets you build perform at software that will scale as your user base does. There are so many things you won’t discover with just coding experience. The output of Academic study is rarely intuitive or obvious, but ironically, knowing abstract academic concepts allows us to make really hard software problems into something that is intuitive and obvious to solve. Yes, the study of software engineering is absolutely necessary to understand software development at its deepest levels. Not knowing it won’t stop you from building great software, it will just make it a lot harder to do so.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I turned 18 in between the two rounds of stimulus checks how do I get the second one even though I wasn't eligible for the first? My mom doesn't claim me as she does not do taxes.
Answer: First off you will have to have been financially independent in 2020. Meaning no one claims you as a dependent on their taxes. You are likely still a defendant if you are under 24 and live with your mom regardless of whether she files taxes. She likely will get a stimulus payment for you and if she does it means you won’t. If, however, you live independently and you make more then $4,200. You don’t have to do anything to claim your check. It will take a while though. When you file your 2020 taxes, you will be able to prove your financial independence for 2020 and a stimulus check will be automatically mailed to you. This likely won’t happen for a number of months after April 15, but you should get it in 2021.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can someone prevent the selling of a family home in an estate though they don't want to buy it themselves?
Answer: Depends on where you live. Where I live in Puerto Rico, the decedents and sometimes parents of whoever owned the estate are forced heirs, meaning regardless of what is stated in the will, they will receive a portion of at least a third of the estate and if there is no will they will receive a portion of the estate shared equally among all heirs. This can get very tricky with properties that have owners with many descendants. Many of whom may not even be on the island anymore, nor even had contact with the deceased ever, particularly when talking about grandchildren and divorced family members. It’s horrible for the real estate market here. If you ever try to buy any property here, you will likely encounter highly discounted properties that have 20 or 30 partial owners and some that are not contactable. Sometimes leading to prime real estate being more or less abandoned simply because unraveling the legal mess is too much. So to answer your question, not only is it possible to stop the selling of a family home, in some locations it’s the default even if you were explicitly written out of the will and have a bad relationship with those who were bequeathed the lion’s share of the property. You do have to own a portion of the property though. You have zero rights being a descendant without ownership.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it illegal for my mom to go through a phone she found in my room? (I told her it wasn’t mine, because it isn’t, and she didn’t get permission from the parent of my friends I access it) she read my friends text messages and went through her photos.
Answer: It is illegal to view someone else’s data on a secured computer device without permission. That being said you are in a major grey area as your parent generally has a legal right to look through your things as they are responsible for your behavior. Your mom could simply claim she was investigating the phone in your room even if it wasn’t yours. To get any response from the authorities, you are also going to have to demonstrate some significant harm that came from or could have come from your mom’s actions. Most likely if any illegal behavior occurred, it would be dismissed as de minimus, meaning the activity was so trivial as to below the court’s notice. Unless your mom used the information on the phone to commit another crime, I.e. blackmail or identity theft, what your mom did isn’t going to rise above that bar. Your solution is to have your friend lock their phone securely and don’t just leave it lying around. This is primarily your friend’s problem for being so sloppy with their private information. Consider this a small price to pay and a valuable lesson learned. Just be happy it was your mom who did it and who I can only assume has your best interests at heart even if it doesn’t seem that way. If you want others to treat your things with a certain level of respect, you should secure them according to their value, even among friends and family.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Years ago I built financial desktop applications in Visual Basic / VB.net. I want to begin anew with web applications (complex multi-page database applications) but there are so many languages, platforms, etc. Where do I start? Are OOP's dead?
Answer: You start with Angular or React. There are other reasonable choices too, but those are both mature and have significant breadth. Angular may be easier to wrap your head around from an OOP background, but your development style and patterns will be dramatically different. You’ll want to forget about doing things as you would in OOP programming where they don’t overlap with the Angular way.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Got tenants in my condo and the HOA wants to fumigate for 3 days. During Covid. What’s the landlord protocol in LA county/city? Do I cover tenant hotel expenses? 😥
Answer: I would offer them either 3 days off their rent that month or offer to put them up in a hotel. Your tenets would likely have several rights in this case unless you have specific language in your contract that says how this situation can be handled. They can challenge the need to fumigate. They could move out on short notice and claim this is a violation of the contract. They can ask for not only the cost of rent for those three days, but any moving expenses incurred as well as costs to lost time. I would just approach them casually and figure out an acceptable date and compensation. Then give them a notice with those terms and have them sign it. The landlord does have the right to make essential repairs with proper notice. You are on the hook for all expenses directly related to that.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: San Francisco has had rent control for decades, yet the housing market is out of control and only the rich can afford to live there, so why do we think rent control is a good idea?
Answer: Rent control is an inequitable idea. It’s terrible for landlords, it’s terrible for transient renters, but it’s really great for long term renters. Being a long term renter is a really weird trait. In most markets, the benefit of renting is that it gives you a lot of flexibility to move around after a year or two at a premium monthly payment to buying the same place with a mortgage. After decades of rent control, prejudicial zoning policy against growth of any kind, and effectively regressive property taxes, San Francisco has turned the traditional reasons for renting on its head. Despite the enormous absolute costs, it’s actually much cheaper to rent then to buy in San Francisco. Tradition mortgage payments can be two or three times what the rent payments are. That has turned the majority of people in San Francisco into renters. A good number of those people who in any other market would buy the house they plan on staying in for the next several years, instead make their homes out of a rental and put down deep ties to the community. Their social networks, schools, even their family ties are all tied to their rental and it’s rent control price. After several years of increasing market rate rents, rent control may be the only thing that allows them to keep their home and the ties that bind them to it. Very few economists will argue in favor of rent control, especially the broad based, market destroying type implemented in San Francisco. Over time as market rates rise to a level only the most affluent can afford, rent control also tends to switch to a highly progressive policy to one that leans regressive and makes rent more expensive by limiting the supply. That being said, when it’s first implemented it helps the least fortunate maintain their homes and is the easiest way help those people keep their kids in the school they grew up in and maintain their family ties. That is political gold. Further more, once it’s implemented and the majority of your constituents are renters, it becomes politically toxic to repeal it. Rent control is a truly horrible way to solve a real and very difficult problem for a large number of voters. That being said, if your only goal is getting elected, it may just be the easiest way to get elected in market of extreme and consistent rising rents.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why did Mitt Romney participate in a BLM protest in June, while also saying he'd vote in favor of Amy Coney Barrett for the Supreme Court, despite the fact she will likely rule against police reform? She'd also tip the court to be right leaning.
Answer: Amy Coney Barrett has a history of conservative bias against Abortion. She is a path to overturning roe vs wade without the perilous legislation it would require Congress to undertake to get there. Despite widespread condemnation of abortion from virtually everyone for one reason or another, very few people want to get rid of abortion and a vote to get rid of it could piss voters off enough to remember it come election time. It’s Regarded as a necessary evil for the vast majority of the US that few would appreciate being repealed completely. The rhetoric may say otherwise, but the when it comes down to brass tacks, the actual debate is on when abortion is appropriate, not if. That being said, full repeal is still an issue the Republican political elite care deeply about as it’s extremely important to the religious right which is a good portion of Romney’s most fervent supporters. A repeal through the Supreme Court is way more practical and doesn’t come with the baggage that legislation would. It doesn’t really matter where Amy Coney Barrett stands on the other issues, other then that she is qualified. She and the other justices are largely untested on police reforms coming from BLM. It’s likely she will have at least a slight right lean, there is not evidence for bias like there is for her stance on Abortion though. She is a sure thing on Abortion and generally a clean justice with a stellar record and no other personal baggage that makes her an easy vote for anyone comfortable with abortion repeal. It is nothing but a win for Romney as he gets his cake and eat it to by getting an abortion repeal without actually having to go on record as voting to remove it and doesn’t even have to stomach a profoundly disrespectful pick like he tried and failed to do with Trump. A partisan supreme court is bad for democracy, but the benefits outweigh that lofty ideal for Romney.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Governor Newsom of California signed an order banning sales of gas powered cars in California by 2035. What other states are also likely to do so, and why?
Answer: We have built most of our cities on the coasts on. a planet with enough land ice to cause hundreds of feet of sea level rise. If that’s not enough, wildfires, droughts, hurricanes, flooding, and other extreme and very costly weather events are all going to increase in both likelyhood and magnitude the warmer it gets, even for us relatively sheltered Americans. It’s really not a question of if other states will realize that extreme change has to happen, it’s just a question of when. We have less then seven years left before we hit 1.5 degrees Celsius in additional warming. An amount the scientific community has unequivocally predicted will bring extreme hardship upon the entire world’s population. Some will be effected way more then others, no one will be spared and it only gets worse after that. The hotter it gets the more rapidly we will see extreme changes. All ICE vehicles will be banned within the entire United States, it’s just a question of how much pain we can take before everyone realizes that the scientists we pay to help us understand what’s going on actually know what’s going on. The next decade is going to get pretty rough. Expect each state to hop on board as soon as they realize having marginally cheaper cars is a quaint problem to have relative to abandoning even small portions of their most productive cities. Have a wonderful and safe apocalypse!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How would Thanos react if I walked up to him on his farm planet and said “You know you could’ve just used the stones to create twice the resources, right? Then people might actually be grateful...”
Answer: During his earlier years, Thanos lived in the Bay Area California. He was the founder of a startup creating digital stones that proported to have 100x the computing power of the worlds fastest super computer at the time. His company was acquired secretly by palintir, but that’s a different story. Anyway, Thanos had a small, but stupendously expensive house in the middle of Palo Alto. It was a beautiful a single story single family home that he inherited from his grandparents and was locked into a property tax rate from the 70s that he fiercely prized. Palo Alto was rapidly growing then as it is now. There was a nice open lot across the street next to a train station that a high rise would allow way more people to live comfortably next and still have a reasonable commute to work, but that wasn’t Thanos’s problem. He was there first and he knew the shadow the high rise would cast on his backyard would slowly wither away his garden. Now Thanos is truly a bleeding heart liberal and the plight of others just trying to live their lives weighed heavily on him, but a high rise would almost certainly cause his house to stop appreciating and if everywhere in the state decided to build enough housing for all the people who wanted to live near work, his home’s value would decline to a fraction of its value. That was truly an unacceptable risk and seemed almost dystopian, even if it would make many more people’s lives better. It would change the home his grandparents left him. At that point, it dawned on him, population control was the only real solution.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Will Google’s plans to build more than 20,000 houses in Silicon Valley impact housing prices and the quality of life?
Answer: In 2019, the Bay Area grew by 21,009 residents. Google’s houses won’t do anything positive for housing prices or quality of life. It is a quick fix that allows the status quo to continue for another year. It does not impact the fundamental problem with the Bay Area that deliberately zones for way more offices, then it does for residential, not to mention having a property tax regime that incentivizes keeping the status quo which in the Bay Area means single story homes along the transportation corridors where tall high rises would easily get filled to capacity. The government is broken. The only fix for that is to fix the government. It’s nice that Google is doing something, but if it really wanted to fix housing prices, it would of dumped the billions it’s going to spend on housing towards lobbying the state government and getting politicians who will take on the unpalatable job of turning well loved suburban neighborhood into medium density urban areas.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Are you happy about the price reduction in the housing sector in Southern California? Do you think it will go further south?
Answer: It seems like a reduction driven by a reduction in demand caused by the Corona virus. It has not come from a change in the systemic reasons that cause housing prices in CA to rise to unaffordable levels for the middle class… zoning driven by extraordinary local control that does not balance residential building with commercial building and a property tax regime that disincentivizes high density building around transportation corridors and other high demand areas where it makes the most sense. The reduction will go further south while there remain individuals who can move out of the state while keeping their employment opportunities and the prices remain higher then the reasonable alternatives. The only way this becomes a sustained reduction is if the local economy never returns to its previous levels. If I were in the market for CA real estate, now would likely be a great time to buy. Other then that, it is simply another sign we are in a recession and that Southern CA is a non-egalitarian market, neither of which is something to be particularly happy about in general.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What will happen in large cities like San Diego, LA, and SF when the prices get so high to the point that the average person can’t afford housing, will it be like the 2008 recession or are we prepared or will it be completely different?
Answer: What’s it like now? I hate to break it to you, but the median household income in the Bay Area is around $100k The median home price is 10 times that and around $1 million. That’s already three times more then what would be affordable for your average person there. It also appears to be completely sustainable as the job opportunities still continue to increase in the most housing constrained areas. It turns out people will flock to job opportunities no matter how much it costs. Of course California is seeing a tremendous slow down in population growth led by lower income workers leaving the state. The highest income residents are still increasing though and will continue to come forcing prices to further rise and more lower income workers to leave. What you will see continue into the future is more of what you are seeing now… a greater division between the rich and the poor. You are likely to see further patchwork fixes, like rent control, that will help a minority of very lucky individuals keep their homes. It will give the false impression that it’s easy for an average worker to live there comfortably, but short of a politically untenable and massive change to zoning laws and the incentives to build high density residential, the majority of middle class individuals who want to live there will either have to substantially decrease their expectations or move out. The only people you will see in California will be those rich enough to afford it or those desperate enough to constrain their comfort to cram into a place with several other roommates or whatever it takes to live there. The Bay Area will become a nicer place to live for very well off individuals as older apartments hosting several families in each unit are replaced with high end townhomes near very nice, high end retail for high income individuals to spend their disposable income on. I know this will happen because it’s worked this way for decades already. If California was going to break from housing costs it would have done so long ago when median household income was just half of what was needed to reasonably afford a place. We can also look to other cities around to world for a dystopian model of the future in places like Hong Kong where 60 sq / ft apartments are a thing. Except in California, they are likely to be in a 2 story building next to a massive open air park rather then a high rise that might disturb the views of the existing residents.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Do the Democrats plan to take back the White House consist of continuing to deny the existence of anarchists among the protestors, and accusing Republicans of the very things of which they, themselves, are guilty?
Answer: Democrats don’t deny that left leaning anarchists exist, nor that those anarchist may consider themselves liberal. Ideologically left leaning anarchists are obviously anywhere from well aligned to well within the same ball park as the official Democratic Party. The democratic party can’t chose who does or doesn’t align with it though. All that they can do is choose the official party policies and tactics which are definitely not anarchist in any sense of the word. The democrats are the party of government. They believe the government should help those who can’t help themselves and be the guardrails first everyone. Sometimes that means reforming a massive institution like the police. That reform is never burn it to the ground and let everyone go at it for themselves. It typically takes the form of replacing a simplistic institution with a much more expansive and complicated one. That being said, protests are a form of chaos in themselves. They can be done peacefully, but they do offer a platform for anarchists to live in and broaden the dispersal of their own message regardless of intent. The difference between the Republican Party and the democratic one is how they react to ideologically aligned individuals who go off message and take an extreme approach to grabbing attention. I have yet to see a democratic party representative condone any violent act during an otherwise peaceful protest. The leader of the Republican Party, on the other hand, accepts the support of white supremicists, suggests guns and violence should be used to solve disagreements, and in general has encouraged the Republican Party to be a populist one with an us vs them mentality rather then one that looks to make deals that benefit a broad base. Both parties have extremists in their midsts. Only one is officially and actively encouraging them.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is there anywhere in the world where you can own property ouright? I.e. free from property tax or seizure by the government?
Answer: Absolutely. Puerto Rico has many ways to beat taxes. If you are merely wanting to avoid paying property tax, just buy a place in Old San Juan. As long as you maintain it up to historical standards, it will be property tax free. Even better. Start a PR based company and export your services to the mainland and you can apply for Act 20 / Act 60, which will slash both federal and state income taxes to 4%. Even better, if you have a substantial amount of wealth, you can apply for Act 22 and slash your capital gains taxes to a flat $10k per year no matter how much income your investments brought in.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I'm a freelance software developer. Should I build proof-of-concept / demo applications for free? Or charge my client for that time?
Answer: Offering software for free is a great way to build a large and robust base of customers who don’t want to pay you for software. You should generally avoid it. Having a portfolio of your past work is good enough. Not getting paid for a proof of concept you spent a small amount of time building is likely not a big deal. The bigger issue with courting a client with a free deal is they tend to be completely oblivious to the very significant up front costs to custom software development. Even if they accept your proof of concept and want more, those types of customers will make you work twice as hard for half the money. They will ask you for more and more, never pay on time, and always ask for discounts. What you really want to avoid is winning such a customer. If you want to build a proof of concept to ease the customer’s doubts, you can do so, but you want to weed out any customers who are going to drag their feet when it comes to paying you. Get them to sign a contract first that outlines what they are willing pay you per hour and spells out exactly what both of your expectations and terms are. Let them know it is non-binding and you will only bill them for the proof of concept if they accept it and want to continue working together. Establish an expected timeline and let them know the risks and the projected total cost of the project.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I’m a California tenant and 100 % disable veteran. The apartment management company is raising the rent from $1400 to $1700 next month. Rent has already been raised twice in less than a year. Is this legal?
Answer: As of Jan 1, 2020, California now has rent control statewide. Landlords are prohibited from raising rent more than 5% per year plus the local rate of inflation. Yes it is illegal. The most your land lord could raise the rent is under $100.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are good ways to reduce the capital gains tax from a startup's stocks?
Answer: Move to Puerto Rico. Act 60 makes all PR sourced capital gains tax free. You do have to pay roughly $10k a year split between government fees and a charity, but after that it’s all gravy. You are still living in the US and get to enjoy island life. I moved to PR from Silicon Valley in 2019 and it reduced my taxes for my ordinary income quite substantially. I still do work for US clients and I’ve saved more in the one year since then then in the previous 5 years I spent in CA. My effective tax rate went from the mid 40% with CAs income tax to around 6% in PR. I also just bought a 6 bedroom house with an infinity pool, incredible ocean views, and in a gated community with multiple golf courses, and near hundreds of gringos doing similar things all for less then what a bottom of the line 1 bedroom studio would have cost me in Palo Alto, CA.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do we allow people to take 30+ years to pay off mortgages when we sell them a house?
Answer: There is no good reason our policy should allow this many 30 year mortgages. 30 year mortgages increase foreclosure risk. They make housing more expensive. They reduce the savings of ordinary borrowers. The interest rates are generally higher then shorter term loans. Still that’s not a reason to disallow them completely, but it signals a major problem when they have become the standard. 30 year mortgages came about in the 50s when the fed raised interest rates and housing prices suddenly became a lot more unaffordable. Rather then lower those rates or let the market correct itself, the fed simply allowed longer mortgages. This did allow individuals to buy more house then they could otherwise afford and it allowed greater profit margins for mortgage brokers. In terms of short term things that everyone cares about, it’s a win / win situation and politically untenable to get rid of it. When it comes down to it, the government allows 30 year mortgages for the simple reason that the unwashed masses are basically goldfish when it comes to making policy decisions. It sounds great now, but over the long haul is usually a poor decision for your average homeowner. It has about as much chance of going away as the government has of solving obesity. At the end of the day, people have to want to make the right financial decisions and quite simply for many that means having a smaller house.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do those who fall in love with all kinds of programming at once, such as mobiles, web applications, websites, desktop applications, and gaming, choose to choose one of all this to start with?
Answer: All software developers have a specialization these days, but a good software developer largely does not choose what they get to work on, their employer does. A good software developer solves a problem with code no matter where it takes them. Sometimes that means giving guidance or handing the issue off to someone who has more relevant expertise and / or greater availability. Other times it means digging in and learning something new. In any case, over my two decade career I have done everything from writing embedded C++ applications, writing REST APIs and database development, to running user experience tests and general user interface development. Largely, I don’t choose what I work on. My clients choose me based on my prior experience, then ask me to help solve a problem that has all sorts of cross cutting concerns. The best software developers are the ones who aren’t just the best at a particular paradigm, but can find ways to fill in whatever gaps come up to get a project done. In any case, when looking for your first job, cast your net far and wide, choose the best offer and don’t focus on the exact technology too much, you can learn whatever you need if you understand software development on a fundamental level already. People tend to love or hate their jobs based more on the company culture and who they work with more so then the technical details of what they do day to day let that be your primary guidance.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: A semi-truck hit my tree on a residential road, and the truck's owner is trying to file a claim against me. What should I do?
Answer: Whether you have any liability for your tree damaging someone else’s property is going to vary by jurisdiction, but generally speaking you will only be liable if you were found negligent in maintaining the tree to a reasonable degree. To be found negligent, it would have to be proved that you both knew the tree was likely, more then usual, to cause damage to someone’s property and failed to take reasonable action despite that knowledge. The precedent where the owner was found liable for just such a situation happened when a branch fell on a passing car and caused it to have an accident, it was found the owner previously had the tree inspected and was explicitly told it was diseased and should be removed. The owner failed to take any curative action and was found negligent. Other owners, even those with diseased trees, were found not liable when the tree fell and caused damage as they simply claimed they were unaware the tree posed an extraordinary risk and the plaintiff failed to prove otherwise. in any case, once an action is filed against you, you have no choice, you need to get a lawyer and file a legal response either through your homeowner’s insurance or personally.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If a Pacific Rim-esque scenario were to happen in reality, what would be humanity's answer to the Kaijus?
Answer: We know the answer already. It’s part of pacific rim lore and conventional military weapons is the first thing humanity tries before building the Jaegars. The Kaiju first appeared on August 10th, 2013 in San Francisco. The beginning of the incident was believed to be a 7.1 earthquake; however, a massive, three-hundred-foot creature, later known as "Trespasser," eventually emerged from the San Francisco Bay and attacked the Golden Gate Bridge. After destroying the bridge, the creature proceeded towards San Francisco and caused significant devastation; it cut a three-mile-wide path of destruction through the city. The massive creature then went on a 35-mile rampage across the West Coast that lasted for six days. It continued on to Sacramento and Oakland, causing massive destruction in its attack. The United States and British militaries responded to the attack and battled the creature for six long days. Despite the use of troops, tanks, artillery and jets, the combined forces of the two armies failed to kill the massive beast. On August 15th, the military decided on using tactical nuclear missiles in the hopes of bringing down the creature. They finally succeeded with three tactical nuclear missiles. With the end of the destruction, three cities were left devastated and tens of thousands of people had died. The dead were mourned, the event was memorialized and humanity moved on. The incident in San Francisco was later known as "K-DAY" In reality though, traveling to other dimensions is so far beyond our capabilities we would pose almost no risk to another civilization capable of it. Either for sport or political reasons they have not destroyed humanity because that was simply not their goal. We can ponder all day on the simpler ways the Kaiju could have been defeated, but at the end of the day, realize the founders necessarily also have to have far simpler ways of ending humanity in an instant. If they have the ability to create creatures capable of surviving in earths climate through bioengineering, my guess is creating an extremely contagious bioweapon that kills off only humans would be trivial for them.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do compilers still have to be written by humans? Why can't they be created automatically from a machine-readable description of the programming language and the target architecture?
Answer: I spent several hours writing code today. I was not particularly productive. On a good day I can write thousands of lines of code. On a bad one I might not even have a write positive number of lines of code. Most days are bad. Most days aren’t spent mostly implementing a carefully thought of design. It’s spent figuring out why after I did everything according to the plan, that things still just don’t work quite right. A lot of times, not working is not even the right word. As a user interface developer most of my time is spent getting the experience right, where things work practically, but are a little off. Like you add a component to a page, but it gets cut off by a few pixels. It’s a black box though and security restrictions prevent you from hacking around it. The hardest to solve problems tend to be those where the majority of the integration work has been automated. The concept sounds great, you just choose a few options and bam, like magic, you have an app customized to just the way you wanted it. A lot of times it works exactly like that, others, it’s close. Frustratingly close, like just a margin is off by a few pixels or everything works until you give it a picture that’s just slightly larger or some other characteristic that’s just beyond it’s capabilities. For whatever reason, that little subtle detail, is a core part of the required design. If that part can’t work better, you can’t use that component at all. This may sound esoteric, but it’s not. It’s the life of a programmer. Problems that can be solved by just a few clicks here and there are the things that programmers write. Custom software development is only needed to do things outside the box and a lot can be accomplished today that needs absolutely no coding just finding the right application and using it. in any case, to answer your question, whether the required application is a compiler or something with a more human friendly user interface, code has to be written and usually lots of it, because nothing exists to do exactly what is required. If it did you would just buy the application and use it. When that’s not the case, actually writing the code to make the computer do what I want is the easy part. The hard part is figuring out the ghosts in the machine to make it work as it was intended. Programming languages are constantly evolving, they are getting higher level and easier to use. They aren’t creating themselves though based on inarticulate human readable requirements. My primary role as a programmer is not writing the code that makes an application tick. It’s fixing all the problems between the different things I’m tying together to make a cohesive whole. As time progresses I’m able to tie bigger and bigger pieces together, but there will always be problems and the lower level and less abstract the code it, the easier it is to debug them. I’m scared of the future your question implies where computers write their own code, not because it will put me out of a job. Quite the opposite, I will be busier then ever fixing the things that your automated system couldn’t account for. It’s painstaking and frustrating work. It takes a ton of time just to find the one line of code change to make it work. programs don’t write themselves because if they did, even if they worked, they would be terrible and are a nightmare to maintain. The capital costs may be minimal, but you will bankrupt yourself maintaining it.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Initial median home prices have reached an all-time high amid the economic crisis. Why is this the case?
Answer: A significant portion of the population also thinks that the best solution to the Coronavirus is to simply let it happen. They believe that the medical community and non-partisan government organizations are lying about the impact of the virus. It was a leading cause of the death in the US in April. It is preventable and social distancing has, in fact, dramatically curved the spread of the disease. The majority of the population is at low risk of dying from Covid, but those individuals are also carriers and spread the virus most when they are asymptomatic. They spread it to high risk individuals like their parents and immune compromised friends and family and can do so with little impact to their own health. Ignoring the disease may be safe to you while at the same time contributing greatly to the death of others. All of this should be common knowledge by now. Unemployment is at record highs. Consumer spending is down tremendously. Companies with household names have declared bankruptcy. Unicorn startups who could do no wrong up to this point find themselves with an unsustainable business model that won’t become viable again for another couple of years. A significant number of customers are now dead and a magnitude larger number are going to try to avoid that fate by not being retail customers regardless of what the government mandates. A significant portion of the population thinks all the economic ills can all be solved immediately, if the government simply opens up the economy again. Many still have their own jobs and benefit from generous government incentives that are propping up the economy. The stock market is still up above May 2019 levels and generally rising. The housing market, while the number of sales are down, has seen significant price increases. There is only one answer to why. Willful ignorance compounded by being able to watch the devastation from a point of relative safety. It will be short lived. Like always, the market will drastically vary by region, but overall virtually no where is totally safe in a pandemic. You can live in your own reality and ignore the effects of the world around you that you are seeing. Denying the effects of gravity does not allow you to defy it. The higher up your are the easier it is to ignore it, but ultimately that perception is just going to make the eventual fall worse. The generous government subsidies are there to lessen the initial economic impact and give us time to adapt, not to allow us to ignore the situation. They are not going to last forever. Take advantage of them now. We have years of hardship ahead of us. Let reality guide you rather then the perception of it.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Are home sales down a lot during the COVID-19 crisis because sellers refuse to lower the price?
Answer: According to the national association of realtors, home sales are down 8.5% in March from the month earlier. Median sales price is up 8% year over year and inventory is down by .4 months of supply. I wouldn’t read too much into those numbers as a reflection of the future. Our perception of the economy has not caught up with the reality that we are in the greatest depression since well, the great depression. Look at the stock market. The S&P 500 is down about 20% from its all time high right before this Covid stuff hit. That may seem bad, but it’s actually still up from where it was just a year prior May 2019. You read that right. Despite seeing the accelerated bankruptcy and closures of household names like J-crew, Jet.com and JC Penny. Despite seeing the decline of massive unicorns that were poised to dominate the world like Uber and Lyft. Despite seeing a nearly unprecedented unemployment rate of 15% and climbing. Despite having a new leading cause of death that didn’t even exist in 2019. Despite seeing the economies and governments of not just the US and the entire world flail in the face of massive uncertainty and tragedy, Wall Street still perceives the future to look as good now as it did in May of 2019. I don’t know exactly what the future holds, but I am 100% confident it’s not economic growth for at least the next two years. There will certainly be some massive individual winners during that time, but volatility never leads to more predictability and predictability is what drives overall growth on Wall Street. In any case, confidence in the market can be a driver of growth and consumer spending. It can’t replace it though. We are currently living in a reality propped up by extremely generous government subsidies and an inability to process an event of a magnitude that has never happened before in most of our lifetimes. We are 2 months in. Our new reality is going to last years and the ability of the government to sustain Wall Street and our old perceptions is going to run out. Housing may not be predictable in many ways, but the one rule it can not deny is that it follows the economy. Our economy is going to shit. We have no choice, we can control it’s decline, but we can’t stop it. It’s not coming back anytime soon. The bottom of the real estate market has already dropped out. Few have looked down to notice it yet, but I have a feeling we haven’t discovered how to defy gravity yet.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Did the U.S. ever actually build the wall that Trump kept lobbying for?
Answer: The wall Trump wanted to build was just a distraction. He did a phenomenally good job at building it. Trump only cares about immigration in so far as it makes a perfect scapegoat to blame pretty much any problem he wants on it. It lets him control the media for the day and distract from any of the administrative actions he performs dismantling the government watch dogs inhibiting or shining a light on his behind the scenes cronyism and corruption. It excites his base and, bonus, excluding people, particularly refugees from hard circumstances enrages democrats… irrationally so making them forget about the practical realities of the hard choices that need to be made to have a viable immigration policy and having them react to Trump personally. This makes for great sound bites that can be used to falsely illustrate the democratic position as being for open borders when the subtle reality is that everyone wants some form of border security, just not everyone thinks Trump’s border wall is a very good use of funds to achieve legal immigration controls. Even better for Trump’s needs, immigration really has no great solution. There are just compromises that force winners and losers to be chosen. Immigration has immense individual consequences, but it’s societal impact on the country is long term and not easily measurable one way or another. Conservatives don’t expect immigration to be ended, even if many call for just that, but just eased by some nebulous amount which will somehow open up jobs for citizens. This feels especially pertinent to rural communities that have seen their traditional populations dwindle as millennials have fled to urban centers, but the reality is employment was near full capacity when Trump took office. What rural America has been feeling is stark inequality more so than unemployment. Inequality that is exacerbated more by hedge fund manager and real estate developers then by immigrants on the low end of the spectrum. Despite that, immigration is still a real issue that needs government intervention badly for other reasons and it is an issue that has become more acute over the past couple of decades as immigrants from Central America have flooded the country in ever increasing numbers. If or how much the presense of more immigrants is a problem or a benefit is debatable, but the change has been palpable over the past decade as more and more immigrants have moved to rural America as the movement of millennials and horrendous zoning policies run by local governments that don’t need to care about expanding residential density have precipitated urban centers becoming unaffordable. Trump also built a physical wall. It doesn’t really look like what he promised, but conservatives don’t really care about how it looks. That was never the wall Trump really wanted. Trump can spin something superficial like what the wall is built of into a win in his sleep. Liberals will take note and point to it as evidence of his lies, but that’s a losing argument when you point to the metric the wall is suppose to tame… illegal border crossings and show its dramatically down. The real kicker is, Trump managed to put a serious dent in illegal immigration through his one true talent regardless of the wall, his caustic rhetoric that makes going to the US feel like a more dangerous journey for refugees then staying put in a highly volatile 3rd world dictatorship. In practice, the physical wall is just a memorial of already driving immigration down. His real success is he has gotten the democrats to waste countless political capital on a an issue that they don’t actually care much about. Liberals do actually want physical border security and want no one to be in the country illegally. The only real issue with the wall is it’s cost, which quite frankly is an easy thing to stomach politically. The thing is actually building the wall isn’t really worth a whole lot to the Republicans. The concept of the wall is valuable in inciting the conservative base and distracting the liberals. Getting $25 billion or however much it would take to build the wall would be the worst possible outcome for the Republicans as they have lost one of their greatest wedge issues and got a wall that doesn’t actually accomplish anything practical. Worse they would then have to explain why the economy hasn’t gotten better for rural America despite having a big beautiful wall. The only reason the physical wall hasn’t gotten to complete funding it needs is it’s not remotely worth it for Republicans to trade anything for something that has negative value for them. Yes, Trump has built the wall he wanted. It’s not a physical one. The country has never been more divided since at least the Civil War.
