Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is buying property during a crisis (like COVID 19) a good idea?
Answer: It’s a risky opportunity now to either lose or make a ton of money. The market is entering uncharted territory. We have had similar experiences in the past and our most recent recession from 2008 saw houses almost everywhere take a significant dive. That’s not the whole story though and should give us some pause when trying to relate them too directly. Despite the following decade from 2008 being one of unprecedented expansion, many of those homes hit by the recession and sold at a loss never came back to their previous highs. Others, not only came back but are valued substantially higher then they were pre-crash. My point is, even if your timing was perfect by choosing the depth of the last recession as an opportunity to buy, you could be looking at a massive loss if you bought in the wrong place expecting it to just return to its previous high as soon as the recession ended or even a decade after. In other words, it means a recession isn’t a good time to buy so much as it creates new opportunities to buy at a discount, but it’s still up to the buyer to find the right deals. A recession is really a gain multiplier, it does not necessarily make it any easier to find a can’t lose deal, but if you predict the market right, your growth will be even better. In any case, if there’s a lesson, it’s the tried true one that you should never buy real estate planning for appreciation, you should buy with a plan of how you will increase its value through improvements or a business plan that will bring out its true potential. Never plan to have the market make your margins for you. What the last recession taught us was that the places that seemed exceptionally expensive during the last crisis never saw a permanent correction in the way many would have predicted, some came back and got even more unsustainably expensive, while other places that already seemed cheap by comparison got even cheaper. The changing prices of some places weren’t just driven by unsustainable credit, but also because the nature of work was changing and going more urban. I’m not so sure we are going to see a repeat of that lesson this time, but it will be just as hard to predict on a specific level. My belief is there is no returning to what once was and that it’s going to take a really long time for society to realize we have to change permanently. In the last recession, everyone seemed to immediately realize the profound unsustainability of credit default swaps and the problem the recession was built on shortly after recession took hold… once it hit, perception was closely aligned with reality. The problem also was created by a relatively esoteric part of our society that the vast majority of people had some stake in, but didn’t know it because there was several layers between them and their mortgage investor. To fix the specific problem that caused the crisis, we only had to change the behaviors of a relatively small portion of society very few regular individuals cared about and life could return to its previous state. Even if there were still massive issues with the system, we could at least ignore them for the most part and return to our lives as they were. This time is different. Perception is not at all aligned with reality. Despite being a few months in since the alarm bells started sounding about the CoVid-19 virus, we still seem to be well behind the curve in realizing the very grim nature of what we have to do to fix the problem. There is no quick fix to this problem. Politicians, in the US, have responses that vary from any reaction that tanks the economy is overblown, to we have to shutdown completely for the next month. None of them are well aligned with what the science says and all of them are a magnitude overly optimistic. We have no cure or vaccine for the virus and, even with extraordinary efforts, the best case scenario is we are unlikely to have one for the better part of a year. I have yet to hear a single politician show a plan that even tacitly acknowledges that that is the best case scenario and instead have latched on to glimmers of hope from the viruses cyclic behavior to offer a deceptive impression that we will get over this soon. The farthest out predictions coming from government policy makers has us looking at things finally getting back to normal in June, yet the only explanations offered as to how that can actually come about seem to be that it is the point when we have controlled the infection “curve”. What they don’t mention is that the control is actively coming from social distancing and fail to offer what is going to replace it. Lifting social distancing restrictions does not mark the point of returning to normal. It marks the point where new slightly less, but still extremely restrictive policies can be put in place to keep control. These may actually be worse for a large portion of society. After social distancing, with extraordinary effort, comes wide spread testing and specific quarantining of those possibly exposed to the virus. It will likely be a very dynamic process not unlike what we are seeing today where every week the restrictions in place will change according to the perceived threat. Those restrictions will hopefully be less restrictive, but under no circumstances will we be back to normal any time this year or likely next. If nothing else, for the next 2 years, cross border travel will be heavily restricted and concerts, trade shows, church, even eating out at restaurants, going to malls, or just going to work at a populated office are going to be extremely risky activities. Whether the government restricts them or not until enough of the population develops a herd immunity, there is no garuntee that any activity done around other people will be safe on a level we are accustomed to. That means profound and likely permanent changes to how we live our lives. With that context, to answer your original question, to correctly play the real estate market now, you have to first figure out what life will look like over the coming years. I don’t know exactly what that is, but I can tell you, it’s not going to look like it did in 2019 any time soon or likely ever again. By the time we are over this, it will have been enough time for people to have developed new habits. Some of which could have huge implications for the housing market. For one, fully remote work may become drastically more common place and the urban centers that have been a sure fire way to make money in real estate over the past two decades may suddenly seem overpriced. Maybe not. As we saw in the last recession, few people fled to areas of better value as the jobs did not find a similar value proposition. This time the question will be whether companies will value having a remote workforce that is more robust to the current threat or simply value traditional consistency more even if it does make finding consistent employees more difficult. Having a general position that bakes in the reality of what is possible will be helpful, but ultimately what is going to make a real estate investment profitable or not for you is going to have less to do with the general macro economics of the situation and more to do with developing a well thought out plan for a specific property that identifies an undervalued potential and utilizes it.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is this the correct time to buy stocks due to COVID-19 sell off, or should we wait a little more until companies announce their first quarter earnings (which is expected to disappoint further and lowering the prices of stocks even more)?
Answer: The current market perception seems to be that the worst of the covid-19 has already been priced into the market and that the US is acting appropriately to keep it under control. I personally believe that it’s not only going to get a lot worse as most medical experts are saying, but also that we have a very hard time imagining the true depths of what that means long term for our economy. My gut tells me this is going to be a lot worse then anything most people alive today have lived through. Unless we develop some miracle vaccine or cure, Covid-19 is going to be a force to be reckoned with for at least 2 years. Our current plan is not to stop it, which aside from those miracles, simply means social distancing to just slow it. Social distancing may get partially replaced by rigorous testing and specific, but far reaching quarantines in places found to be affected. In any case, there is no going back to what we know as normal. There is going to be a new normal and no one knows exactly what that is going to be. Imagine, for the next two years, there is only very limited hand shaking, dating, concerts, cruises, conferences, and other large gatherings in person. New social contracts will be formed. Virtual will become bigger and more commonplace. Once wide spread testing is implemented, a new dichotomy will form between people who have had the disease already and have immunity and those who don’t, maybe there are new ids cards with it and only those people can go to bars, eat out in restaurants, or travel internationally. What you can do will probably vary by state as our current federal government has been unwilling and very slow to make any strong moves to curtail this thing socially. Our president, who is leading our efforts to combat this thing was quickly found to be an idiot after suggesting that we would be through the worst of this thing by Easter despite every expert directly telling him before, during, and after that that wasn’t even remotely possible even with a miracle cure. In any case, I think by this point everyone knows the type of leadership we can expect from our commander in chief, what is a little less clear is an actual date when we will be past this. Lots of politicians and business leaders are floating dates like May or shortly thereafter, but that’s not coming from the medical experts, thier opinions tend to be along the lines of summer may lessen the virus’ contagiousness, but aren’t really offering up any clear dates other then timelines of a year or two before this thing completely runs its course. By that time we will have forgotten what normal was and will have simply created a new baseline upon which the world and the businesses in it will adapt to serve. This is what happened during the Spanish flu, which was bad when it first came out. It seemed like it went away during the summer, but came back even worse in the fall. That is a roller coaster ride with lots of ups and downs and our economy is surely going to follow it. You may be thinking this time will be different then the Spanish flu. We can use our knowledge to lessen the deaths. You are right, but social distancing and other extreme measures is how we use our knowledge. There isn’t some no compromise solution or magic technology that can help us that doesn’t also have a profound effect on how we live our lives. Our technology is going to keep us healthy by telling us how to avoid each other, it’s not going to give us a way to continue to partake in risky situations. The good news is the virus is mutating slowly which means a vaccine may be effective, but that’s still at least a year away if we are lucky. If not, the steps we are taking now that slow the spread also prolong the pain and the need to control care contact for longer. It is an exceptionally risky time to buy stocks, but also a great opportunity to get some insane deals, but keep in mind people’s behavior is going to be changed, not just for a few weeks, but for years, possibly forever and that’s going to kill some bedrock businesses. After Q1 results is likely going to be just as volatile. We still won’t have a clear path of how this thing is going to play out, particularly with a conservative administration trying desperately to save what we had rather then acknowledging the worst is still yet to come and preparing for the long haul. In any case, play the market with the things you know… it’s going to be very volatile for a while. If you can deal with the volatility, there are deals to be had. If you can’t easily see those deals, play it safe and invest in some low risk bonds or simply open a savings account, or just stay the line and do some dollar cost averaging in a broad based mutual fund with a long term outlook. The market will come back. It will just come back different then what anyone can generally predict and it may take a relatively long time, but it will come back.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does the government have the authority to force corporations to use their cash pile to offset the effect of coronavirus? Large cap tech companies are sitting on piles of cash that are really useful in times like this.
Answer: Yes. It’s called the tax code. When the government needs to redistribute wealth or provide a service the private market is unable to implement satisfactorily, the government can change the tax code to incentivize the practice. Want to have a company create medical supplies… create a tax credit for doing so. Want to make sure no one gets laid off, create a tax equal to a years salary that must be paid for anyone laid off in the next year. It can be targeted only at corporations of a certain size or even be a tax on corporate wealth. There are so many possibilities. It’s not a direct seizure of assets, but it doesn’t need to be. Corporations are driven almost solely by profit and taxes hit directly at the bottom line. All it takes is agreement among the three branches of government and the government can get corporations to go in whatever direction they deem fit.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why was global warming (climate change) used as a reason to stop construction of a third runway at Heathrow?
Answer: Airplanes contribute about 2 percent to global warming. If that number seems low, that’s because it is. Most of the world can’t afford to travel by air. For semi-frequent fliers, meaning at least 3 or 4 flights a year, flying contributes more to their carbon footprint then all other sources combined. Flying emits particulate pollution high in the atmosphere that has an additional warming effect. There are lots of factors that effect how polluting plane travel is from the distance of travel, height of travel, efficiency of the plane, to where you sit on the plane, but in virtually all cases it’s the most polluting way to travel sometimes by a 50x margin or more per mile traveled. Worse still, planes are not going to get much greener anytime soon in the future. Where as trains and cars have a clear path to electrification, batteries simply don’t have the energy density appropriate for air travel and using hydrogen or some other source of greener fuel is completely unproven. In other words, the only way we have to make flying greener in any substantial way now, or likely for the next couple of decades, is to simply do less of it. To answer your question, global warming was used as a reason to stop construction at Heathrow, because it happened to be the most legally expeditious way to stop construction. I’m not so naive to believe climate change awareness is more of a motivating factor then pure NIMBYism. With recent regulatory changes though, air travel’s disproportionate contribution to climate change is very easy to prove in court, not because those regulations were written badly, but because it actually is! Much more so then trying to prove irreparable harm from say the noise and disturbance from a few more planes flying over your neighborhood, you can’t move off the earth to escape climate change and there still ain’t no way to unmelt the Antarctic ice sheet that can practically be implemented this millennia. Many other forms of travel exist and this case was not about stopping air travel just limiting it, perhaps just to flights that can’t be easily accomplished by train. Sadly, climate change is not just the best legal reason to stop construction, but is also the most practical reason to stop building it as flying truly is one of the absolute biggest contributors to climate change for the people who use it. The statistics are truly horrendous and make for an easy objective win in court. We just think as coal plants as enemy number one for climate change because so many more people are using coal for their energy needs on a daily basis so the total numbers are simply staggering, but if an individual who flys a few times a year wanted to lessen their carbon footprint, they would be better of putting their efforts into taking other means of transportation then say installing solar panels on their house or shutting down their local coal plant.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I live with my sister, her partner and 2 children. How do I explain that me paying 1/3 of the utility bills is unfair? Hers come in at 600$ mine have never been above $300
Answer: First of all, you need to realize this is not objectively unfair. Part of the costs of living in shared spaces is you give up some freedom and costs to essentially buy in bulk. You may pay more in utilities, but you have a deal you likely won’t get anywhere else… living with someone you presumably like to be around and at a cost that is likely dramatically less then living alone or with other roommates. The first thing you should do is look around and compile a list of realistic alternatives, maybe tour some other apartments or see what is available in online ads. My guess is you will likely find the deal you have now, assuming you like living with your sister, is probably both cheaper and more beneficial then any other alternative. If that’s the case, chalk the extra utility bills up to the cost of getting a great overall deal and be happy you not only save money, but the extra you do pay goes to your sister, not some corporation you don’t care about. On the other hand, if you find something cheaper that you think you would prefer more and are truly prepared to move out, then you should be frank with your sister, tell her how much you appreciate living with her, but it’s getting expensive for you to continue. Mention why you think the utility bills are unfair, but don’t belabor the point. It’s not a black and white issue. Ultimately you just need to show her you have better options and be willing to use them if she doesn’t want to compromise. Maybe she has better options too and she has a friend who would be happy to take your place without any complaints. In any case, don’t make this personal. If she doesn’t want to renegotiate the arrangement, that’s her decision to make and makes your decision to leave for someplace better easier. If you find that makes you uncomfortable and you really don’t want to leave your sister even if you think she is being unfair, you just need to get over it. Accept it as something you do for your sister because you love her and don’t think about it again unless you truly want to move.

Question: It's often said that if you raise corporate taxes, the business will leave for another state or country. What actually happens to the original state or nation's economy when this happens in the short and long-term?
Answer: In the US the statutory corporate tax rate is relatively disconnected from the effective tax rate corporations pay. Significant changes to the corporate tax rate are almost always accompanied by equally significant changes to deductions and the closing of loopholes. Note both the sharp decline in the statutory rate in the mid 80s is accompanied not by a sharp decline in effective rates, but rather a substantial increase due to closed loopholes! The rest of the timeline is also very disconnected and illustrates that the statutory rate the government sets usually plays only a very tangential role in the effective taxes corporations pay. The health of the overall economy as well as how well corporations are able to restructure to take advantage of the tax code plays a much bigger role as well as the structure of the country’s tax code in question. That doesn’t mean that taxes don’t play a big role in shaping the economy, but the effects tend to be subtle and take decades to play out in ways that can only be completely understood in retrospect and are always way more complicated than as a direct result of a statutory rate change. Incentives and deliberately shaped loopholes tend to be a much bigger driver of where businesses move to. When it comes to taxes, the carrot tends to have way more of a shaping effect on the nation as a whole then the stick. The simple answer to your question as to what happens to the economy as the result of corporate taxes being raised in OECD countries is… nothing happens in the short term. Governments will go out of there way to make sure effective rate increases are minimized when the scrutiny is on after a statutory tax raise and any significant increases are phased in over long periods of time. In the long term, companies will adapt to the new tax code, sometimes in positive ways that match the intention of the behaviors the changes were trying to drive, sometimes in negative ways, the only thing that is clear is that the statutory increase that comes with major changes to the tax code is least predictive metric of the health of the future economy.

Question: Why won’t $4.5 billion from big tech end the California housing crisis?
Answer: The median cost of housing in the Bay Area where the big tech companies are is $1.5 million. The median household income is around $125k and means a $600k home is at the top of what the typical household could reasonably afford. That’s a huge gap. If we forget about the poor and those struggling the most in the Bay Area and just focus on those middle class households, which should be the low hanging fruit, that still means that those billions of dollars makes just 7,500 homes basically affordable. 7,500 homes may seem like a lot, but the Bay Area is huge. 8 million people huge. That $4.5 billion works out to about $562 per household. The entire Bay Area has also grown by about 50,000 residents per year over the last decade. 7,500 homes won’t even cover the growth that happens in 2 months in the Bay Area! $4.5 billion won’t end the housing crisis, it won’t even make a dent in the problem, at best, it will let you keep the status quo for a couple months longer. In any case, by the time this money gets allocated and spent, the housing crisis will be worse in the Bay Area then it is now, just maybe marginally better for the handful of people who benefitted from the tech generosity! None of this really matters though. The good news, if you could call it that, is that the housing crisis in the Bay Area doesn’t require money in the form of charitable contributions to solve. Simply allowing typical market forces to play its course would fix the housing crisis in several years. The housing crisis is currently artificially supported by decades of zoning restrictions, property tax regulations, and onerous permitting processes that make building extraordinarily expensive and subsidize existing residents regardless of income to incentivize them to live in inefficient housing in dense urban areas. A streamlined permitting process, changes to zoning to just impose infrastructure improvements and quality of life standards without limiting the number of units possible, and a property tax that is directly proportional to the density the land could support would end the crisis.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why does a 5-year-old company with 1500 employees call itself a startup?
Answer: A startup typically means a company is pursuing growth over profitability to an insane degree. Although, such a large company may have both massive revenue and a sustainable business plan already, rather then returning the profit to the owners or shareholders, they use all of it to grow and usually seek additional funding on top of that to grow even more at an even quicker pace. For certain industries like tech where the word startup is often used, capital costs tend to be significant and a company’s greatest asset is daily active users which can be expensive to obtain, but cheap to maintain. Network effects also mean that once you are a leader in the space, new user’s will come to you with little to no active marketing because everything interesting already happens there. Shareholders of a startup will care more about growing users exponentially with little care to the cost as the assumption is even if you spend $10 to acquire a user worth a $1 in revenue to you today, if you reach critical mass, those costs will come down and the users and associated total revenue with them will be 10x or 100x what was invested. A company that is funded with the expectation of being a $10 billion company is a money loser for the investors, even if it is profitable, if it only ever gets to $1 billion in revenue. In other words, user growth is often a much better metric then profit for startups and why size doesn’t matter so much as whether the company is planning for exponential growth or not.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If an American can move to Puerto Rico and not pay taxes, why isn't everybody moving there? What's the catch?
Answer: I moved to Puerto Rico in 2019. It cut my taxes substantially. It was an easy choice for me, but it took some extraordinary and dystopian circumstances aligning to make it viable. First of all, I have my own business and I am able to work remotely for companies in the states. You absolutely need those two things to get the tax savings Act 20 offers which gets you to a roughly 5% combined state and federal income tax rate. I say roughly because you still pay taxes on a nominal salary that must be a fair salary for the work an average person with your skill set in Puerto Rico would make. Effectively, the tax break is only on the corporate profit after that salary. The economy in PR is relatively bad so salaries here tend to be 2/3rds of what they would pay in the states. That 1/3rd in tax savings isn’t worth it though if you are just bringing in revenue roughly equal to an average stateside worker. There are additional fixed costs. You need to pay an accountant and lawyers and regulatory compliance in Puerto Rico makes the heavy hand of California regulation seem downright conservative. The people who move here are at the top of their careers and bring in revenue that is a multiple of what your average worker can do. Look on glass door for the national average salary for your position. If you aren’t making 2x or 3x that number or don’t have a high performing remotely manageable business, Act 20 is not for you. Also, realize Puerto Rico has some costs that may seem extraordinary if you aren’t coming from a high income area. PR has the highest sales tax in the nation that was just recently lowered to around 11%, which is pretty close to the Bay Area where I came from, but won’t seem too great next to some other states. You also will optionally want to get yourself a place with a generator, cistern, and multiple internet connections. I’ve only had to rely on my backups a couple of days this year, but a couple days of downtime is more than enough to make the additional cost worth it to me. With those things, my office has been far more reliable with a higher speed connection then what I had in the Bay Area. Those are the hard cut offs. High income, remote, and self-employed is narrowing the number of people who can do this tremendously. Maybe 1 in a 1000 will have that capability. There are other ways you make Act 20 work for you and also other laws like Act 22, but they are dependant on having substantial wealth ($1.5 million+) or some risky investment strategies like BitCoin. I was lucky enough that the former applied to me and I am on the path to the latter, however, even with those circumstances it would have been impossible for me to move here outside of this year. Prior to this year, I had a wife, a son, and friends in the San Francisco Bay Area. The tax savings are nice and the 45% effective rate I was paying in the Bay Area makes it seem doubly so, however, there is no amount of money that I would leave my son for. My wife made just as much as me and could not work remotely. She is also not someone who island life would appeal to even if I could have convinced her the numbers were still in our favor if she quits her job and we live off my salary alone. Puerto Rico is just not the type place that she would ever consider. That all changed last year. My son died and an extremely contentious divorce followed. My wife poisoned my relationships with all of my friends in the area. I had no other family in the area. I suddenly found myself in an area with no friends, no family, and no local job that tied me to it. What was once not even a consideration, now became a no brainer. I met lots of other Act 20 residents here. Most haven’t had their personal lives devastated to the degree I have, but may meet a somewhat unique set of professional criteria and most were in a time in their lives with some fairly untypical circumstances, others are just non-conformists, and some always wanted to live the island life intrinsically. Don’t take that to mean that Act 20 is only for the super wealthy or executives like many other legal tax schemes. A typical upper middle class worker from an urban area would likely see a good deal of upside. In any case, pretty much anyone who moves to Puerto Rico can apply for Act 20, however, only a select few will be able to effectively see the tax savings and of those that can only a very select few of those will want to uproot their personal lives and move to an island. So far moving here has been one of the few bright points in my life and well worth it. I love Island life, living with an ocean view, and being right right next to the beach with summer weather year round. I’ve saved more in my first year here then the 5 years I spent in the Bay Area and that includes going from a dual high-income household to just me. Others here have struggled a bit more both with dealing with island life and have more complicated business structures that make complying with Act 20 requirements more expensive. Still, it truly is an amazing deal you won’t find anywhere else in the world. It is not a scam, but it only works if you have just the right circumstances to take advantage of it.

Question: Why do many developers feel they are unqualified to design user interfaces?
Answer: Only a poor developer doesn’t take responsibility for ensuring the design of the user interface is appropriate. That doesn’t mean they are the best to lead the design or spend the majority of their time doing high fidelity mockups. That means when it becomes obvious that the cost / value equation is sub-optimal for a certain design choice, the developer should propose new design changes rather then try and implement something that will take substantially longer or work in a way contrary to a good user experience. Sometimes that does mean creating mockups or building a prototype that demonstrates a better approach. Other times, it simply means voicing your concerns with enough explanation to allow the product managers to make a more informed decision whether your opinion is validated or not. In any case, not only are developers qualified to play a role in the design, you can not build an optimal application without expertise in how the technical implementation will work out. Many organizations don’t empower their developers to take an active role in design. Some developers simply don’t take the initiative to work outside the box that they feel they are in. In short, the reasons good design doesn’t happen are far more numerous then the criteria under which is does happen. What is clear from my experience is that an application of any type of complexity requires everyone involved in the development process to take an active role in the design of the application.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why don't companies advertise salaries after a tax deduction? For example, you are paid $2000 and you pay $1000 in taxes, why do they advertise a salary as $2000 instead of $1000 after taxes?
Answer: I paid my accountant $800 this year just to figure out exactly how much I made after taxes. My tax return was around 100 pages I do have a few investments, but capital gains only made up about 10 percent of my income. It really should not be hard to file my taxes, but it is because our tax code is crazy impractical. Absolutely everyone prepares thier taxes electronically these days, yet it’s still based on paper forms. Also, I filed married filing jointly which substantially changes your tax owed if your spouse is in another tax bracket. In any case, the United States is one of the most complex tax codes in the world. The real question you should be asking is why doesn’t the government tell us how much we owe in taxes as many other countries do. The fact that we self report information that other sources have already told them about baffles the mind. The only people that should be filing taxes are those that want to contest what the government has already recorded about you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I am in the middle of getting my GED but I also want to learn how to code to become a software developer. What should I do first?
Answer: The GED for sure. If you really like software development, you will likely lose motivation to go back to other things like the GED that will help your career, but will seem like a step backwards once you have conquered basic coding. Also you don’t need things like high school level math to get started in coding, but it will help and is absolutely integral to building robust algorithms and solutions to nontrivial problems that even the most junior of developers will be expected to solve to get a job.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If software engineers in the Bay Area are really paid more than the rest in other areas, why do some of them still complain as to how expensive SF is? Are the high salaries not enough?
Answer: I worked in the Bay Area up until the end of 2018. I made an above average wage and was married to another tech worker who also made an above average wage. Neither of us struck the equity lottery, but we were certainly an example of what two high performing individuals could do. Our income was high. Like nationally, one percenter high, but in the Bay Area, I would call us typical high performing career tech workers for our age and skill level in the Bay Area. However, in California, that means you get hammered by taxes. Our effective combined state and federal income tax rate was 45% last year! On top of that you pay another 10% of everything you buy in sales tax. To live a familiar middle class lifestyle reminiscent of the one I grew up living in New Jersey in a suburban home a similar distance from Manhattan that I was in the Bay Area from San Francisco, we were paying $7500 a month in rent and utilities and spent another $5k a month on just living expenses. That’s at least 3 times what a similar home in the neighborhood I grew up in would rent for. After generous retirement savings and savings for our kids college fund etc, there wasn’t much left over. It felt like we were paying top bracket rates living a middle class lifestyle. Still I’m not saying we weren’t doing well. These are first world problems indeed. We were spending a lot more than what we could have to just get by even though it wasn’t buying us nice cars or fancy clothes. My complaint was never that I wasn’t making enough to get by in the Bay Area nor that there weren’t enough things to like. California weather is amazing and there is no place on earth that offers the same number of opportunities that Silicon Valley does. There is definitely some positive value there. The problem is there are much better deals in almost any urban location, especially when you are mid-career and have more ability to set the terms of your employment. The complaint is really about relative value. The cost of living is enormous and doesn’t get you what you expect it would, especially as a software engineer with a high ego and dreams to buy a house as nice as what your middle class parents were able to afford on their relatively modest salaries for the time. The enormous rent we were paying in the Bay Area was also actually a great relative deal as the mortgage on the place we rented would have been $18k a month if we bought it at its current market value. That was completely out of our price range even with our high salaries. It wasn’t a mansion either or in a trendy location in the city, just a typical single story home in the Bay Area in a suburb an hour from San Francisco or San Jose. 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms, and a single car garage. It was close to work more than anything else. Our Bay Area life style was basically good enough we could live there indefinitely as renters, which is actually a really high bar, but to put down real roots and buy a place would mean major compromises on where and how we wanted to live. After California, I moved to Puerto Rico. The government practically begged me to come by offering a 5% federal and state tax rate for the next 20 years. On top of that, the cost of living in PR is super low, even living in or near San Juan where there is tons of stuff to do. I work remotely and get paid hourly. Something easy for most software developers in the Bay Area with a good reputation can easily transition to. Even before the insane tax breaks, my gross income went up as I don’t have to deal with lost time from traffic or any of the other time consuming problems I had to deal with in the Bay Area. I live right next to the beach. The weather isn’t quite as human friendly as the Bay Area, but it’s sunny almost every day and never ever gets cold, it’s always a little hot, but overall it’s still a very close second weather wise to the Bay Area. In any case, my stress level is a fraction of what it use to be. I pay a fraction of the rent I use to, but live in a place twice as big. I do basically the same thing I use to, but I am more effective now that I don’t have as many distractions and time sucks. I won’t say there aren’t significant compromises, but relative to the significant compromises in the Bay Area, the overall value is absolutely insane. I have saved more in the 6 months I’ve spent here then the previous 4 years I spent in the Bay Area. I miss certain things about the Bay Area terribly, but my life away from it is better in so many other ways. I do have a somewhat unique situation and the path that brought me to the island is one that was forced on me by the choices of others that I did not get to make for myself and the result of circumstances that no one would choose to have thrust upon them regardless of the eventual outcome. Now don’t get me wrong, moving 4000 miles to an island in the Atlantic is not an easy choice and likely impossible if you have any real roots in the Bay Area you care about. In any case, my point is regardless of how you get out, high performing software engineers can do way better outside the Bay Area pretty easily. My complaints may not resonate with others who have more basic affordability problems, nor would I say they should or they are at all comparable. However, when the rest of the world offers you higher value and enough opportunity, it makes the Bay Area look pretty poor in comparison. That’s a legitimate complaint to me, not that I’m expecting anyone to shed a tear over it, but it’s why making a ton of money working for some of the most interesting companies in the world is not all it’s cracked up to be. Some high earning engineers complain about the cost of living in the Bay Area because even though they may have more opportunity to get a high salary there, at the end of the day, they only need one job. It’s eminently possible to earn just as much elsewhere with the right skills and luck and be able to live in a place where you can afford to buy the house you live in and have way more disposable income.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do so many Californians drive expensive cars even though many studies show that many are still struggling with rising housing price and stagnant wages?
Answer: When I lived in Silicon Valley CA, I was earning a multiple of the median income of the area. Still I struggled to buy a place given that starter homes start in the 7 figures and places I could see myself living in for 30 years were closer to $3 million. Rent was less then half the price of what a mortgage for the same place would be. I was able to live in a nice place that was affordable to rent, but I couldn’t remotely afford to buy it. Despite that my money couldn’t be used to buy a house I wanted, I could easily buy a $100k car in cash. That wouldn’t be a great financial decision, but it would still be more affordable then what the average car buyer does when buying a new car. Given that for the 4 years I lived there, the home prices went up way more each year then what I was able to save, saving to buy a house in CA is an intractable problem for the vast majority of its residents who don’t yet own. At some point you just say to yourself, saving isn’t the answer to your housing struggles, you might as well buy something that lets you enjoy your life.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: NRA members are statistically less likely to commit a mass shooting. Why are people attacking the NRA after shootings?
Answer: When Mary Landrieu (D-LA) proposed a relatively straightforward change to the federal background check system to include gun purchases at gun shows and over the internet, a proposal that is supported by 90% of US voters (90% of Americans back background checks for all gun sales?), the NRA purchased ads that deceptively oversimplified her position and said that she was trying to take away your gun rights. She subsequently lost the next election. All the NRA members I happen to know are registered gun owners who went through background checks when purchasing their firearms. Universal background checks wouldn’t meaningfully effect their right to bear arms. It would effect the gun industry in a negative way. Maybe some of the people attacking the NRA feel that felons and those convicted of serious crimes, the number one reason background checks are failed, really shouldn’t own guns. The NRA is a big reason why those individuals can still easily purchase firearms despite it being against the law to own one and against what most of thier members believe is right. NRA members and the NRA organization both strongly believe in the right to gun ownership. However, they are not well aligned on what should be a priority. Maybe those attacking the NRA feel it would be better to protect just the rights of its law abiding members rather then those individuals who have not demonstrated a proper level of respect for a gun.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I have been a web application developer for 15 plus years and I want to transition into management. My resume seldom gets picked up for manager positions. What can I do to get a job as a manager?
Answer: Start managing. A title follows the work, it doesn’t precede it. As a developer you should have lots of opportunities to perform administrative tasks no one wants to do and a range of tasks that your manager doesn’t want to do. Do those and do those well and you will be trusted with more. Start with things just outside your role and keep expanding them until there is nothing left or things so large you can’t do them on the side while getting your work done. At that point go to your manager with ideas of how things could be done better and a plan that you will execute that will make things better. Don’t go to them asking for work you have never tried to do. Bring them a complete package and make it hard for them to say no. Explain the expected costs and how to deal with any downsides. Then rinse and repeat until you become a defacto manager. Finally, resumes in general don’t get picked up. If you have 15 years of experience and are handing out resumes to random companies, you have already failed. Use your network. You should have a ton of ex co workers who are familiar with your work and your management abilities who can get your foot in the door. Cold calling with a resume is necessary for individuals straight out of college or when looking to transition to a specific company you would love to work, it’s hard though. Build a reputation for going above and beyond your current role and the opportunities for doing those things will find you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is working for a tech company company worth it in Silicon Valley, after all of the everyday expenses?
Answer: Rent in Silicon Valley is expensive, but no more than a typical city, The big difference is Silicon Valley is a dense suburb that may or may not have many amenities within walking distance and it generally won’t be nice or what you would call luxury living. It could be though. You pay for size and proximity to work here and I’ve seen high-end places with top of the line appliances rent for very similar prices to bottom of the barrel apartments. You will be driving most places and traffic will be horrendous. Where the cost of living hurts the most is in buying which is now at levels that mean a mortgage is easily double what rent on the same place would be going for. So if a stable home and buying a place is not something that’s worth a lot to you, Silicon Valley may be a good value. If you are currently driven by work and opportunity, the downsides will be relatively minimal, but you will likely never be able to afford a house you would currently imagine yourself living in long term. The average tech worker will make substantially more in Silicon Valley working for a medium to large size tech company. If you are working for a startup, your financials will almost certainly take a major hit unconditionally unless you get lucky enough to land at one of the startups that has an exit big enough for the grunts to see a big payday. Even then working for half your salary for several years is a lot to give up and that big pay day that only the lucky get is going to be taxed at top federal and California rates which will cut it in half. IMHO, don’t even think about coming here unless you get an offer that’s substantially more than what you are making now. Unless you are a founder, the opportunity for your average tech worker, even early tech workers, should be defined in tangible dollars and cents and if you don’t find it to lure you here, you likely won’t find it to keep you here either. The medium to large size companies will offer equity that comes close to doubling your salary to the workers they want to keep and are a pretty safe bet to both grow your career and grow your savings better than other cities, if you rent cheaply. That being said, if you are good at networking and getting stuff done, you can do better than average in even second tier tech locations and that combined with the cost of living savings, it will make Silicon Valley look like a bad deal. In any case, the younger you are and the less success you have had in the location you now live makes Silicon Valley a better option. The more roots you have and the bigger the need for a stable home (i.e. you have a spouse and kids), the less value you will find in Silicon Valley.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does the leadership of San Francisco have a solid plan for the homeless?
Answer: No. There is no viable plan. To have any success at addressing homelessness, you have to address the sources of it and there is no bigger source then the housing crisis. The continual rise in the cost of living drives more and more individuals into homelessness. Unfortunately, if they want to get re-elected, local politicians really don’t have any viable options. Addressing the housing crisis would mean building way more housing of all types for all income levels. It would mean more sky scrapers and more pubic transportation. People living in the city now would have to adapt to having massive new complexes and lots more traffic. Many would have to give up thier cars and, quite literally, thier backyards. That would infuriate local residents, many of whom have both the time and the money to protest and control those who get elected. Unlike every other city outside of CA, San Francisco has no natural downward pressure forcing residents to move to make way for new development or incentivize them to upgrade thier homes or rental properties to something that supports higher density living. Prop 13 means residents never have to worry about property tax increases making thier single story home in the middle of a growing city unaffordable. It effectively provides them with a subsidy based on how long they live in a place and doesn’t care if there are both better places for them to live or more efficient uses of the land that could make housing affordable for someone on the verge of homelessness. Solving for homelessness is one of those paradoxical situations. The residents of San Francisco truly want to solve homelessness, they are just not willing to pay the true costs. That’s completely understandable, even if any outside observer could see it as the wrong choice for the city’s future. No one in thier right mind would vote for something or for someone who would decimate the value of thier home to build something that will primarily benefit others. The leadership of San Francisco will never willingly touch the real source of the issue unless they are forced to. The state could do that as they have started cracking down on some cities in CA that have blatantly failed to build the housing that the cities themselves declared was absolutely critical to meet the needs of existing and incoming residents, but simply chose not to do it when the local residents became upset with the idea thier way of life may have to change. Having the state force the issue is a long and a politically fraught process. Forcing someone to do something they do not like and has tangible and immediate consequences, even if it’s for thier own long term good, creates enemies of the people who are most needed to ensure things go smoothly. It’s like getting a toddler to eat vegetables. It can be done, but the process breaks many adults who try. Failure is not really an option over the long term though, assuming San Francisco continues to be a thriving metropolis. San Francisco will have to eat it’s vegetables to survive, just don’t expect the plan to do so to come from the local leadership or happen any time soon. The city is still growing. Ironically, the best time, politically, for reforms on this level are in declining economies when you have no other options left and declining growth. Despite a growing majority experiencing the pain of the cost of living, San Francisco still has a lot of very substantial winners. While San Francisco continues to be a place businesses want to be, new residents will have to pay whatever costs are necessary and local politicians have no other option then to do what thier longest and most connected residents won’t get too upset about.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Since tech roles are in such high demand, if you leave your tech job for another and reapply some time later, will you be blacklisted by the company?
Answer: I have worked for 8 different companies in my 20 years of professional software development. Only 3 of those companies still exist. The rest were acquired of met some other demise. These weren’t just small companies either. One was a Fortune 500, some of the others were listed on the stock market. My point is, loyalty to a company isn’t worth much in today’s world. The average age of a corporation these days is substantially shorter then a person’s career and you have zero control over most of the events that happen to a large company as a worker be. Despite that and jumping around to different companies every couple of years, I’ve never had a problem finding work. Going back to a previous employer has never worked out for me though. Not so much because I burned bridges, which I have inadvertently done in my earlier years, but because the companies just don’t exist anymore and the ones that do, the people I knew have moved on. I still keep in touch with some of them though and I go work with them wherever they are at. Corporations aren’t people. They are cold and uncaring. Be loyal to your professional friends and you will never be without work. That doesn’t mean you can’t stop working with them, just be there when they need you and they will be there when you need them. Build your network well and it doesn’t matter where or for how long you work at any place. Impress your coworkers and they will always be there for you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do software Developers manage the cost of living in San Francisco?
Answer: Assuming they neither bought in a downturn, nor won the equity lottery, they rent. Buying is nowhere remotely affordable on the median household income, but rent has been stable in San Francisco for the past few years. It's easily affordable on a median software developer salary. Add a roommate or a high earning spouse and you have options. All of them will likely be compromised in some way and take some finesse to acquire, but will get the job done. It may not seem a great deal in absolute terms, but there is no place else in the world where you can routinely rent a 7 figure place for under $3k a month.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are your thoughts on San Francisco banning new companies from offering employees free onsite food?
Answer: This is kind of like going out shopping for new clothes while your house is on fire. Sure, maybe you will need new clothes to replace the burned up ones, but it would be a whole lot better to actually try and put out the fire now, then to simply ignore it and do something else. San Francisco’s myriad of problems primarily come from the ridiculously high cost of living. This doesn’t address that. It deals with it as a way of life. Rather then having a community that could support diverse restaurants that may not have constant foot traffic or charge enormous prices, it acquiesces the fact that prices are completely unaffordable to your average individual on the median income and looks for a way to keep the burden, but lesson its impact for a select few restaurants at the cost of the local businesses and its workers. The painfully obvious solution is really quite simple…. build enough supply to meet the demand already created. Instead, rather then upset the NIMBYs and take on the politically hard task of reforming California’s zoning, environmental, and tax laws that create the housing imbalance, the San Francisco government has simply added yet more legislation that may treat some symptoms, but like most quick legislative fixes, it will ultimately just make the housing crisis worse.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do software engineers get annoyed when business majors come to them saying “I can handle the business side, you just do the coding”?
Answer: Context matters, of course, but stating the obvious in a condescending matter is always annoying. Moving past that faux paux, the bottom line is a function of both costs and revenue. While you can argue many software projects have nearly infinite scalability and all that matters is building the right product no matter the cost, the reality is resources are limited and success often comes from being first. My most valuable skill as a senior software engineer is eloquently telling a product manager their idea is dumb from a resource cost to customer benefit perspective. That often results in esoteric discussions where I am wrong just as often as I am right, but on the times I do have pertinent technical insight from spending every waking hour working with the internals of a project and learning the business needs around it, it can literally save years of development time. It’s quite often magnitudes easier to change certain arbitrary aspects of a business process then to build nonsensical tech to make it work anyway. You pay a junior engineer to just code, you pay me to make them code less. Just hire the former if you want to spend years going over budget and getting exactly what you asked for, hire a senior engineer if you want to be constantly questioned and only finish half of what you thought you initially wanted in your first version, but do it with an order of magnitude of more time and budget to spare. You can then iterate on it until you build something no one could of imagined when the project started. The first thing you learn after releasing a product is usually that no one actually knew WTF to build in the first place on either the engineering or business side. That being said, up front collaboration and input from all sides can limit the time you spend building something no one actually uses and get to discovering what is actually valuable. The quicker you realize that, the better your product will be. Software engineers get annoyed when someone says they don’t need input on the business requirements not because it makes clear that they know exactly what to build, but because it’s flatly untrue. Optimal business requirements can only be discovered.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can I still be a software engineer if I minor in computer science?
Answer: Yes, but there is a good chance your career will be short lived. Software engineering is frustrating. It gets easier, but still a good amount of your time will be spent in highly unrewarding pursuits trying to finish the last 1% of a feature that is just about there. Others may have some insight, no one else has the answer. You have to dig and dig until you figure it out and once you figure it out you will just have another issue come up. That takes a love of the art and commitment to see it through. A lot of people go into computer science and tough out the early years thinking once they have the skills, they will just be able to see the answers. That is true to a degree, but there is a plateau. After you become an expert at software development, what is left is problem solving and many problems defy clean, well architected solutions that fit anything you learned. On some level, you will always be a student. Some hard things you experience will always be hard. The challenges will change, but they won’t always get easier. I mention all this, not because a minor in computer science isn’t more then enough to give you the capability to start developing. Heck, all you need is a computer and access to the internet to get the skills you need to start a career in programming. A degree makes getting a high paying, stable job easier, but is hardly required. I mention all this because good programmers are really dedicated to the pursuit. If you are minoring in computer science because software engineering just comes naturally to you and you want to spend your hardcore academic time pursuing something that will expand your capabilities and knowledge in a particular specialization, Godspeed, you will likely do great. If your minor is a way of hedging though, in hopes that if your true love falls through, you can pursue something lucrative that isn’t particularly interesting to you, you will likely burn out quickly. That still may not be a bad thing career wise as those who can’t code can always manage those who can or possibly find a more rewarding career in QAing others code, but others who I have worked with who don’t put software engineering first and like it that way, don’t end up being software engineers for very long.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is every company copying Apple's notch? Even Google is reportedly bringing the notch in the next Pixel. Why does everyone follow Apple's design failings (yes it is, Apple had to go so far as to hiding it in the presentation with that wallpaper)?
Answer: The notch allows you to put a bigger screen in a smaller phone. Big screen + small phone = better

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is something that I can do in Bay Area and not anywhere else?
Answer: Pay $5,000 a month in rent and still live in a tiny, shitty single story apartment IN A SUBURB an hour commute from a major city and with bottom of the line appliances and no washer, dryer, or air conditioning. The kicker is, you still think it’s a great deal because it’s half what a mortgage for a similar sized fixer upper would be.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is the best way to go from being a software engineer with professional experience (startup) and a BS in computer science to a computer science graduate school candidate?
Answer: Knowing few details of who you are or what you want, my first recommendation would likely be to not go. Most people need a masters in CS either because their undergraduate degree is from a non-prestigious or foreign school, or they are pursuing a very specific career path in academia or research. If you are just pursuing a masters to up your pay or expand your opportunities in general, it likely won’t have nearly the effect you would expect. That being said, I found getting into grad school much easier then undergrad. There wasn’t a real trick to it. I did have a high GPA and was a native English speaker. Grad schools appreciate the cheap, highly skilled labor that is in short supply to help teach thier booming undergrad courses. If that sounds like it applies to you, just start applying to schools you like, but, back to my first word of caution, make sure you have a very clear idea of what exactly you want to get out of the program. It’s not a necessary or worth while choice for the vast majority of programmers. Figure out a specific discipline you want to study and realize you will be trying to evolve your understanding of the science of computers, not put computers to practical use in cutting edge ways like you would in a startup. Your goal will be to theorize the best ways to solve problems, but you likely won’t actually solve any problem in the real world. If you like programming, you won’t be doing much of it in grad school, instead expect to focus very deeply on some real challenging problems and theories to help solve them better.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would you consider leaving your freelance job to join a startup as the first full-time employee if you really believed in the product and vision?
Answer: No. Personal belief does not make money. Even if you believe really really firmly. What you need to signal a successful product is belief from a ton or strangers who have nothing to gain except being able to use your product. I think of products that don’t exist several times a month and can envision them being profitable, but that don’t mean a thing. That’s a start, is trivial and may be exciting, but it might as well be the ramblings of a madman and often is. What’s much harder is developing a sustainable business plan and gathering hard proof it’s viable. It takes some skill, some luck, and a ton of elbow grease, but doesn’t require much expertise or a real product so much as persistence and a legitimate goal. A founder has to do that work before convincing me to come onboard full time. Validating an idea can be done through a prototype thrown out into the real world and virally adopted, numbers from an ad campaign or survey with fantastic buy in from ordinary consumers, or a business or individual willing to pay you some cash up front for delivery. Get creative as you want, but show me some hard numbers that when your idea is put out into the real world in some form, more then friends and family get excited for it. That being said, I often help friends build prototypes that help them get validated in my free time, but that leash is short.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Could Apple shrink drastically or even go bankrupt in the next decade in spite of its current $1 trillion valuation?
Answer: Sure. Just look at yahoo. They were worth 125 billion at thier peak. A year after the dot com crash they were valued at under 5 billion. They managed to rebound to about 60 billion and made some investments that turned out to be really smart. Despite that, they stopped being an innovator even with Herculean efforts. They were eventually sold off for around $5 billion despite having a stake in alibaba worth over $30 billion that was first divested. They had the cash to basically continue at thier current size indefinitely, but they just could not catch a break and it became obvious thier culture was not breeding the innovation and products they needed to grow. Yahoo never learned how to compete with google after they lost search to them and never found another product consumers really wanted after thier initial success. It took a little over a decade to see the complete downfall despite tons of cash, but after being a market leader, Yahoo was widely regarded as a hasbin within 5 years of being the hottest place to be on the internet. Still, I wouldn’t blame Yahoo’s downfall on its actions so much as the actions of others. Innovation isn’t something you can predict and it’s impossible to plan to build the next big thing. Yahoo was just a year or two behind the curve when it came to recognizing the power of search and google ate them for lunch because of it as well as having a much more likable message of being simple and ad free. In any case, I digress. When I see the downfall of Apple, it comes not from Apple making a bad product so much as someone else beating them to making a substantially different product that redefines computer hardware. Despite the cash on hand, if a competitor develops a closed off eco system and grows quickly enough, they will disrupt the market and all the money in the world may not be enough for Apple to catch up. Even if Apple has a ton of cash, like Yahoo, if they don’t have a viable play to make it work for them, its not going to make sense to spend it. Still, none of this is likely since Apple can buy any competitor it sees far enough in advance, but I do think Apple’s walled garden approach that super charges thier profits now also makes them more supseptible to missing the boat on some great change that happens to revolutionize computing while they are trying to do it the Apple way. Imagine if Magic Leap wasn’t a steaming pile and suddenly you don’t need a phone or a PC with a screen, just a small device that never comes out of your pocket that projects a screen that is whatever size you need it to be. There will be future revolutions in technology. All it takes for Apple to lose is to simply be late at catching on or for thier answer to be obviously subpar to a cheaper redefining product.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If I already have a job as a software engineer, will my growth ever be stopped because I don't have a degree, or is experience more valuable?
Answer: Depends on what domain you work in. Academic / research / government affiliated organizations will care about your degrees or lack there of long after proving you have lots of experience. Even research divisions in hip srtartups will lean heavily towards having an advanced degree. Some will have hard requirements not only on a degree and what type, but GPA minimums, most however will just be guidance given to the recruiters as educational requirements that will be ignored for someone who is otherwise a good fit. Saying that experience is more valuable then education is really comparing apples to oranges. They do different things at different times. An education from a prestigious university does wonders for getting you past the gate at HR. Tenor at a leading tech firm with a household name like Google can also do wonders, but if you don’t have the box checked for education, you still might be filtered out by the recruiter. None of that actually matters though if you are not cold calling and sending your resume out to random companies you don’t know anyone at. The majority of hires at large companies come from referrals and is what you should be leveraging after your first job. After your first job, you should have lists of people who worked with you and can vouch for your abilities. Some of those will go onto bigger and better things both inside and outside the company you work at. They will be your ticket to your next job and will get you past HR as long as there are no hard degree requirements. I wouldn’t say education is more or less valuable. Experience is typically the dominant thing that will get you hired, set your role, and set your salary after you get through the door, but you may not ever get that chance without a degree and it will raise serious competence issues to a stranger who only knows you by what a piece of paper says. Your growth won’t be stopped by the lack of a degree, but your paths to obtain that growth may be more finite.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Out of all the code you’ve seen in your career as a software engineer, what piece of code left the most lasting impression in your memory?
Answer: Definitely edge finding algorithms in image processing. 20 years ago, I studied them in one of the hardest graduate classes I ever took. I just used practically the same code I learned there for a gaussian blur and a sobel operator in a current project. They were just rewritten in JavaScript to build a card scanner that works on mobile web pages. A feature that only became possible recently when access to a video camera for image processing purposes became widely available on mobile browsers. It’s a cutting edge application of really old software. Despite decades of advancement and being in a problem space (recognizing objects like a human does) that has substantial and broad value. The basic algorithms haven’t improved much. They don’t work great either. It’s still really hard to detect the edges of objects consistently in the general sense, a task that humans do with ease, even on 2d photographs. Machine learning has been revolutionizing object detection recently and is certainly how humans recognize the edges of objects so well… by knowing what discrete things look like on their own, but requires lots of specific input for training and is far from trivial even with the right skills and tools. As humans, we recognize edges so intuitively and don’t think about things like we only know where a wood table ends and a wood floor begins because we know what a table looks like and the difference between wood grain and a cut edge. Trying to do that “simple” differentiation of what’s a texture and what’s an object without that context is extremely hard to do in a generalized way on a 2d image. Machine learning is a good answer, but it feels a little Rube Goldberg. I just want to know where one object begins and another ends. It’s something I can tell you definitively and precisely as a human without much effort at all. It also seems easy and possible just by looking at local pixels, it is anything but. It seems we reached the extent of what naive algorithms can do decades ago.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I read that "the Bay Area housing market is slowing down" last month. Has the downward trend continued, or have the prices stabilized?
Answer: No. You can look at a chart like this and see that Freemont saw an average $50k decline since the start of the summer, but buyers are still paying over $200k more than they were last year. And that's for a place that’s going to take you an hour plus to get to where you actually work at rush hour. It’s also still 30 times the yearly market rent where one would expect to see 20 times in a typical market. If that’s price stabilization, I’d hate to see what a seller’s market is. If you want to predict trends in the housing market in the Bay Area, you should not be looking at housing prices, you should be looking at the local economy. By all means, that's doing great and means offices are being built in greater numbers then housing. Ask this question again when a recession hits and you start to hear about layoffs and slow downs in commercial construction. Until that happens, demand is going to substantially outstrip supply in the residential market as the zoning boards always support office development over residential development throughout California whether they think it's the right thing to do or not. Building offices means your government coffers stay filled and not spent on really expensive things like schools and police that only have to scale when the number of residents do and means the local voters won’t complain to you about the dense condos being built in thier residential neighborhood. Property taxes do get reset to market rates when new housing gets built, but over the long term, residents here are incentivized to rent out property rather then selling, which means new kids and declining revenue per student as the costs of supporting residents rise with the market values, but property taxes do not. The state laws mean local municipalities are financially disincentivized to ever build enough supply to catch up with demand despite the rhetoric that recognizes a housing crisis at the state level. The only relief is that demand can shrink while supply stays static. Home prices don’t really have a top dictated by median incomes as the workers who want to live in the Bay Area simply rent at far lower prices. Rent has been stable in the Bay Area for about 3 years and allows the area to continue to function, despite that buying a house is now unaffordable for everyone in the middle class that is only driving rent prices. Housing purchase prices are dictated almost exclusively by investment potential and whether a home buyer thinks the house will be worth more when they want to sell it. Buying is a luxury. It’s also volatile month to month, but the yearly trend is clear. Housing goes up as long as companies are hiring more workers. A small shift by a small percentage of buyers over a month means wild swings in prices happen, but isn’t a trend. The only true down cycles that have happened since the 70s in the Bay Area have been tied to a slowdown in demand driven by a greater economic slowdown (most recently 2001 and 2008) and not any increases in supply. When another recession happens again, expect housing prices to come down to be more inline with the rental costs as investors tend to be weary of buying rapidly depreciating assets.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: In California, why don’t people sell each other’s homes for a dollar, gift the rest of the value, and then pay low property taxes?
Answer: The price you pay in property taxes is assessed separate from the price the house was sold at. Of course, the home’s selling price typically factors heavily into that assessment and if you paid a bit below the assessed value, you could have a chance of getting it lowered on appeal. If you bought the house for a dollar though, the chances of that are non-existent. The gift tax is also limited to $15k and would also mean you would lose any possibility of a 1031 exchange.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If Apple will announce for the first time ever a bezel-less iPad in their September 12 event, why is it so hard for them to at least shrink the top bezel of the MacBook Pro and get rid of the huge iMac bezels?
Answer: A bezeless screen is primarily an aesthetic choice. You can argue you get a little more screen space in a smaller package, but that also effects how long the battery lasts so it’s not a free trade or always beneficial one on the MacBook. There are also significant aesthetic negatives. You may have a cleaner looking screen, but you will not be able to have a gently curved cover that gives the MacBook a much thinner appearance then it actually is. The MacBook, arguably looks better closed because it has that big bezel that’s visible when it’s open. The MacBook also has a screen viewed in landscape mode and means if you make the screen higher by getting rid of the bezel you will change the aspect ratio or have to make the entire laptop wider or go the other direction and make it not as deep which will change the dimensions of the touchpad and typing area which is one of the exceptional features of the macbook. In any case, the aesthetic change will have implications on usability in a much more significant way then on the iPad. I don’t know if hard is the right word to describe getting rid of the bezels… risky may be a better description for the laptop that’s widely regarded as one of the best designed in the world even if it does have its fair share of compromises.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is an internship at an antivirus company good for profesional development as a software engineer if I don't want to work in that field in the future?
Answer: Guys with options don’t ask questions like this. If you had multiple offers and they are reasonably competitive with each other, you take the one you are most passionate about. If not, take the one that offers more money. It usually means the company is serious about investing in you. When you only have one offer and Im guessing it’s an offer to pay you likely the most money you ever been paid to do a job, you take it. You don’t have to think twice. It’s super easy, your only option is your best option. It’s far more likely to be both more productive and better for career development then sitting around waiting for a better one, especially considering it’s likely already time limited. If you have other passions you can still pursue them on the side. Take the offer, even if it’s a mistake, they will pay you and you will learn from it. In any case, As a software engineer, the domain doesn’t matter much. Software engineers care way more about how good you are at architecture, algorithms, libraries, languages, and just the state of the art in your chosen software specialization. Domain specific knowledge isn’t going to hurt, but they aren’t hiring you for that, they are hiring you for your power to spit out robust and performant code. Of course every company is going to want you to learn thier product specific knowledge and taking responsibility to know how to deliver the next big feature for a product and how important it is before the product owner even tells you about it is what sets an ordinary developer from an extraordinary one. Knowing that domain specific knowledge is incredibly important, but it’s also way more specific then just a general category that’s easily transferable between companies or even between divisions. It’s at the product level and knowing the specific company’s strategy for that product more so then say having previous experience implementing a similar feature before. You bring your coding skills and knowing how to quacking figure out where a company needs the most help and where you can go above and beyond to fill that need. At the end of the day all problems can usually be broken down into easily recognizable patterns, those will transfer between jobs.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What would you do to improve public transportation in the San Francisco Bay Area and are they financially viable?
Answer: None of this is remotely politically viable, but it’s incredibly simple and well understood solution. Getting more creative is not the answer and asking for more public transportation without corresponding walkable residential infrastructure nearby is asking for disappointment. Really, the only thing that has to be done is get past the NIMBYism by changing a few laws that make it so pervasive in California.
