The bad news is, until you do that, every solution is doomed, but succeed in that and the market can solve the problem on its own.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What moments of brutal honesty from a doctor have you actually appreciated in hindsight?
Answer: Honesty is complicated. My son was diagnosed with severe ADHD and moderate autism halfway through kindergarten. This was strange as, for the first 5 years of his life, you could not ask for a calmer kid. Not strangely calm either, just really well behaved. He was social, had no tics or weird behaviors. He was at level or above in academics. Describe an easy kid and this was it. He largely followed the rules, potty trained in a week, rarely threw tantrums, great eater, dressed himself, went to bed easily. We signed him up for various different activities as he got older. When he was 4, he started soccer. This kid, later diagnosed as extremely hyperactive, was the one who would sit in the middle of the soccer field and look at the butterflies and entice the other kids to pick flowers with him while the rest ran around in circles chasing the ball. Things started changing in kindergarten. He was getting sent to the principal’s office on almost a weekly basis for behavioral problems. Nothing mean or aggressive, more things that can be described as not having any concept of proper manners, like peeing outside the urinal or wandering off while someone else was talking. He became an escape artist, but a terrible one. He would leave the classroom. Slowly and unsneakily, but you wouldn’t notice because it was just so unexpected. He just didn’t know he was breaking the rules. He would be able to understand something was wrong afterwards, but still couldn’t grasp why you were mad at him. As time progressed, things got worse. We took him to therapy and they explained to us we just have to learn to cope with autism. It’s not a disease, you live with it and adapt to deal with the world. Behavioral problems are solved with increased repetition and more consistent structure. We tried that. We tried everything. Our frustration was palpable. Every time we would visit the psychologist, we would explain how improvement didn’t really seem to be happening. Our psychologist would chalk it up to dealing with a hard problem who sees nothing but frustrated parents all day. My wife started asking if there was anything else we could do and alternative explanations. He wouldn’t refer us to any other medical doctor, just more therapists. He seemed honest and sincere. It convinced me enough as I had zero previous experience with special needs kids. My son became incontinent later in the year. He stopped reading. He was talking only in sentences with a few words. Our psychologist still thought this was another expression of behavioral problems, but now thought he might have been misdiagnosed. He was showing clear signs of severe autism! We then showed him a video of our son, with “severe autism” from when he was 4. Singing and socializing and behaving as a normal, but highly social 4-year-old. The contrast with his current behavior was stark, to say the least. Autism is not something you catch; you are born with it. You can adapt with it or not, but you don’t suddenly get better or worse. The video did it. We were finally referred to a neurologist and as soon as possible. The battery of tests took a month. First was the EEG. I have reason to believe it was slightly abnormal, but our neurologist chose her words very carefully and said there was nothing that was clearly a problem. She was honest, but in retrospect I get the feeling there was more than she was letting on. The MRI was next. Where the EEG was nebulous, the MRI was lit up like a Christmas tree. There was the problem. After a year of listening to therapists tell us how both we and our son weren’t working hard enough to overcome his difficulties, the stark reality was sitting right before us. This was a degenerative disease. None of this was treatable by behavioral intervention. His brain was being physically damaged and getting worse. At this point we had another symptom and it was exclusionary of what we had been treating him for. The question now was what was causing the brain damage and, even more importantly, how do we treat it. You have never really experienced a roller coaster until your only child has been diagnosed with a white-matter disease. All forms of these are horrible, but some caused by infections are completely treatable and, if caught early enough, can be completely reversed. The others are horrible in every way. Our neurologist told us nothing on the MRI showed permanent damage. We had a kid who we believed had severe autism and were just told there’s a chance he could be cured. We were preparing ourselves for a lifetime of taking care of a kid who would never be able to take care of himself and now has a disease that might be able to be treated with medicine. Time to ride the roller coaster up. Unfortunately we’re not at the brutal honesty part yet. White-matter disease is a very generic term for anything that affects the white matter of the brain. Our neurologist knew exactly what she was doing. His MRI was not specific, though, and while there was a chance it could be caused by an infection, that was an unlikely scenario. She didn’t share that just yet, but sent us for a battery of about 50 different tests for everything under the sun that could be possible. Our son’s brain was actively being attacked and, after a year of doing nothing but the wrong thing, time was of the essence. Both my wife and I had some connections in the medical community and found we had some very high-up resources who were immediately motivated by a kid with brain damage looking for a definitive explanation. Over the next two weeks, I reached out to everyone who had any type of medical background doing the trust but verify thing with our neurologist. We felt more comfortable with her than any of our past therapists, but we also now had direct experience of the limitations of a medical diagnosis and the risks couldn’t be higher. I managed to get the help of a retired Fortune 500 CEO who got us direct access to specialists at Stanford who were the guys to talk to. Turns out our neurologist was already in contact with them and they had the same conclusion that more tests were needed. On another contact, our old neighbor’s cousin was a head of radiology and he gave us another breakdown of the MRI. His recommendation was that if he saw this, he would never have let his kid leave the hospital after it and would have had them start treating him for an infection. We started to freak out. We were at the top of the roller coaster and going down fast. Was this treatable and were we just wasting time? We made a late-night call to our neurologist. She picked up. We’re still not at the brutally honest part yet but, at this point, she explains to us the MRI wasn’t really presenting as one that would have an infection as a source. It just didn’t fit the other typical presentations either. Our son had a rare disease or a rare presentation of a more common disease. Still she said she put a rush on the more definitive tests but, since they weren’t back yet, she would schedule us for another far-more invasive MRI the next day that would require sedation and be the path to start treatment for an infection. Hours before we left to go to the hospital, our neurologist calls us. Another one of the tests results had come back. It was positive. It was also definitive. Our son had the gene for adrenoleukodystrophy, a degenerative neurological disorder. There is no treatment once symptoms present themselves. It can be treated with a risky bone marrow transplant, which is highly effective if done before the slightest sign of behavioral problems. But if done after symptoms start, at best your body rejects the transplant and you die quickly; at worst, it leaves you in a partially vegetative state blind, deaf, immobile, and with very advanced dementia, but your body is otherwise healthy and can live on virtually indefinitely. Our son is now mostly blind. He doesn’t talk, can’t understand language, has virtually no emotions. All the unique things that made him the little person he was were the first to go. His dementia is substantial. There is no comforting him from an emotional standpoint. He doesn’t seem to recognize anyone on his best of days. This actually makes it easier on him as he didn’t care when he went blind or care about his other numerous issues. He largely doesn’t show emotion unless he has physical pain. He is largely a zombie. He can still move around pretty well and feed himself, but doesn’t care what he eats like a typical kid would. He won’t eat mac and cheese anymore, his favorite food, as it’s too soft, but vegetables, rice cakes, any food whether it has sugar or not, as long as it’s the right consistency, he eats mindlessly. This is where the brutal honesty comes in. This disease is horrible. About as bad as it gets. It takes years and you just decline throughout all of them. It takes your soul, then it takes your abilities. Then you die. There are no experimental treatments. There’s not even hope of experimental treatments on the horizon for his state of progression. The cures are for the thing that causes the brain damage, not the brain damage itself. No one in his state in all of human history has ever had a good outcome. Everyone asks, “Have you gotten a second opinion, have you pursued X?” It’s not like that. There’s nothing. It’s just bleak, but it’s clear. All the puzzle pieces fit together perfectly and you don’t need to be an expert to see the big picture. That bleakness is comforting in that way. You stop worrying about whether you are doing the right thing. You are just doing. You don’t have to choose palliative care. It’s chosen for you. Your options are persistive vegetative state kept alive by machines — or death. It is definitive and, unlike so many other diseases, there aren’t Hail Mary options with extremely unlikely cures that are extremely painful and then you can die anyway. Our neurologist was anything but honest until she had to be. Once the diagnosis was confirmed, though, there was no sugar coating. I understand why she did what she did when she did it and hold her in very high regard. Especially relative to our earlier experts. At the end we did get honesty and it was brutal. There is one path we have now and while it’s about the worst one you could ever imagine, at least it’s known. Not knowing made life even worse. We put our son through hell in his last lucent year thinking he had autism. We can’t make him better now, but we can make him feel better and by knowing what’s in store, when it’s time, we can make sure he dies quickly rather than artificially prolonging his life on false hope. While there are no words to describe how it feels to know your only child is destined to die a horrible death with little quality of life left, it’s far less stressful than knowing that’s a distinct possibility, but holding out hope and constantly searching for a diagnosis with no end in sight. I feel guilty about it, but I appreciate the brutal honesty of a definitive death. This is my son. He may look perfectly normal in this photo but when this was taken, he was anything but. He had already lost all ability to understand language among other things. This was the last time I saw him really laugh. It’s a priceless memory and one that I have only because we knew his path and weren’t pursuing therapies that were useless to him. Edit Adrenoleukodystrophy (ald) can be tested for at birth with a simple and relatively cheap blood test. It is now required in only a handful of states, but not others. It is an x-linked genetic disorder where girls are carriers and boys have a 50% chance of getting it from their mothers. 1 in 18,000 are affected. It is on the list of recommended tests to get at birth by the federal government, but still not done routinely in many states. If you are pregnant ask your doctor if an ALD test will be performed as part of the screening at birth. Pay for it if your insurance won’t cover it. It’s around $100. We had no family history of the disease. We followed every recommendation of our doctors before he had any symptoms. We had no reason to suspect anything and a perfectly healthy 5 year old until we didn’t. Getting the test at birth would’ve made the cure viable.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Uber wants people to start using electric bikes for short trips instead of cars. Would you do it if it was accessible and cost effective?
Answer: Bikes are cheap. Electric bikes less so, but still can be bought with what I spend in about six months on my car. Bike racks are also easy to install on a car and cheap. Accessibility and cost isn’t really the problem. The problem is there are too many cars and not enough infrastructure to support bikes. Car infrastructure is unsafe and slow in urban areas and mixing in bikes makes it worse. Renting a bike wouldn’t fix that. What would would be getting cars off the road during business hours in highly urban areas. The outskirts of those areas would have electric bike depots where you could park and ride. From say 8 am to 6pm it would be illegal to drive a automobile into the city. All traffic lights would become circles for bikes. The speed limit would be 25 mph everywhere. After hours, streets would still be limited to one lane with the rest reserved for bikes and vehicle traffic would be optimized for deliveries with no long term street parking. In a city like San Francisco, which has perfect bike weather year round and is only about 7 miles wide and 7 miles high, you could get from anywhere to anywhere in the city in under a half hour at rush hour. That would make me get a bike if I lived in the city and rent one from Uber if I didn’t.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If you live in California and are working on a side project, and then take a new full time position, how do you prevent the new company from owning your side project?
Answer: Every large company I have worked for usually asks you to declare any inventions or preexisting IP you have in your employment contract when you start with them. Fill that out and don’t make a big deal about it. You start asking specific hypothetical questions and they will refer you to the legal department which will find risk with hiring you if you give them a reason. Otherwise as long as your project is broadly unrelated to your day job, you shouldn’t have a problem and I’ve never had anyone in management who wasn’t supportive as long as I made it clear I was only working on it in my free time. You can also let your manager know at any time you started working on a side project in your free time at any point after you start working and he will likely have you fill out a declaration. Even if you don’t do that, there likely be won’t be any questions asked when you quit especially if it’s on good terms. Just don’t burn any bridges or do something blatently unethical. The few times that I heard of IP conflicts with employees that led to lawsuits was when either the employee was blatantly stealing IP and bragging about it or there was another somewhat unrelated suit between companies and the lawyers tossed in a stolen IP accusation from an employee who happened to be at both companies.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As a programmer/software developer, do you prefer sitting or standing desks at work?
Answer: Standing all day is hard. Sitting all day is less hard. I choose sitting despite having generous access to standing desks. While some may argue standing is better exercise, being the smug asshole programmer trying to fit into my stereotype that I am, I am happy to point out, standing is not exercise as you are not moving. The other health benefits are a mixed bag. The important thing is to change up any repetitive activity periodically. If a standing desk helps you with that, go for it and don’t let anyone call you a hipster. As to me, I like to change up my sitting by laying down and taking a nap. I call that my exercise.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do you think San Francisco will look like in 10 years as the high cost of living and increased inflation continue to put unsustainable pressure on the working class?
Answer: The pressure is really only unsustainable for a certain segment of the population that have expectations of how to live, but aren’t rich enough to afford traditional middle class standards. The area’s low income workers may live in relatively cramped housing compared to pretty much anywhere else in the United States, but by international standards, the city is hardly dense and looks pretty damn good compared to some other cities. Coffin homes are a thing in places like Hong Kong and make living with 3 or 4 other families in a small house look pretty good. San Francisco may seem like rock bottom to your average american trying to live on the median income there, but it’s actually no where near rock bottom of what a human can endure and some individuals who have seen the true rock bottom will find San Francisco a welcome reprieve even as a low wage worker. In other words, you can toss on a whole lot more weight on the backs of the lowest wage workers before your break them. What is really happening in San Francisco is the whittling away of the middle class worker and family unit, not the worker in general. Those who don’t make enough to make living in the Bay Area worth it, but have enough resources and opportunity to find viable employment elsewhere will move out. Richer and richer individuals will continue to come in greater numbers to be around where the money is, even if its just to try to make their mark before moving onto easier living. Poor people in ever more desperate situations will also continue to come as the place provides guaranteed employment for those who can use extremely creative and dystopian ways to control their own cost of living in order to maximize their savings. More than anything else, San Francisco will become more transient as renters form a greater and greater portion of the population and will move in and out of the area as they discover whether they can personally make the substantial benefits outweigh the substantial negatives long term. Over the next 10 years, expect inequality to get even worse. This won’t cause a shortage of workers so much as a shortage of middle class workers. Both workers who live below the poverty line and those who make several times above it will continue to come to the area. As the area’s existing middle class residents who take advantage of prop 13 die off, their homes will be inherited by their families who already live somewhere else and will turn them into rental properties as the state will subsidize them quite generously with a substantial property tax write off to do so. There is no pressure to sell on those who own the land. Sitting on a piece of property that consistently increases in value quicker then the stock market with virtually no expenses is a great investment even if it’s no longer a great place to live in. The area’s housing is a financial windfall for those who own here and the legislation that artificially makes housing rise exponentially is just getting more popular among voters who are also affected by the cost of living, but see the tax breaks and zoning that is highly responsive to existing homeowners complaints as a great thing. It is personal source of relief and seen as a fix for them despite driving the cost of living up for the community as a whole. A repeal of the true legislative sources of the drivers of the cost of living is politically untenable regardless of the hardships future generations have to endure. The only change that can be expected from the government as things continue to get worse are band aids like rent control and subsidized housing that will make special winners of a small segment of the population and politicians look good, but make the problem as a whole worse for everyone. Low wage, unskilled workers like house cleaners, nannies, and any others who can avoid the areas mandated minimum wage, taxes, and other quick fix regulations will find lots of work and be generally available. High skilled, middle class workers like teachers, plumbers, electricians, firefighters, and other government workers will both become more in demand and lower quality to the point where you won’t see any of these positions filled by anything other than a transient population of young workers without families unless they marry someone from a much higher income bracket or fill a niche position. The area will still continue to function, but inequality is the name of the game and certain functions that are taken for granted will be open to only those with means. Schools will see great disparities between neighboring districts and the declining quality of teachers will leave the public schools with only the most substantial of resources due to private donations from residents as still providing a decent education. Private schools will become more and more popular in the other districts and leave only the neediest of students left to public education. Highly social retail workers will also likely decline, but the workers who are not so visible will take on some of the less visible work. Efficiencies will bring both welcome changes and growing pains as businesses find ways to cater to their new customer base. There will be no shortage of amenities or fun things to do. Some will even be fairly affordable if they are high volume and require little space and human hand holding. You will have walmart and you will have whole foods, but expect places like Target that cater to those who want quality at reasonable prices to go away. I know this will happen, because living in the Bay Area, you can already see it has taken hold quite significantly already. What can and will change over the next 10 years is just the magnitude. The frequent retort that San Francisco is culturally dying is just wrong. Culturally it is changing, but that’s nothing new nor at all unique. It will lose many family oriented things, but in terms of nightlife and trendy places, it will only get a greater number of places and likely even more niche places, but those will only be open to extremely high earners. The buildings will both get crappier as rent controlled units age and much nicer as new buildings catering to the prevailing market are put up and gentrify the few areas that can overcome the pervasive NIMBYism. As long as you can pay for it, you will be able to find anything at any time. San Francisco has a way of preserving the truly exceptional places despite the market telling them it's time to go as well as the stupid large amounts of disposable cash for the select few that support fun things that wouldn’t be possible most other places in the world. San Francisco will continue to be an extremely desirable place to live even if you can’t afford it. You may not be able to live there and curse it for being so, but you will still want to. In 10 years, San Francisco will look like paradise if you are an exceptionally high earner who owns property there able to fulfill every need you have without needing to interact with the unwashed masses. As a low wage worker, it will look like a necessary evil if you are willing or forced to use your flexibility to cram yourself into a cardboard box that will have the benefit of being colocated with your best revenue stream as well as some nice public amenities that you will probably never use because you are working too much. It will have virtually no middle class and as a resident, family will be something that is either elsewhere for you or you are rich. All that is decimating to the American dream, but is quite sustainable.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can Donald Trump pardon himself out of tax bills that might arise from his IRS audits?
Answer: No. A sitting president can not be indicted in the first place… arguably so. This has never been tested in court so the supreme court has yet to lay down any precedent, but it’s widely agreed, the proper way to penalize a president is through impeachment and a federal crime like tax evasion would be an impeachable offense. Furthermore, the IRS can levy both civil and criminal penalties and most likely it would be the former which is a lower bar. The presidential pardon only applies to criminal offenses so he could not pardon himself out of any civil fines levied by the IRS.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: When taking a computer science course, how can you determine what content is extremely important to my future as a software developer, and what exercises are just training me on how to solve problems at hand?
Answer: Don’t sweat the details. Learn the stuff to get the grade, then make sure you code on the side as much as possible. No new grad should show up to an interview without significant coding experience on real world projects. When I interview someone, I don’t care about what theory you know, I care about if you know how to use it in the real world effectively and that goes for new grads. Coding is a virtually free way to produce a new product. You have no excuse for not having a few projects to your name even if no one has ever paid you to build anything. The important stuff you learn you’ll repeat often and retain it pretty quickly. You are also never going to be able to stop learning either. Custom software development is about doing things no one has done before and that’s often only possible using new libraries that push the state of the art and have to be learned a new. The theory you learn in school will help you connect those dots, but you will only have to retain a cursory understanding of them to apply it to the new stuff you will have to learn. My advice to you is if you have free time and studied enough to pass your tests, don’t waste anymore time on trying to understand the theory, just code. Put your skills to use and make something. There are no words or tutorials that can show you what’s important better then actually trying to produce something real and seeing where the pain points are.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If I am having trouble finding a job in software engineering, should I go back to grad school?
Answer: If we were in a recession that might make sense, but in the current economy, finding a software engineering job is about as easy as it ever gets. In the 2 years or so it takes you to graduate, that might not be so and a master’s degree does not do much in terms of hirability unlesss you are looking to go into a very specific role. A graduate degree in software engineering without working in the real world first is also just a bad idea in general. A little real world experience will give you first hand knowledge of exactly what skills you are lacking and how useful certain theoretical knowledge will be. I did get my masters right after my undergrad and I feel I missed out on reallly pursuing things in a way that I would better retain and be able to use in the real world. It does help with justifying higher pay, but I don’t think any job I ever got was because of my grad degree and pretty sure it never got me in the door to a place I wouldn’t of already been a fit for. Assuming you have the grades to get into a decent graduate program, you should have the minimum skills to get a job. There is something else a miss and grad school probably isn’t a solution to it. Finding your first job is hard, you may have to expand your search and apply to places you didn’t think you wanted to work. Also get someone to review your resume if you are not getting interviews. If you are not getting offers after the interview, ask the recruiter for more specific feedback as to why, which they may not want to tell you honestly. If that proves fruitless ask someone you know in the industry to do a mock interview.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What would you suggest to reduce the number of hours a software development team spend in meetings?
Answer: Work remotely more often. This makes the cost of a meeting less as most will be virtual and attendees can vary how much time they are actively listening. It also makes meetings less differentiated then other virtual communication methods and offers less of an incentive to have a meeting vs say hashing something out over email or just over a phone call. You tend to not wait to do this in person as there is no in person. There is of course a cost to that magical word, synergy, but I have found that substantial increases in productivity have far outweighed any hypothetical gains from it and if you are in an organization that has fully embraced remote work, qualified individuals will make communication work just as effectively as in person.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How good are bad software engineers?
Answer: A poor software engineer does exactly what they are told. Seriously. Most of the bad programmers I have had the displeasure of cleaning up after asked for and received very specific and painstaking requirements. They then implemented them, sometimes using dubious architectural standards too and made just what they were told to work somehow. Sometimes in a nonsensical way and they took no time to actually understand what they were doing, but just did it to meet the specs. In some cases, the programmers knew what they were doing was a piss poor way to do it, but because they did not feel empowered to do the right thing, which often would have some effects on the design requirements, they simply did it the wrong way. Management and culture often share a large part of the blame that make otherwise good, but inexperienced programmers perform very poorly. In other cases, the code is beautifully written, well commented, and sometimes even architecturally flawless, it just doesn’t work well. In any case, the issue starts when a programmer lets the task of programming take priority over solving the problem. Bad programmers may or may not lack programming skills or experience, what they universally lack is an active and overriding sense of responsibility to solve the problem no matter where it takes them. Also, by problem, I actually mean everything that’s a problem from how the app works to how maintainable the code is. No matter the task, a good programmer is the one that identifies the thing that is not good enough and works against whatever friction there is to solve it. So to answer the question, bad software engineers can actually write great code, they just don’t follow through to make sure it solves the problem well.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How would you reform the structure of San Francisco’s government to make the city run better?
Answer: San Francisco really only has one root problem worth mentioning. The cost of living. Everything else is exasperated or realitively minor in comparison. Unfortunately, a significant driver of the cost of living that has left San Francisco unable to cope with the phenomenal growth of the Bay Area comes from laws at the state level. Like the environmental regulations that have been abused by NIMBYs to cause a 6 month permitting process to drag on for several years and of course prop 13 that both makes offices more sustainable for government revenues and subsidizes people who stay in inefficient housing situations. That being said there actually lots things that could be improved by restructuring the local government to deal with the idiotic state laws that have in turn driven local towns to make short term fixes that cause bigger long term problems. Specifically, the entire Bay Area from SF to San Jose should be a single government entity that has complete and unilateral authority over zoning decisions. Kind of like the boroughs of New York, just much much bigger. This would allow the region to build public transportation that works by having a single consistent transportation corridor with high density residential buildings along it to meet the current and future housing needs. This is opposed to what happens today where a town along the line simply declares they don’t want a train going through thier surburban neighborhood or bigger buildings despite building office space for 3 times the number of residents the town can house. This means any other town that did the right thing, usually at great expense, has to cope with not only the expense of its own office workers who live there, but the nearby towns too. Residents tend to want things like schools and police that offices don’t need in quite the same level and tend to eat up the majority of a towns budget. In any case, a single political entity would solve this problem and more by balancing the revenue between related towns and making it less advantageous to build just offices. Fix that problem and balance the number of offices with residences and you have solved the housing crisis.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it a good job offer if I'm getting 2.7% of employee stock option pool at a B2B startup that just raised $6M in Series A funding?
Answer: No. It’s shit. Nearly 90% of series A funded startups fail to exit. You can qualify that a little more given by what you know about the company, but chances are you still have a better chance of winding up with 2.7% of nothing then anything else. You haven’t mentioned other compensation or the value of the opportunity to your career and you haven’t mentioned other offers that may make this look better. This is better then nothing, but a 1 in 10 chance of something more then zero doesn’t seem too great when top established employers offer equity packages that can easily double your salary with easily liquifiable options. A good offer from a startup is one that makes up for the insane risk of thier equity by paying you more in base salary or giving you a resume builder that will springload your career. Those good offers are not too common. Expect to get dicked over at a startup. Still, they are usually fun to work at so make sure you at least take that away. Most startups are about as good for your long term financial health as a night in Vegas.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it bad that I want to become a Java developer? Everybody tells me that I’ll never succeed as a programmer if I want to only use one language. I like Java and I don’t see the issue with that.
Answer: Let’s suppose you were a fire fighter and you said I only want to man the fire hose to put out fires. You end up being very good at it and put out fires quicker then everyone else on your team. You quickly become known as the amazing firehose guy. Your reputation runs far and wide until one day, not too long into your tenor, you get called to rescue a cat from a tree. Not just any cat mind you, the mayor’s cat. The chief tells you the mayor has asked for that hot shot firehose guy to handle it personally. You show up at the tree, aim your hose at the cat and fire away. Perfect aim, problem solved in no time flat. No one could of used that fire hose with more precision or more quickly. Congratulations, you got the cat out of the tree! For some reason, neither the cat, the mayor, or your peers recognized the amazingness of your skills, but saw only incompetence. Suffice it so say, you are now known as the wet cat guy instead of the amazing firehose guy. While you still get to put out fires and people appreciate you when they are fighting a very specific kind of blaze, it feels like no one trusts you with the big challenges with lots of unknowns, most of which you are confidant could be put out with a firehose, but it’s always someone else leading the way into that blaze as they only trust you with things they already know can be solved with a fire hose. There is no problem with learning Java, nor is there any issue with saying you are going to solve most of your problems with Java. It’s just a tool though. Your job is still to solve problems in the best way possible, not to write as much Java as possible. As long as Java is never an impediment to solving the problem the right way and you recognize when it is, use it all you want and it’s quite possible it will cover the vast majority of what you will need to do. There is a line though where creative use of a language becomes a kludge and if you cross that line because you are resistant to learning new things, thats when you become an impediment to getting things done well. Don’t be the wet cat guy.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are the most persuasive arguments to convince someone to stay living in SF Bay Area who is doing well in their job and is convinced that rising housing costs is cause to transfer to another office in an area with lower costs of living?
Answer: Your kids are already enrolled in school here and your wife also has a job here. The choice to move really isn’t yours to make.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do liberal progressives think about the living conditions in San Francisco?
Answer: Ugh. It turns out the romanticized moral of the story of David vs Goliath is, in general, profoundly bad. San Francisco is your evidence. It turns out, big slow moving entities that sometimes harm the little guy often do so for the greater good. The proverbial David may have been smaller and protecting a minority, but he crushed Goliath then used his righteous indignation as justification to force his Christian identity on the Pagan majority. A similar thing happens in San Francisco. I was driving through the city this weekend, coming from the south bay. I didn’t want to do anything in the city, just get through it as quickly as possible. That’s just not possible. San Francisco hates cars. I do too, but that doesn’t change the reality we currently live in. California has been seeing massive growth for the better part of a century and seeing the problems of rapid growth during the age of the automobile is most acute here. San Francisco’s hate of cars is a long held belief thats been in place since the 60s when highway 101 and 280 was being built and had plans to cut through the west side of San Francisco. Growth and cars bring lots of problems with it. Cars may not be the best solution particularly in urban areas, but they are a net benefit over nothing. Of course more cars means lots of changes, that will have some very adverse effects on individuals. Houses would be lost, public places would be disturbed. It sucks, especially so for the handful of individuals who live in the path of that highway. I am a vocal advocate for building more public transportation and prioritizing walkability and bike lanes over highways and street parking, but I also have the common sense to realize thats a slow change that requires massive agreement on zoning and infrastructure to happen over time. Not building a single section of highway is simply not a viable option when the rest of the state has already made it the defacto transportation mechanism. The entire Bay Area is built for cars and the highways are how everyone gets around as there really are no other good options for a majority of uses case. In any case, protests in the 60s were successful. Despite the plans for the highway that were open for public comment and went through years of permitting and a drawn out planning process to find the least disruptive compromise, days before concrete was to start pouring another city council vote triggered by massive protests passed on a 6 to 5 vote cemented the lack of a highway to this day. For the perceived benefit of a handful of NIMBYs, everyone who lives in the area has to deal with significantly increased commute times. Unfortunately those protests were not “lets find a better transportation solution that works for everyone”, they simply found fault with an imperfect proposed solution and left it at that. No effort was expended to address how to better correct the worsening growth problems the solution was targeting. To this day, highway 101 ends in San Francisco, then continues after you get past it. The trouble is, even though, the highway doesn’t exist, the traffic still does. Traffic from a 12-lane highway is dumped onto city streets with lights and lots of cross traffic whether you want to end up there or not. Everyone, including the NIMBYs still lose. Ultimately the city has to deal with a massive amount of cars for longer. The noise, the pollution, the danger, the time wasted is all worse then it would of been by building a highway correctly. Cars remain in the city for more time. Public transportation also remains largely unsuccessful as the rest of the Bay Area doesn’t have the density along the transportation corridor to support it. 50 years on, demand for highways has only increased. It turns out that Goliath is big and less sympathetic to individual concerns because it has to be, not because it is inherently evil. Highways are the natural extension of how you support people who want to live in low density suburbs. That is but one anecdotal story, but it extends to the most acute problems of the Bay Area housing crisis that has become a epitome of inequality. Well intentioned individuals see a compromise and ignore the forest for a couple of trees. There is nothing wrong with caring for those individuals trees, but the government needs to care about the forest and weigh the individual losses accordingly. Individuals from every demographic can do great in the Bay Area and are protected in California, but not consistently or fairly and it comes at the expense of the vast majority who don’t have enough of an individual claim to care about. In California, political vigilantes choose a wedge issue and pursue it with blind vigor and no responsibility for the future outcome of their decisions beyond the immediate effect on their targeted special class. California has a participatory democracy that easily allows individuals to partake in legislative affairs that are normally left to city councils who have to at least have a little care about the long term repercussions of their actions on the area as a whole. This is definitely a hard sell in our current political environment, but legislation should be made by professionals who consider the long term ramifications of the issues at stake not individuals who will always be biased to what is going to effect just their own backyard. What do I think of about the living conditions in San Francisco? I think fixing the living conditions have exceedingly well-understood and viable technical solutions. However, fixing it will appear to cause a little bit of harm to a very sympathy inducing victim, long time home owners, in order to bestow a benefit to everyone including high earning new comers. David needs to lose, but no one has written a sympathetic story for that moral yet.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As a software developer in Silicon Valley, what percentage of your income typically goes to rent costs?
Answer: Before taxes or after taxes? With or without my wife’s income? Does income include equity and do you subtract out before tax expenses like retirement and child care? A small portion of my income is taxed at the highest rate and that means I go out of my way to have several write offs, 2 of which let me expense different portions of my rent. I rent out an above average place in Mountain View that special circumstances require me to. It costs a shit ton of money in absolute terms and is at the top end even for rentals in Silicon Valley, but is less then half what the mortgage would be. At the end of the day, we are saving more here then we were in our previous state. That’s the win, but the shocking thing is you would expect to be in a city with way more amenities and density when you move to a place half the size at several times the cost. We’re not even demonstrably closer to our employers then we use to be. The only thing that Silicon Valley really gives you is being close to a ton of employers who you don’t currently work for. So you don’t get to see the true value of what you are paying for unless you quit the job that lured you here in the first place! In any case, I’m not trying to be an ass by not telling you a percentage, my point is, nothing about rent or compensation in Silicon Valley is typical. Equity makes up a much larger portion of income for tech workers here and varies wildly. The vast majority of renters I know seem to have some special scheme to lessen the load… roommates, rent control, tax write offs, etc. My numeric answer isn’t going to tell you much as it most likely won’t apply in the same way to you. What I can tell you though is that almost every tech worker who recently moved here both has more disposable income after paying for housing and lives in substantially more compromised accommodations then they use to. There are also a few that come here and end up both living worse and saving less so make sure you do the math first. It’s not hard to afford to live here as a software developer, it just doesn’t happen automatically and those who don’t actively work at being very miserly with housing tend to not stay here very long.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What should I do if I really struggle with finding freelance clients?
Answer: Go get a full time job. Impress the hell out of your coworkers for the next year or two. Find another better job, then repeat. Keep in regular contact with as many people as you can, particularly the ones who seem like they are going places. Young people will actually be the best as they are most likely to switch jobs often and will want to bring thier friends along. After another year or two, you should know enough people who know you intimately on a professional level to get hired as a consultant.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is your view on the recent news about San Francisco authority looking forward to ban free lunch at tech companies?
Answer: The ban is just on new campuses. The reasoning for that is to build mixed use buildings that make neighborhoods more walkable and put offices next to residences, next to retail including restuarants. So if a tech company opens a new building that growth happens uniformly, not just in office growth. The inability for towns in the Bay Area to zone for what’s in the best interest of the future of the town rather then zoning for what will bring in the most revenue is why the Bay Area is in a housing crisis and why Google made free lunch popular among Silicon Valley companies in the first place. Google sits across from a 10 lane highway between it and downtown Mountain View where all the restuarants are. it’s easily a 15 minute journey each way given the number of traffic lights. Lunch out is not quick or easy because of the way the campus was. Anyway, back to the meal bans. They are kind of about correcting a wrong and if the ban really results in robust mixed use development that means more people can live near where they work, it’s all good. More then likely though, this doesn’t have a chance in hell of facilitating mixed use development over the objections of th NIMBYs at a level where neighbors become more walkable. It really just means workers will lose out on free lunch and likely won’t see the benefits of working in a walkable community. What the Bay Area needs is less restrictions on building high and dense and infrastructure to support it. The free lunch ban, indirectly supports initiatives that are a perfect complement to high density building. However, by itself, without making the hard compromises, this isn’t going to make it cheaper for restuarants to hire workers who need more and more money to live here and is the real threat to small restaurants. It’s silly to think you can save mom and pop businesses who are struggling with the costs of supporting thier customers by giving them more customers.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do you think of "San Francisco Bay Area cities are cracking down on free food at tech companies — here’s why that’s a good idea, according to a startup cofounder"?
Answer: Restaurants in the Bay Area are suffering because they can’t find enough employees who can afford to live there and work on a waitresses salary. Giving them more customers seems a poor fix , particularly ones use to getting food for free and will balk at going out if lunch starts to cost $20. Build more housing, then maybe we can talk about the restaurants. If you really want to create a vibrant downtown with lots of restuarants, build some tall residential buildings, make the first floor retail and restuarants. You don’t have to force corporations to operate against thier interests and you solve the real problem to boot.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is the best, tax minimizing way for my parents to give me ~100K to make the down payment on a mortgage (my income is enough to easily make payments, I just don’t have the cash on hand for the down payment)?
Answer: Your taxes could likely be minimized with a trust. The trust would be setup by your parents to purchase the house, you would be a beneficiary. You would make rental payments to the trust used to pay the mortgage. You wouldn’t own the house until your parents die. You may lose out on the mortgage interest and property tax deductions personally and it may have tax implications for your parents. Managing a trust gets complicated. This is something it is worth paying a financial advisor to guide you through the process and may have better suggestions that take in more context of your situation, but this is something you have options for significant savings with.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is the most demandable in the recent world, a web developer or a software developer?
Answer: A web developer is a software developer. A good software developer should be an excellent problem solver who uses the tools he is familiar with to solve whatever problem he is given. Almost always, that means learning something new in the process and even if not, learning a new tool often pays dividends. Now back to the question at hand, if a web developer is being distinguished as a separate thing from a software developer, that likely means they don’t want to or are incapable of taking on certain types of more general problems. They find some excuse why it’s not a problem for them. That’s not to say that a web developer should sign up to take on a well defined role to be a machine learning specialist , etc., but if a customer defines a product and machine learning will be part of delivering the best solution, a good developer will find a way to take advantage of the state of the art no matter where it takes him. My point is, a good web developer IS a software developer, a bad web developer, well I don’t know what to call that, but I don’t want to work with them and everyone else would likely be better served by just posting to Facebook or another existing platform. A web developer who thinks only in web technologies and not more general problem solving isn’t much use to anyone who wants a novel custom solution to a specific problem.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As a software engineer, can you transition your high-paying salary you earn in the Bay Area to another cheaper city without taking much of a hit in total compensation?
Answer: Base salary. Absolutely. The base salaries in Silicon Valley are more then most other tech hubs, but usually within the range of other positions. If you have a champion bringing you into another company and aren’t just cold calling, get a base salary match or even a bump should be quite doable. The equity is likely going to be a bit harder to match if you are at a top silicon valley name, but that would be true even if you moved laterally within Silicon Valley between companies. Of course, you have many more options that could offer comparable stock options in Silicon Valley, but there are also a lot of private companies that don’t have a liquidation path or a solid valuation to compare to. Silicon Valley also has more companies that are engineering first and tend to have much higher ranges for engineers, but move to another company that is engineering focused and compensation will tend to be similar. If you moved from say Facebook’s Silicon Valley office to Amazon’s Seattle office, you would likely not take a hit. Mid-size businesses in Silicon Valley, however, will often be competing fiercely with the big names in tech and will tend to offer much better compensation then you find in another mid-size business in say Austin or another tech hub. In my experience working both for east coast companies and in Silicon Valley, it matters more on the opportunity you are moving to more so then where they are located, but the best opportunities these days tend to be in high cost of living areas. So you will not take a hit if you find a similar opportunity, but good luck finding those outside of Silicon Valley.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Pandora considers my corporate browser too old, so I can't use it at work. Are they trying to go out of business?
Answer: Use your phone. If you don’t have Wifi at work, you can download and play offline. The better idea is to quit your job and stop working for a bureaucratic dinosaur. Your employer is who should go out of business, not Pandora.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Do you think progressive income tax rate can be viewed as a form of punishment for being relatively more successful than others?
Answer: Of course. The only thing you did was make more money and now you getter bumped into a less desirable tax bracket. That’s punishment. The thing is, it’s not a very effective punishment. It stands very little chance of actually disincentiving earning more income the way it is structured. Even at the highest rate, you still get to keep most of what you earn and those higher rates only kick in for those earning extraordinary amounts of money. People whose jobs are far from hourly compensation. They make money by delivering a product or service or closing a sale. In the vast majority of cases your income isn’t going to be tied to how much overtime you worked, but more on how successful or lucky you were. Working less is only tangentially related to your earnings and not putting in the required level of work is often an all or nothing proposition. Even if you made the income tax rise all the way to 100%, those top earners would likely do all the same work as not doing so would jeapordize all thier earnings, not just the upper end.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Have tech workers ruined Silicon Valley?
Answer: No. The housing crisis is a California problem, not a Silicon Valley one. It is systemic and not something that you can blame easily on individuals on any side. The seeds for the current discord were set at the state level decades ago and would make for a great case study in unforeseen consequences from well intentioned voters. The housing crisis may be most acute in the Bay Area, but LA, San Diego, and all the big CA urban areas all have million dollar prices that are far in excess of what would be found in similar US cities. More to the point the suburbs surrounding them that usually provide relief for middle class families are as expensive and sometimes more so then they cities they surround. Although all growing cities tend to expand endive places to live, California’s urban growth problems are special and distorted by well intentioned laws that don’t balance growth. The problem becomes readily apparent when you visit the heart of Silicon Valley in Palo Alto and find it’s not a city, but it’s a community of single story single family homes with a couple of tall office buildings at its outskirts. The next town over is Mountain View which has the same issue and is home to Google and has 3 times the number of workers as it has residents. They are over an hour from the nearest city during rush hour and since they are suburbs, public transportation is not readily available for most people who have to drive through several miles of single family homes to get to a train station. All these problems are ultimately failures of a government supported by a complacent constituency who see direct benefits from the rules that cause the profound inequality, but casually ignore the indirect negative consequences that also come from them. There are several laws that cause this inequality. Prop 13 stops taxes from rising on long term residents, but that lack of downward pressure means they are no longer motivated to move when the area needs to become denser. Well intentioned environmental laws protect the many green spaces, but environmental reviews can be initiated by ordinary citizens with ulterior motives who simply don’t want any new construction by them and can drag out the costly permitting process. The lack of property taxes and pressure from NIMBYist residents who have unusually strong powers in California’s participatory democracy mean local politicians still find far more revenue and less resistance in building offices over housing. Quite simply the people who vote are likely to already have housing, while they don’t appreciate the traffic and other issues that the housing crisis exacerbates, they love watching the value of thier homes appreciate and enjoy living in a single family home with a large backyard with retail and commercial amenities that are more akin to denser cities. You don’t kill the goose that laid the golden egg when it bites a few neighbors, you simply find a way to have less neighbors! The government should establish zoning that keeps the amount of offices in check with the number of residences. This is a fundamental job of local government, not of tech workers. They should build transportation corridors that are surrounded by enough density to where public transportation can work as the area grows. This is simply how cities work and while getting people to adapt to changes that are caused by population increases is not easy, it is a well understood problem with great solutions that can work for everyone. Tech workers are attracted to the money and the jobs. If the workers weren’t wanted, all that would have to be done is simply make building offices harder. Those solutions may seem obvious, but I make no presumption that they are at all practical in California’s current legislative environment that is essentially deadlocked between homeowners who don’t want to see thier quality of life or home values decline at all and legislators who know the obvious things that must be done to correct the issue, but also know it’s a sure fire way to make enemies of thier most loyal and vocal voters, homeowners. If a dam collapses because it couldn’t support the predictable amount of water it was built to contain, you wouldn’t blame the water for causing it to fail. That’s just what it is suppose to do. Similarly, you can’t blame the tech workers for going to where the most interesting and lucrative jobs are, that’s just what they are suppose to do. The failure here is failure to account for the predictable outcome of what happens when you build more offices then housing.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why should foreign nationals in the US receiving public financial assistance for themselves or their children be permitted to send money out of the country?
Answer: Undocumented immigrants do not qualify for welfare, food stamps, Medicaid, and most other public benefits. Legal immigrants, presumably paying taxes already, cannot recieve any of these benefits until they have been in the US for at least 5 years. If someone that meets that criteria and they do happen to have large amounts of money they are able to send out of the country, they are most likely committing fraud which is illegal and those people are quite simply not permitted to do it. If it’s a small amount, then we’ll good for them. Those welfare payments rarely even cover necessities. They must have another source of income that’s not quite good enough to get them out of poverty, but at least the are working and forgoing some pretty basic things to help thier family back home. In any case, the sums we are talking about are both small and temporary as the vast majority of states have hard limits on how long you can recieve welfare for. Meaning, you will either use welfare as was meant to be used and find a job and start paying taxes again or not and either get kicked out of the country or welfare and probably both. If you are concerned about immigrants not working. Holding out a small carrot that forces work requirements To get them to actively search for work seems like a good idea. I don’t really care about how you spend the money. Micromanaging is never a successful strategy. If having more money to send home to rescue your family is what motivates you to start being productive, encouraging that seems like a great idea to me, the welfare is just the cost of doing business.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Can my employer request that I (a programmer) bring my own laptop? Isn't that part of the necessary tools I need for work?
Answer: That sounds wonderful. I once did some work for a major financial institution who had more money then common sense. They somehow thought it a good use of money to equip me, being a senior software engineer at the time, with an underpowered thinkpad that already had a couple of years on it at the same time as paying me for the hours I worked, or in this case, the hours I spent struggling to work. They didn’t give me administrator rights and locked it down so tightly I literally couldn’t do my job. I used my own PC to do most of the work, then would transfer my work to it to check into thier network. It was what I call stupid hell. They paid really well though and respected my work even if they didn’t listen to my opinions on thier equipment policys. That was the exception though. Most employers I worked for had fairly liberal equipment policies that would get you a decent machine, but still not quite up to par with what I would buy myself. In any case, most employers won’t let you use your own machine as it muddies the legal waters as to who owns the work product and more importantly whether they can access the machine and everything you do on it at any time. My guess is your real problem is this company is kind of shady and not paying you nearly enough where you don’t have to think twice about buying your own toys that you will use day in and day out for years. If that’s not the case and they are both paying you market wages and letting you bring your own machine, take advantage of the situation. The liability is on them. Its all gravy to you!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is the best way for a newcomer junior software engineer to get a software job in the Bay Area?
Answer: Move there. Then interview with local companies and network as much as possible. That gives you the best chance of success. Companies love convenient new hires who don’t need relocation and are much more likely to take a chance on interviewing a seemingly weaker candidate if they don’t have to fly them in. Also be sure to bring your “A” game and lots of relevant extracurricular projects, but I’m sure you already knew that part.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are some practical solutions to California's housing shortage?
Answer: Easy question. There is only 1 solution, albeit, with lots of ways to get there. Build denser housing around transportation corridors, enough to account for all the nearby offices the town has already and is zoned for.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How much does a nanny cost in San Francisco?
Answer: I have had several nannies in the Bay Area. The answer varies wildly between what you are asking of them and what you are offering. Generally expect to pay between $10 and $25 an hour in and around San Francisco, with $20 being a pretty typical amount for a typical nanny situation. $10 would be someone who you are generally offering something else. i.e. A full time live-in aupair who you also provide food and shelter to. Experienced nannies will charge a few dollars more if there are additional children and responsibilities like cleaning up after the parents. Hourly rate is also a very poor indicator of performance. It is very important for retention though.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is an average rent increase in Sunnyvale, CA? Should you expect to pay more every year?
Answer: No. Rent in Sunnyvale is relatively stable compared to home prices which have been going up 10% to 20% every year. Homebuyers in the area tend to see much more value in a home purchase then a renters see in living here as a substantial part of the value of a home here is based on speculative growth potential not simply as a nice place to live. Most workers who live in Sunnyvale can’t remotely afford to purchase a place at current market rates and rental rates are more tied to average incomes. That doesn’t mean it’s cheap to rent. Rent is now affordable only to high earning tech workers or those on comparable salaries, but it’s still an incredible deal compared to a mortgage on a typical single family home. A mortgage here can be 2 or 3 times the average rent and is getting worse. Unlike a typical market, rent is not tightly coupled to the rise in home values, but rather salaries, which don’t go up at the same rate. If things continue going well for the economy at about the same pace they have been, expect a rent increase every other year, maybe every 3 or more years renting from an individual. It will likely be around 5% and closely tied the inflation.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would a software engineer from 1998 fit in with a software team in 2018?
Answer: Yes, a good software engineer is a good software engineer. Software engineering is problem solving. The tools you use may change and gaining expertise in those tools is a significant challenge, but it’s also a typical one for even engineers who haven’t mastered time travel. The most important qualities in a good software engineer are timeless. Languages, libraries, and the state of the art are always in flux. This is the double edged sword of software engineering. It’s very easy to stand up something new and the cost of failure is thus very low so you can take on a new development paradigm quickly, see what’s its like and if not toss it out. And that’s what happens. Constantly. You are always learning. Or, more to this point, your existing library expertise continually becomes nearly worthless on a 2 or 3 year time cycle, not a 20 year one. The things that a developer lacking 20 years of progress has much of the same deficiencies as someone who simply has been working on a legacy project for the past couple of years. When I make hiring decisions, skills in the libraries we use are important. However, it’s not the top priority. if I interview a 1998 developer who can explain both the optimal and suboptimal ways to solve various algorithmic questions along with pros and cons of each then can go on to explain how to diagnose real world performance issues, he’s doing pretty well. Admit he will welcome the challenge to learning a completely new stack and he would stand a good chance of getting hired and doing just fine. Particularly if you compare that to a modern someone who can go pretty in depth on the intricacies of day to day implementaion of a particular library, but you ask them a question that shows problem solving initiative, like how do you diagnose and optimize slow running code in production and they respond with, that’s what the IT support team does or ask them what level of unit testing is appropriate and they respond with whatever my manager says and thier modern language expertise suddenly doesn’t hold the same charm. I want to work with engineers who can help me solve the problem, not with ones who only know how to configure existing solutions. That’s not a universal commodity among professional software engineers, despite that it is a fundamental requirement. A 1998 engineer who brings problem solving qualities in spades fits right in, even if he is rocking the starter jacket, Reebok pumps, and refers to things as “fly” a little too much.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why are there so few companies willing to train Entry Level software engineers?
Answer: Writing software is accessible to virtually everyone. Particularly any computer science student. All you need is a computer and the will power to complete a project or two. When I hear “entry level software engineer” it makes me think of a number of candidates I have interviewed and some I have had the displeasure to work with who simply completed all their classes as checkboxes on theIr way to get to a lucrative career. They have the requisite book smarts, but lack real world problem solving ability. In many fields, that’s acceptable as you simply can’t practice your craft outside of a professional and highly regulated environment. In computer science, that barrier barely exists. An entry level software engineer is someone who didn’t take advantage of the unique opportunities in the field of engineering that software development offers. A computer scientist can apply their craft to almost any personal or extracurricular problem as the cost of entry to starting a project is extraordinarily low. Unlike other engineering fields where you have to build stuff using expensive materials, using specialized equipment, and following strict safety protocols, in software engineering, the cost of entry is access to a computer. Failure is also often very low cost in production environments for brand new applications without user bases and opportunities are virtually limitless. In other words, the only thing stopping you from getting experience is a lack of desire to do so. If you want to point the finger at someone for not wanting to train you, just look in the mirror. You can get more than enough experience and knowledge you need on your own to ace an interview for a low level software developer. A little guidance here or there that you will get working in a professional environment is still helpful, but largely, if you want to be good at programming, you need to be good at self instruction. Those candidates are not that hard to find in individuals fresh out of school who make through a software engineering degree. Would you hire someone who has both had the skills and ample opportunity to practice something they say they want to spend the rest of their career doing , but lacked the motivation to do it?

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is San Jose such a shithole with such an extraordinary tax base and Silicon Valley right next door?
Answer: The tax base is only extraordinary in how unequal it is. San Jose is in California and it has prop 13 and oddly regressive income taxes. New residents get absolutely hammered with taxes as existing ones only pay property taxes on the amount they paid for a place which is often several times less then what it’s worth now. Income taxes are both state and local and rise with rising income. Those existing residents may also be making far less then what it would take to move into the area. All this equates to a highly variable tax base. Many areas are shitty because a great number of residents pay next to nothing in property taxes regardless of how much they make or what they do. It also applies to corporations and all those startups tend to lease thier space from a corporation that’s paying taxes on thier assess value in 1970. Corporations use to pay 50% of property tax revenues, it’s now closer to 25%. Quite simply areas are shitty because they have no money. Those new tech people may be paying through the roof to live thier, but 20% of the population can’t make up for the remaining 80% paying next to nothing. The area also struggles with a highly progressive agenda that sometimes prioritizes homeless shelters and generous government pension plans over things like fixing aging infrastructure.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What should San Francisco Mayor London Breed do about the anti-tech backlash that's becoming more disruptive in SF?
Answer: Build more housing! The backlash is driven by the extreme cost of living. Build high quality housing that is both dense and provides lush public amenities for both the existing residents and the new ones and it will solve all problems. The cost of living will go down and the quality of life will go up. The existing residents do fear change and are taking it out on tech, but if it wasn’t tech, it would be something else. The real problem is balancing the zoning out so that corporate development is kept in line with residential development. Dense housing where the jobs are means people walk to work instead of commuting and sitting in traffic. If done right, it means massive and well maintained green spaces paid for by development fees on high rises. It means lots of retail shops and amenities that will be attracted by all the consumers living and working nearby. Everybody likes good change and once you’ve built nice new things and make them accessible to everyone, they are adopted immediately and those decrying the apocalypse of change start preaching how the new way of life is the old way of life and should never be changed. Change is the key though. Do whatever you have to, but build enough housing to make it affordable, do it with quality of life in mind, and the unwashed masses will be happy.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do liberals feel about Bill Maher's suggestion that we might need a damaging recession to get rid of President Trump?
Answer: Trump’s policies have already had severe negative consequences on many of Trump’s constituents in certain rural areas that are as bad as a recession in that locality. (https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/many-maryland-watermen-deny-a-crab-crisis-is-trumps-fault-except-it-is/2018/05/07/0703a6c2-5205-11e8-9c91-7dab596e8252_story.html?noredirect=on ). Despite being both easy to trace directly to both Trump’s rhetoric and the policies he has implemented, those Trump voters still believe that Trump is better for the country and whatever harm is either the cost of making this country great again or the true source is some far fetched liberal priority that may have had some effect, but requires a significant and far fetched conspiracy theory to be true to create the magnitude of impact that is claimed. The simple fact is that politics is not simple. No decisions can be made in a vacuum and it really does take a wonky expert to explain where and why a lot of policies are bad for the prosperity of the country even if they satisfy an immediate desire. Belief in those experts doesn’t happen automatically and often times they are not exactly right. If the media does not take pains to honestly break down that subtlety and explain why it is relevant even if it hard to hear, the message is not going to get through. To answer your question, no consequences don’t matter to hard core Trump voters when they agree with the rhetoric that says otherwise. A recession will only matter to Trump voters if their trusted media sources explain it in a way that resonates with them and makes Trump part of the problem. That could happen if the recession effects certain monied interests who have power over conservative media sources and suddenly feel they will make out better with the highly liberal candidates the Democrats are running, but a recognition of your average Trump voter that Trump is the predominant source of the nation’s most pressing ills and not the resistance is not going to happen based on critical thinking based in reality. That being said, Trump just barely eeked out a win and he did it by flipping some traditionally democratic voters. They voted for him to give him a chance and because they had become disillusioned with the political machine. They aren’t so tied to his policy positions as they are to the idea he was an outsider promising great change. Trump actually has a bigger problem then creating a recession, he is presiding over a time of great economic success and despite that is failing to keep the voters at his margins behind him. A democratic wave is coming and we haven’t even seen the effects of his policies to a large degree. We don’t need a recession to get rid of Trump, nor are his true followers likely to be swayed by it. Presidential elections are won in this country by swinging the independents and by the believability of your rhetoric regardless of its truth. All we need is for Trump to continue blasting our inane statements on Twitter that strengthen the resolve of his base, but alienate those on the margins who voted for him because they expected him to govern. We may get a recession, but regardless, Trump has little chance of sticking around past 2020. He is a polarizing figure. Whatever harm or good he does will be looked at by his true followers as validation of his policy direction and backed up by highly partisan media sources. Conversely as we are seeing now, even during great economic times, his polling and support from everyone else is being driven away by his rhetoric and failure to deliver on a populist message that was suppose to drain the swamp and bring practical change.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If a computer programmer went back to 1983, would he be able to do anything special on the IBM PC? I.e. strictly software - must use only the hardware of the day.
Answer: The best programmers today, regardless of age are not linguists they are problem solvers. A talented new grad should have no problem figuring out the systems of yore with time. They will have to learn some new (old) tricks, but that is part and parcel to the trade. There has never been a time more volatile then now where success in technology is defined by how quickly you are able to learn and put to practical use new time saving languages and concepts. Yes the technology of 1983 will be foreign, but learning it will not. It may be frustrating, but so is learning the latest version of a hot new trend. If I went back to 1983, I would be able to build for what’s coming without guessing. Amazing in 1983 would be building a competent spreadsheet or word processing application and I know exactly what one looks like that has 30+ years of design iterations. Heck, I know the internet exists and everyone and thier mom wants it. I could be AOL before AOL and not make all the same mistakes. I could be google simply because I know competent search will crush categorization and walled off content plays. The greatest company of our generation are actually based on some really simple technology. Certain infrastructure has to be in place too, but that’s a solvable problem when you can garuntee there’s going to be a market for it. I know you seem to be asking the question from the point of view that learning antiquated computer systems is too hard. It’s not. Learning the syntactical nature of a system is easy for a programmer. Especially one that has a limited set of commands. The harder part is knowing how to put that to use to make a desirable product. Computer scientists can and do pick up languages and new architecture all the time. It’s not a fundamentally different mindset, you are problem solving using the available tools. Even today programmers are constantly resource constrained. Amazing is also not doing some tech demo that pushes the limits of your hardware. Truly amazing is technology that changes everyday lives. VR headsets were around in the 80s. They were amazing to see, but not to use.
