Building a tool that would allow you to instantly share your life with distant relatives very simply, aka Facebook, is truly amazing, technologically simple, and more an idea then sophisticated software. If I went back to 1983 I wouldn’t know a lot about the current hardware, but all of that is easy to learn. Computers come with manuals. The future though is unpredictable, but not for me and I would use that knowledge to build in 1983 what people actually want.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why don't we build park-like villages of 500-1000 square foot houses and give them to those who can't afford a housing?
Answer: Better idea. Why don’t we just build housing until it becomes cheap enough that anyone above the poverty line can afford? That means no matter how much you make housing will be cheaper. It’s a win win all around if your goal is to give everyone an affordable place to live. Giving stuff away for free simply creates different winners and losers. Sure it’s great for the person lucky enough to get one, but what about the guy who makes $1 too much. Maybe he makes rent every month, but just barely. Any type of accident or set back is going to devastate him though. He will now have the goal to make slightly less to qualify and those who did qualify certainly are going to want to stay under that limit. Government should come in and build shared infrastructure that’s open to everyone. Building private homes simply distorts a market that would naturally balance itself. This is not a hard problem, we simply need to build housing until it becomes affordable for anyone working the most menial of jobs full time. Doing anything else is stupid prior to fixing that issue.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I get blisters on the arches of my feet when I run long distances (I have kind of fallen arches). Do I need wider shoes?
Answer: The last time I got blisters on the bottom of my feet it was from the soles of my shoes being worn out. The shoes were less then a year old and otherwise looked pretty good. I didn’t notice it until I upped my run from 2 to 6 miles either. Inspect your soles see if the soles are faded or have a different texture where you got your blisters. I resolved my problem simply by replacing the soles.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: When will the current housing bubble finally burst?
Answer: The current housing bubble is driven by two factors more than anything else. A very high demand in metro areas where the jobs are and a lack of housing in those same areas. There is largely not a national bubble. Although some housing has far exceeded its peak during the last housing bubble around 2008 that’s only true in certain areas. Many rural areas and some lower demand cities have still not recovered from the last housing crisis. Housing is also being driven by a higher than average number of investors and speculative buyers who took advantage of an over correction during the last bust to buy up property at fire sale prices. They are less likely to be subject to foreclosure risk than an over-leveraged primary home buyer would be, but are also more likely to liquidate the property if they believe the investment potential over the next several years looks poor in comparison to other investments particularly if transient renters start leaving their properties in droves and can not be replaced. If you want to know when this housing bubble will burst, it will be less about whether owners can’t pay their mortgages and more about what will shift buyers to look for more value based properties in currently less appealing places. Right now metro areas, like the Bay Area, are extremely expensive and that expense is already driving out lower income residents at an increasing pace, however, high income workers are still attracted to the area due to the better opportunities and are more than able to make up for the massive exodus. Supplies are also still getting more, not less, constrained due to an inability to zone for housing relative to office space that makes only a small imbalance in incoming residents having a disproportionate effect on housing costs. This trend is true for almost all metro areas where housing prices are soaring and amplified in places where suburban sprawl took priority over denser, more walkable, and more livable cities. The cost in housing is rising directly with the unrestrained growth in office space in the same locations where residential housing is more constrained. This is unlike the previous bubble that was driven by unqualified buyers getting into the market and buying more housing then they could afford. This bubble is very much driven by a hot employment market and healthy companies with lots of cash at their disposal they can use to continue to grow. That means if you kill the jobs, you will also kill housing. Those same high income residents who recently moved to the high demand metro areas are also likely to have shallow roots and won’t have diversified reasons for staying. That may sound obvious… recessions always kill housing demand, but in this market, expect a recession to have greater then normal effect on housing. It still may not be as acute as the last housing crisis, but lots of investment properties will likely come on early after the signs of a prolonged recession become apparent and as rentals make up a greater portion of the market then that have in the recent past, existing residents are not as tied to high cost areas. The smart move for investors will be to sell in those high costs areas where values are at all time highs and buy up properties in low demand, but high value areas where the low income employees will be drawn and high income employees will no longer be tempted to leave to the major metro areas with fewer available opportunities. Houses in the bubble are out of whack with rental prices and out of whack with the intrinsic value that competing areas offer As to when that will actually happen, that’s hard to say, but we just paid for the past year of employment growth with debt financed tax cuts whether we needed it or not and can likely live off that at least until 2019, maybe longer, but over the next 5 years, the tax cuts for the middle class expire and if nothing else that is going to get politicians trying to do big things when we have no runway for failure. The tax cuts eroded the safety net and unlike every other developed country that is now paying off debt and positioning themselves for better long term stability, the US did the opposite and bought itself guaranteed volatility during the next down turn. There will be a recession at some point, it will be significant, and housing in the most volatile areas will see the greatest declines.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do rich people moving to San Francisco justify being a large part of the problem that forces out families who have lived there for generations?
Answer: The housing problems that plague the Bay Area are caused by both the lack of housing density and job growth. Both the world’s population and the nature of work has changed over time. Both of which are a direct result of decisions made by previous generations and progress in general. The problems that arise from those decisions are also just simply not things individuals are responsible for. They are a function of government regulation. The zoning, building codes, and tax incentives are what create the massive imbalance between housing and offices in the Bay Area. It is an eminently solvable problem and one as old as civilization itself. The reasonable solution does not require anyone to move out or to prevent anyone from moving in. It also does not require giving up quality of life. It does, however, require change and competent planning that forces quality of life to be factored in when creating new zoning. That does not mean limiting density. The more walkable a neighborhood becomes, the more people like living there. It does mean existing residents living on acreage they make relatively poor use of will have to move into newer and better housing that would be paid for by massive equity gains in thier existing residence. That being said that’s not how the Bay Area works. The new housing that is built is tempered by density limits and because of that walkable infrastructure is just not possible in most places meaning cars and commute times keep going up even with the small numbers of houses built. Existing residents are incentivized to stay exactly where they are even when there are better places closer to family and work by property taxes that may greatly escalate if they move. Still you can’t blame existing residents for making the decision to stay when it’s made vastly in thier financial interest to stay, nor can you blame the “rich” new residents for wanting to come here when a similar financial argument is made. The blame does fall squarely on the government and that government is a reflection of the people who vote. If you want to blame someone, blame those who were around in the 70s who voted for prop 13 and blame those who continue to make choices that may protect residences, but also force the government to get revenue from corporations who are more then happy to supply it to continue thier growth. Smart growth is possible and no one would be forced out if the decision was made to design the area in a way that accommodates all the people who want to live here and not simply acquiescing to those who are afraid of change, even if it is better for society. The “rich” new people are not afraid of change if they came here and gave up thier old life. They are not the ones who are supporting a government that is not balancing the needs of the area. They also make up a small portion of the voting population. They jusitify thier move here by knowing if existing residents really wanted a fix, it is solely on those residents to band together and make some obvious choices with regards to who should be in charge of urban planning.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would it look bad on the resume if a software engineer changes jobs every year for a decade?
Answer: Depends on the type of software engineer. I do mostly front end work and I complete most projects in 6 months to a year. That doesn’t mean they are done, but at that point the product team either realizes you built a fundamentally wrong product and need to rewrite it or you enter a maintenance mode and may take on new responsibilities or a new direction. In any case, it’s an opportunity to leave a job in a completed state. That’s certainly not the case everywhere, but working in the same project for several years is not a position that’s helpful no you grow and is usually not good for either the company or yourself. That doesn’t mean that job hopping every year is good, but in the right context it’s good. I have interviewed and hired quite a number of developers. I’m more surprised when I find someone with several years of experience and it’s all from one place. Still in either case, the first thing I notice is that in the first 5 minutes of the interview have you impressed me. If you have and you don’t majorly screw up on any of the other questions, you got the job. If we didn’t hit it off immediately, but you still did strong enough throughout the rest of the interview, I’m going to fall back to your resume and see if it syncs up with the person I interviewed. If you are a hopper and you seem desperate for a job and have any unexplained gaps between them, it’s not going to be a happy ending for you. If, on the other hand, you’ve jumped from job to job, tell me how you crave the challenge of new projects and learning new things and have a diverse skill set to prove it, it’s going to work in your favor. Especially if you are young. You should hop around early in your career, then gradually settle into a place that you know is pretty good. What does look bad is an early career where you had a decade at one job, then several more that you just couldn’t keep for more then a little time. I will also ask you what your long my term plans are and it will be more important that those are in alignment with our needs then what you have done in the past. In general my advice is, it doesn’t matter what is in your resume, assuming it’s relevant, so much as you have a compelling story that is highlighted by your resume and vice versa that fits in with the needs of the project you are being hired for.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How long would it take an experienced .NET web developer to learn ReactJS and Node.js?
Answer: You should be able to complete a hello world application immediately, but not understand it much. You should be able to slowly fumble your way through architecturally simple real world tasks within a week, be able to write and understand a reasonably complex application in about 3 months and at that point realize almost all of the dumb mistakes you made in the 3 months prior. The next two years will be about getting faster and writing more optimized and reusable code. Also realize that ReactJS and Node.js are fundamentally different things and not any more complimentary then say a ReactJS front end and a .NET restful services backend. You may use Node.js as an integral part of your build chain, but you don’t need much expertise in it to do that. My recommendation would be to use .net for the backend, if possible and react for the front end, then learn Node.js once you have a better understanding of JavaScript as learned through react.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As an early employee, I own a part of a startup that's about to IPO. These shares constitutes almost all of my wealth. As an aspiring conservative value investor of age 30, how much and at what rate should I sell off my shares after the IPO?
Answer: Sell all of it. There is one trick to being a good investor. It’s diversification. The current direction of the stock does not matter. Intrinsic value and every other metric that so-called experts tout is dwarfed by being properly diversified. Stop looking at charts and past performance, those are for different questions. Investment advice on what and when to trade is for help on which stocks you should invest the small fraction of your income on and you should have multiple stocks across a broad range of categories. Talk to an accountant who can help you figure the best way to minimize the tax implications when selling, that may effect when you want to sell, but you do want to sell and sell as soon as possible. If you still want to be invested in a risky new IPO stock after selling, buy similar stocks in similar categories with a small fraction of your assets. Unless you are an executive and can take advantage of some inside knowledge, there is no benefit to you being overly invested in your employer. Assuming you want to continue working there, you will continue to be defacto heavily invested in the company by your salary. Everything else should be sold and diversified.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why didn't all Bay Area "natives" buy when homes were $75K/$175K/$275K? In prime locations or any location for that matter instead of getting priced out now?
Answer: Because it was a really poor investment relative to investing in something like Apple stock at that time.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why are Democrats against a merit-based immigration?
Answer: They aren’t. In 2013, Democrats fully supported the Border Security, Economic Opportunity, and Immigration Modernization Act of 2013 - Wikipedia It passed the senate with the support of all democratic senators and a small minority of Republican ones. It would have increased border security by adding up to 40,000 border patrol agents. It also would have advanced talent-based immigration through a points-based immigration system. That sounds pretty reasonable to me and hardly a bleeding heart liberal bill. The bill failed because the Republican led congress never scheduled it. Democrats would gladly accept a shift towards more merit based immigration and literally have done just that in the recent past, however, they are loathe to just accept any old bill if it means decimating the existing immigrant population and a shift to a merit based system that results in a net loss of working immigrants particularly at a time when unemployment is at near all time lows. Trump won on a platform that focused on the concept that immigrants were taking away American jobs. He is unapologetically xenophobic. The administrations actions thus far have been more about securing the border and making sure that fewer immigrants get through then making sure more of the right immigrants get through. I’m a little skeptical Democrats are the ones who don’t want more immigrants working here. The leader of the Republican party called immigrants murderers and rapists in general without being very careful to qualify the statements. That’s not the type of statement that’s going to build trust, particularly when your average illegal immigrant is less likely to be the perpetrator of a violent crime then your average US citizen. He followed that with promises to build a bigger wall, then as an after thought, tosses out the idea to move to a merit based immigration system. It’s pretty clear the intent isn’t to control immigration to optimize for the talent based needs of the country, but rather use it as a means to control immigration to appease those who see immigrants as the cause of the cultural as well as economic decimation of this country. “Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses, yearning to breathe free.” That is what is is inscribed on the Statue of Liberty. That may be a bit dated, but it’s still what I want to think makes this country great. That doesn’t say it has to be a free ride and and making capable immigrants work is fully compatible with that, but if you are going to change immigration to exclusively be “Give me your active, your greedy, your individuals without baggage, yearning to make a quick buck. Everyone else need not apply.” I’m a little hesitant that’s an improvement over the massively broken immigration system we have now and seems down right unamerican.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Did Obama actually think the Obamacare penalty would help make healthcare affordable, or does he just not want me to have a tax refund?
Answer: You are confusing affordable for you with affordable for society in general. Obamacare was initially designed to both tackle cost and coverage, however, by the time it passed through congress the things that would introduce major cost controls were largely whittled down to toothless provisions. There was still hope it would produce meaningful savings for all participants in the healthcare system, but anyone who took an objective view of what was left would have little belief it would do anything more then simply control cost growth at best. Obamacare, as implemented, was a play for better coverage for healthcare, not cost. It was to make healthcare affordable for those with preexisting conditions and those too poor to afford insurance, but too “rich” to qualify for existing healthcare services. It was not targeted at controlling costs of our healthcare system in general despite being advertised as such and having that as an early goal. Along those lines, Obama was thinking, when Obamacare passed that he would bring the US into line with almost all other developed countries in offering universal coverage for its citizens. It did well on that front and reduced those without coverage by more then half and would likely get even better if the individual mandate wasn’t repealed and other provisions weren’t gutted by the Trump administration. As to whether he wanted YOU to not get a tax return, that’s kind of a secondary concern. What we do know is he didn’t want YOU to go bankrupt if you came down with a serious ailment and to be able to afford insurance no matter your income level. The individual mandate is how we ensure no one is doing something profoundly stupid and does not have catastrophic coverage. Obamacare largely didn’t address cost and we still need to do that. Repealing the individual mandate isn’t going to help with that. Neither will single payer or most of the big ideas the democrats are talking about now, but they may put you on a path where controlling costs becomes easier. The big problem with healthcare costs is that even though it is private, it is not market based. It is almost impossible to shop for care when costs really matter. The provider you go to is the one who is in network. If there are multiple, you still can’t really make an informed decision as costs, in most states, are not transparent and in many cases, like emergency rooms it is actually illegal to advertise prices as in the 80s some ERs told impoverished patients the exorbitant prices they might have to pay to get care there when they didn’t want to Treat someone they didn’t think would be able to pay them. Similar things happen with prescription drugs. You have to buy the drug you are prescribed even when there are cheaper alternatives unless you consult your doctor again, which isn’t a convenient thing to do. On top of that, the drug companies actively work against any type of competition based cost controls by offering things like copay coupons that will reduce the drug price the patient sees even when the price the insurance company pays may be ten times what a perfectly acceptable alternative might cost. There are simple solutions to these problems, but they will require drastic changes and upset those who are making tremendous profits right now. In any case, the individual mandate is the price you pay for universal healthcare. There are other ways to pay it, but YOU, as a US citizen have to pay something. Access to healthcare is really a bare minimum to being a developed country these days. That being said healthcare costs are really fucked up in this country. Complaining about Obamacare is a witch hunt though. You should be complaining about the cost of care and ask the government to reduce that. How they achieve that should be immaterial as long as your costs get cheaper.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As far as freelancer marketplaces go (for a freelancer to list themselves on), would you recommend Fiverr, Upwork, or a competitor, and why?
Answer: You try them all and figure out which platform your mojo works best on or, better, maintain a presence on all the platforms that are worth your effort. The buy-in is ridiculously low and they are not mutually exclusive. If you are highly skilled and price to the market, you will eventually have too much work. At that point you can be more choosey about where you spend your time and optimize for a single platform that has been the most lucrative. I do tend to find upwork has bigger projects and Fiverr seems better for smaller tasks, but that’s not a hard and fast rule.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is socialism so popular with young Americans even though it worked nowhere?
Answer: You are watching too much fox news. Get out in the real world and actually talk to someone young. I have never heard any statement uttered to the effect that we should get rid of all privately owned companies and let the government handle all means of production. By anyone in the real world. Not even anything remotely suggesting that. There is perhaps no more universal belief in this country among both young and old that it should be based on capitalism. You need to realize it is perfectly acceptable to believe the government can do better and more then it is doing now and still believe in capitalism. Regulation and capitalism are not mutually exclusive. They go hand in hand. Regulation ensures a smooth running economy over the long term. If that’s not a goal of capitalism, I don’t know what is. The young people I met simply think the government can control excessive pursuits of profit at the expense of society better then the market will self regulate. That’s a really painfully obvious common sense statement. If you want to have a legimate discussion, it needs to be on where the line should be on that regulation. You are the only one talking about socialism and, as a young person, it’s hard to relate to you when you start talking about such crazy things.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What companies in Silicon Valley are welcoming older software engineers?
Answer: That’s a complicated question. It’s not that Silicon Valley companies don’t like older engineers. When you are going to be paying upwards of $300k for an individual, you want some garuntees that they are a good investment and there is no better predictor for future success then past success doing a similar thing. The problem is that older engineers already have families. They have kids in school and likely have become accustomed to certain way of life. In Silicon Valley, a spouse and 2 kids is a $2 million problem. Telling someone that you will pay them a lot more money, but when they do the math to live in the area, it means thier kids will have to suddenly share a room, their commute will at least double, and their discretionary income will now be based 100% on equity and the performance of a company that they only have tangential control over, it suddenly doesn’t seem very welcoming. There are many older engineers in Silicon Valley. They came here right out of college and found a way to scrape together the money while living cheaply as a single person. Several years of compromise that would be unacceptable for someone raising a couple of kids, isn’t too bad when you have the flexibility of not having the baggage that comes with living your life for a decade or two after graduating. They built highly successful careers and used them to get around the earlier compromises. They then buy in when the getting is good. There are many older engineers here and they are well respected in thier roles and have many opportunities and head hunters knocking down thier doors. The hiring in Silicon Valley is not age biased, the cost of living is!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What JavaScript book would you recommend to someone who understands just the basics of the JavaScript language?
Answer: I would recommend war and peace. It’s just the right height to use as a stand to put your monitor on while you get to coding. If you understand the basics already, you should be doing. When you come to something you don’t know how to do, you google the answer, then get back to work. Get a couple small projects under your belt, then pickup a framework like Angular or React. A book might be more important here as you will want to understand more abstract architectural concepts that won’t become clear when building on your own until you get into some very advanced situations. The tutorials do a pretty good job at getting the practical usage down, but understanding the theory behind it explained in a book will make it go down easier. Quite honestly, there is no practical middle ground for JavaScript knowledge though. You need to know the basics and once you are an expert coder, you will want to know in depth how JavaScript works to properly optimize things, but it’s unimportant for your average junior developer to make progress.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What can the pro-housing movement offer existing homeowners to get more of them on board?
Answer: Existing homeowners are already PRO housing. The majority of existing homeowners in hot housing markets are in the same boat many renters find themselves in. Their problems may not be as acute as they don’t have to worry about escalating rents and certainly enjoy the rising value of their investment, but unaffordable housing prices also effect them greatly. Over time their incomes have increased along with their families and need for more space, however, the increase in household income has not been nearly enough to ever let them move up to a more accommodating place. They bought in, but they now have golden handcuffs. Everyone hates traffic and when you are stuck in a home, you are far less able to adapt to new traffic patterns or a more remote job. Quite simply, you don’t have to offer most home owners anything to get them on board with building more housing. It benefits them all the same as those who don’t own homes, albeit in slightly different ways. What you do have to get them on board with is that the new housing will improve their quality of life, not diminish it. The problem with the pro housing movement is that it is almost always championed by those who simply want more housing and their approaches come off sounding like that out weighs all other needs. That’s not really always true, but it does turn off existing homeowners who suddenly find themselves in a position where they may be stuck in a house that is depreciating in value, next to a high rise, with even more traffic then they have now. The YIMBY movement in particular, makes NIMBYs out to be greedy, self centered individuals. When really most just want to make sure whatever gets done, improves the quality of their neighborhood. What most home owners would be happy with is more housing options that increase the quality of their current housing while also offering more options to move to a more accommodating place. All of that is in favor of building more housing. What it comes down to is making an argument for building more towards quality of life then just simply building. That shouldn’t be hard. People are drawn to density. They like the amenities that having lots of people around affords. Per capita, cities are more environmentally friendly and mean you don’t have certain expenses like transportation and lower electricity bills. There are also some major drawbacks that come with that, but the good outweighs the bad. Why else would cities attract so many people at the really high prices they are at. That’s not always true though and change is hard. Cities are also associated with slum’s, terrible schools, wasteful spending, and lack of green spaces. It doesn’t have to be that way and some cities have found very good paths to growth that are just universally better. If you want to convince home owners and really everyone, that building more is a good idea. You need to make what your selling as better for everyone. That means sensible building that emphasizes walkability, green spaces, and balanced building codes. You offer density bonuses for things that improve quality. It should mean you take out the junkyard across the street and replace it with both amenities for the existing home owners and lots of places to live for the new ones. The schools should get better, not worse. The traffic should get better, not worse. Being outside should get better not worse. If the pro housing movement wants to appeal to everyone, they just have to stop making it about more housing and start making it about better housing. Don’t build housing to allow new residents to live there, you build denser for the benefit of everyone. The argument that others want to live here doesn’t really hold weight. The argument that you can bring others here and together they will make this a better place for everyone to live does.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do you like and dislike about Gavin Newsom for governor of California?
Answer: I like that he recognizes California is in a critical housing crisis. I dislike that all of his plans lack aggressiveness and bite. Hes put together a list of sound bites that won’t piss anyone off, but also won’t do much to make an impact. We need to take on prop 13. Even starting with the easy wins like no more subsidizing corporations, secondary homeowners, or those with high incomes through generous property tax breaks. Zoning needs to be reformed and public transportation needs to simultaneously be implemented on a regional level that will allow us to give up our cars the closer you live to the city. He needs to find a way of combating the polarization of NIMBYs vs YIMBYs and focus on quality in people’s backyards regardless of density that is appealing to everyone. Newsom needs to grow a pair and think bigger. The housing crises is immune to business as usual. He needs to look at Toronto and follow thier plan that makes people want to move to the big cities not just because the jobs are there, but because they present an affordable way of life with walkable amenities and smart building that gets both density and quality of life right.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Do you think a top exec at Amazon, Apple, Google or Facebook would ever leave to co-found a start-up with someone that's not in the SV (Silicon Valley) circles? How would you approach them?
Answer: Just like an investor, you need to convince them you have an idea that has real potential to be worth 100x thier investment. When you are talking about people making 7 or 8 figures a year and asking them to invest the next several years of their life, that means you need not just a $100 million idea, but a $10 billion one. You literally need to convince them you really do have the next Facebook. Now I’m sure that your idea is brilliant, but Facebook wasn’t so creative as much as it was broadly and instantly appealing for the time it was created in. No amount of words or even nifty demo could convince a person that Facebook was even just a real MySpace competitor. The one and really only reason it generated so much early interest from Silicon Valley insiders was it went viral and had the metrics to prove it. It was already built and working. The heavyweight help comes after you have already proven your idea to help scale it, not to build the first iteration. Now you know what you need, there’s only one step left before you can walk into an executive’s office and have a chance of him quitting his job and walking out with you. You need to build your idea give it to at least 10 users and overnight or in a pretty short time frame see it spread to at least a 1000 users. There’s lots of ways that you can do this, but it is going to be just you or just you and a couple people who already just trust you and can help you out for a minimal amount of thier time. You don’t have to build the actual product. Just an ad describing it or build anything that plays off the same emotions and can be tracked to show it being virally shared. No, before you ask, that’s not what the executive is going to be able to help you do. The when, who, what, and where of what you build is going to be critical to your product going viral, but no one can tell you exactly what that is, at best an expert could offer some advice on what’s probably a bad idea, but when you are talking about a revolutionary product, even that is hard to predict. You are likely going to have to build and test something several times before you find the right combination that anyone will really care about hearing about.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do tech startups still so heavily favor the highly taxed San Francisco and New York City areas, even though the internet connects us everywhere and the low/no taxes plus low-rents of other states offer a substantial financial advantage?
Answer: They don’t… its kind of the other way around. The area heavily favors founders. It takes a lot of time and money to see a startup through to its conclusion and it is an effort that is usually a massive loss for the founders. While you may see the most expensive places in the country as a bad place to start a company you are trying to run with your own money on a shoe string budget, the ones who are most likely to be able to be both financially qualified and skilled enough in tech to succeed at a startup tend to already live in those areas. What’s more, both those areas are defined not so much by the expensive prices, but, in this case, by the massive inequality between the people who live there. The median income relative to the cost of living may put more people in poverty then almost anywhere else in the nation, but that doesn’t tell you that those who are doing well are doing exceedingly so. The Bay Area in particular has been on an inequality tear lately. Housing prices have more then doubled in the past five years in what was already an expensive area. Due to California’s very peculiar and highly regressive property tax scheme, it means founders who purchased their home several years ago don’t have to worry about the rising cost of living. The lucky ones are also likely sitting on massive piles of equity that rose along with housing in the area and have had a double windfall that lets them have paid off their home and have a them have a very favorable tax scheme that belies the fact they are occupying some of the most expensive land in the country without having to worry about a comparable income stream to support it. If you were doing well in your job a few years ago, things are fantastic for you now. Those people can become founders with hardly batting an eye. They may be building their startup out of their garage, but it just happens to be a multimillion dollar garage with no expenses on it. The area is also rich with investors and having lived in and built a network and reputation in an area means when you do need cash and resources, you don’t have to waste as much time seeking out investors or proving your ability to them. The same goes for early workers who likely already know the founder and are flush with cash from the same exit that gave the founder the ability to strike out on his own to pursue the dream. Additionally since a startup is likely hemorrhaging lots of cash for the founders, the income tax doesn’t really matter. That’s not to say its all smooth sailing, your startup is going to have to sink or swim by the time it gets to 10 employees when you will need real office space and super inflated salaries to pay the grunts that will take you to the next level. That’s when you discover why growing a startup in an expensive area is a terrible idea, but the hardest part is getting started and showing initial exponential growth. If you have done that, investors will pay exorbitant amounts of cash to fuel the next level, because you have already proven you know how to 10x an idea. Paying a 2x cost seems like an inconsequential thing to do when you are pursuing a 100x rise in value. Still, I think your conjecture is a bit flawed. Startups aren’t really flocking to Bay Area or NYC now. It’s a stupid place to move to to build a tech company, particularly one that can be built virtually. A starving founder could no longer afford to even rent a garage in Silicon Valley. Startups, however, are still just born there naturally. It is a really great place to be born too, but only if you already have the means to be self sustaining and the cost of living is a non-existent issue for you. Inequality is a bitch. The most expensive areas of the country aren’t home to more startups then anywhere else because they are expensive, the most expensive areas of the country are home to more startups because that’s where the rich tech people who can afford to start them already live.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why did Apple abandon the Aqua interface design? Are end users left unsatisfied about the result? I found the interface incredible at that time.
Answer: Traditional user interface design is mostly art and tends to be subjective. However, user experience design is more of a science. User experience design is about analytics and using an iterative process to see what impacts a particular design has on how well users are able to interact with and perceive what is going on in a particular user interface. My guess is Apple hopped on the user experience design band wagon. I don’t have any particular insight on why the design team at Apple specifically moved away from the Aqua UI style, but I can tell you it fundamentally violates a couple design standards that current state of the art user experience guidance provides us with. It’s pretty clear they started to think a lot more about the little things about how users will perceive the minutiae of a user interface. In general, a good user experience says less is generally more when talking about stylistic only elements. Gradients, shadows, gel like appearances, brushed metal effects, etc. They certainly can look cool, but they are an unnecessary complication if they don’t actually provide any context to the user. By making all buttons have these cool looking doodads and sophistication, it makes it harder for things you truly want to emphasize to stand out. Text is harder to read on a textured background and draws your focus to things that may not be important. Early user interfaces also focused on making things look like their analogous real world counterparts, like a circular dial for a volume control. That is most like what a user would see in the real world and is certainly immediately intuitive to a use, but it’s also not as easy to use with a mouse. A vertical slider is both intuitive and easy to use even if it does have a uniquely virtual look. Everything should have meaning. If you are going to use a gradient, it should be to emphasize part of a user interface in a way that helps the user. That doesn’t mean you can’t also have style, but style should always be secondary to usability. Apple’s move away from the Aqua interface was one that seemed to follow the greater industry trend of moving to flatter simpler looking interfaces that put function over form. People get tired of looks, no matter how good they are if they become frustrating to use. No one ever gets tired of good usability.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How good should a front-end developer be, if he claims to have 4 years of experience?
Answer: He should be expert level in his chosen language and frameworks. He should be able to answer every basic question on the specific workings of those things he has expertise in. He should be able to answer advanced general questions and give you a very specific answer in his chosen framework that eloquently answers it. He should be able to talk about performance and how to achieve it. What you need to optimize and, more importantly, the things that you don’t need to waste time on. He should know HTML, javascript, SASS or LESS, and CSS. He should know at least one major javascript framework and familiarity with a build system like grunt, gulp, angular, etc. and how to combine with a CLI like jenkins. He should be able to prove his depth in all those things. He should have opinions on what the best debugger and development tools are and why he thinks that. He should be able to provide you with anecdotes of where they have failed him and where they have saved him. In short, he should be at peak performance in terms of grinding out code in his core frameworks and language.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Golang vs NodeJS vs Python? I am currently working to improve my knowledge and skill to become a back-end developer. Which should I focus more and why?
Answer: All of those languages are actively used so I wouldn’t say any one was a bad choice, but there may be a better choices and better ways to make a choice. First you need to figure out what you want to do on a little more specific level then just back end developer. One way would be to look for places you want to work at with job openings. They will describe the relevant skills they are looking for as well as give you a clue as the types of projects that would be open to you. You could also pick a side project to build on your own and try it in all three languages or look for relevant examples for similar things of what you are wanting to build and pick that one that comes the easiest. In any case, pick a more tangible goal first and your choice should get much clearer.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Are Christians frowned upon in Silicon Valley?
Answer: Do you use blind faith to as a way to justify your positions and lecture others on proper moral conduct? Do you have a hard time accepting logical conclusions or abstract, but well validated scientific evidence that directly contradicts positions laid out in the Bible? If you answered yes to any of those questions, you will have a hard time making it in tech circles in Silicon Valley. Christians in general are not ostracized. Far from it. There are 8 churches in Mountain View alone, the city that has more people who work there for Google then people that live there. Christians are a diverse group within themselves. If you are a tolerant one and use the religion more as a guide then an absolute way of life, you will be in good company. Start spouting off that using contraception is a sin and others who use it are going to hell or try to win an argument on the historical accuracy of certain miraculous events in the Bible and you may find your friends start to disappear.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What income should I target in Silicon Valley to live a middle-class life if I have a family of 6 people?
Answer: There is no income that a company will pay you here that will let you live a middle class lifestyle for a family of 6. You can compromise or roll the dice that someday you may strike it rich through the equity lottery or hope for a repeat of the past housing crashes that doesn’t also crash you, but the middle class career that gets you to middle class homeownership for a family of that size is a white elephant. The middle class here is a dying breed, kept alive by prop 13 that lets existing residents live here without being Uber wealthy, but it’s not going to help you as a new resident. California has indirectly decided it has all the families it needs and no place can that be seen more evidently then in Silicon Valley. The 5 bedroom houses now rent to 5 tech bros all pooling thier resources. Just let me save you the trouble, it’s no longer a solvable math problem for your average middle class worker. If you are not rolling in wealth already or coming here because you have been aquihired with a multimillion dollar equity grant, you are not going to be on a path to a middle class lifestyle.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why are employers these days starting to be employee-friendly, employee-caring and employee-supportive in ways that they weren't earlier?
Answer: Where do you work? Employers use to pay a salary that grossed, in a single year, half of what was needed to buy a reasonable house for you, your spouse, and your two kids. Employers use to offer pension plans that would offer a defined benefit that would allow you to retire at a certain age no matter how much longer you lived. Employers use to be located in places that were a 15 minute commute, at the worst, from where you would want to and be able to live. The employers you speak of are taking in record breaking profits and passing lots of it to share holders. Some of that goes to employees, but it’s not spread out evenly and only tangentially ties to work effort. In Silicon Valley today, the place that has the reputation for “employee friendly” workplaces that your question evokes. The salaries may seem high because everyone else in the nation makes less on average, but the median salary of $125k is more then 10 times less the median cost of housing that’s within an hour of work. There are no pension plans. The 401k plans can be generous, but still if you plan on living to a ripe old age and continue living in the place you raised your kids, you are going to need savings beyond the maximum contribution and that’s going to be based on equity with a roll of the dice. Silicon Valley is not alone either. The world's top jobs have urbanized. That’s not a problem on it’s own, but NIMBYism, suburban sprawl, and simply poor planning and a lack of funding have made many cities a bastion of inequality. Employers didn’t create that problem on thier own and even complain about its existence, but they aren’t making the hard choices to address it head on and continue to feed it. Sure, you may get free lunch, massages, and busses to work, but that seems of relatively low value compared to a time when you could purchase a large house in a good school district on one spouse’s salary and be home within time to see your kids before bed. That’s not to say previous generations didn’t have hardships that we couldn’t even imagine living with today, but despite tremendous advances in technology and productivity people are working more for a lesser quality of life. Your question shouldn’t be why employers are giving these benefits that they weren’t before, progress should be shared amongst the world’s people. Each generation should have it easier and certainly not regress if we can help it. No matter your political orientation, I think everyone agrees that fair work should have a fair payoff and these fringe benefits are trying to make up for an unfair system… on the cheap. The question should be why are we ok with losing fundamental benefits that previous generations worked so hard to get instead of supplementing them with a new easier way of life for all that technology should make possible? Looking at where the money is going, it’s pretty clear the world has not been getting intrinsically harder to live in. Technology has made life easier. However, since the 80s more and more of the world’s productivity gains have been going to a smaller percentage of people at the top. You have to look no further than how employers reward work to see the impetus for this change urged on by favorable tax policy that doesn’t discourage employers from treating lower level employees inequitably. I would not say the defining quality of the benefits of working in the modern era are these fringe things employers are offering. The inequality is. Employers are giving more fringe benefits these days because it’s far cheaper and easier than addressing the real problems associated with how the nature of work has evolved in the modern world. It is hardly what I would consider more supportive to give you free food while ignoring that you don’t have a stable place to live. Not that fringe benefits are a bad thing and are far from universal. Many employees don’t get them and are certainly far worse off, but when your average new employee at one of the world’s preeminent companies comes to work and a typical career path gives them zero chance of ever affording a place of thier own, I would expect an employer that cares about its employees to see that as a untenable situation and move mountains to make it right, not simply find more and more creative ways to hire more people to come and find the same exasperating situation.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If democrats campaign on repealing this year’s tax cut will liberals vote for them because they don’t want lower taxes?
Answer: I’m 25+ years away from retirement. I live in a high tax stake. I make a decent amount to be taxed at a high rate, but not nearly enough to see the windfalls the top 0.01% will see. The tax “cuts” give us a trillion dollar deficit at a time when we should be taking advantage of the economy to pay down debt, not finance luxuries for already profitable businesses. Social security is on a death spiral and we are on track to pay more then 50% of all descretianry spending to debt service. The tax cuts are not paid for. It is a loan the baby boomers have taken out and passed onto thier children. I will vote democratic because I want to pay less in taxes over my lifetime and avoid the costs of financial mismanagement. I want those trying to pass on thier debt so they can retire wealthy to pay thier fair share. I don’t care if taxes are high or low, what I want is value from how my money is spent. Taxes that get me good schools and a stable middle class lifestyle with robust support structures to support me is money well spent. The Republican tax plan robs the government I rely on of the revenue that’s needed to sustain middle class living and uses it to pay those gaming the system and not paying thier fair share. Many government entities are horribly bloated and need reform. Robbing them of money does not make them nimbler, it simply takes away all the good and leaves only the most disfunctional parts that are willing to cheat to stay afloat. I would vote Republican if thier policies were aimed at cutting costs by making government services more efficient, instead tax cuts are down without thought to whether the revenue was being spent efficiently or not. I will vote democratic because they know that tax cuts have the be paid for and the ones we just got are going to cost me way more over the next decadethen they are worth now.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Will the housing market crash in the Bay Area any time soon?
Answer: It is a crazy time to be buying in the Bay Area. It’s been ridiculous levels of expensive relative to the median income for some time, but what really tells you about sustainability is how much people are willing and able to pay to live there. The cost of owning is approaching 40 times the yearly rent on some properties (10401 Phar Lap Dr, Cupertino, CA 95014 | Zillow). That says to me the market is not based on what people are willing to pay to live here, it’s based on speculation and the idea prices will see much further growth. There are so few homes on the market here relative to buyers, it doesn’t take much to fuel it though. The converse of that is you only need to scare off a scant few buyers and you will suddenly find the market for people who actually just want a place to call home is far below where those speculators are and happy to rent a place for half of what the mortgage would be. All that tells you is that despite the current demand being exceptionally strong and the ability of current homeowners to afford the places they are buying, which are the typical signs of stable housing market, there are fundamental things wrong with the market that make it unsustainable. It will crash. You asked when it will crash though. That’s also easy, it crashes and crashes hard in the next global recession. Companies will stop hiring and lots of current high earning residents who suddenly see thier equity tanking will no longer find it worth it. People will move out and won’t be replaced. Rents will drop first, housing goes next. The smart speculators will sell off early causing a precipitous drop months later. That’s not a date though. A date is hard, but the good economic times the US is currently experiencing is a house of cards. We our debt financing luxuries. Rather then paying down the national debt and running a surplus, we gave tax breaks to corporations who are currently taking in the cash hand over fist. That bill comes due in the next 5 years. We are likely to see confidence wane well before that as the obvious starts to take hold in the minds of the American public. If the democrats take back the house in 2018, it’s going to destroy any confidence in the current administration to get anything done. My guess is we get a recession before 2019 if that happens and if not then, 2020 seems prime for a correction. You have at least a year, but likely 2 to 3 and at most 5 before you see a major correction.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is there anyone who still enjoys living in the Bay Area? All the forums have a lot of negatives and talk about people moving away in droves.
Answer: Of course. The negatives of the Bay Area are driven by profound inequality. The haves here have it really good at the expense of everyone else. If you are lucky enough to call yourself a homeowner, congratulations, the average equity in your home went up by more then the average worker grossed in income from working. On top of that, your property taxes raise at less then the rate of inflation so you get a built in raise every year too just for staying by at home, doing nothing. Yeah, the traffic sucks for everyone, but less so for those who live in a single family home that’s walking distance from amenities you would only find in dense urban areas elsewhere. What’s more, California’s constitution gives ordinary citizens substantial veto power to determine what gets built in their town. If you are a renter, all those things make it so you can barely make ends meet on large six figure salary. That sucks and sucks more knowing that the substantial taxes you pay don’t go to making CA this liberal Mecca where everyone gets treated equally, but instead goes to a fortunate few of the previous generation to subsidize thier own homes that are larger then what you could ever dream of affording here. Lots of people do better in the Bay Area then they would anywhere else in the nation. It has great weather, great jobs, lots of things to do, and suburban living that is comfortable, but defies all societal sensibilities. The Bay Area has few downsides when you don’t have to worry about the cost of living. Unfortunately, if you want to fix the bad things you are going to have to tear down some of the things causing the inequality that some people love.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is Stormy Daniels even an issue? It was prior to his presidency. What about Clinton/Lewinsky?
Answer: Clinton / Lewinsky was the thing that got a president impeached. It was partisan and it really came down to judgment call in Clinton’s character. Clinton never really had a sterling reputation as an upstanding family man, but he kind of played one on TV. Lewinsky shattered that image for anyone not watching too closely before, but still it wasn’t a huge shock. That is even more true for Trump. This is the same Trump America knew when they voted for him. No one in their right mind is going to be surprised at the revelations involving infidelity that comes out of the Stormy Daniels trial. The direct facts of the case are salacious, but are likely not going to matter much, even if Trump loses the case. What the real issue for Trump is discovery that happens during the trial. Clinton’s problems started during the trial at which he was sued by Paula Jones. Clinton won that trial, but during it, he made some incorrect statements under oath that later became the primary impetus for his impeachment. Trump has led a notoriously secretive presidency. He never released his tax returns, he has substantial financial ties to Russia and countless other countries and organizations, and his blind trust is run by his children whom he communicates with very frequently. He is also an amatuer politician. Trump may be a media spin doctor, but government officials have to stand up to not just extraordinary public scrutiny, but legal ones as well and Trump is definitely dancing with disaster with his devil-may-care attitude. Whether any of the things he is hiding are illegal is one thing, but he almost certainly has things that fall into a grey area and won’t be very flattering, particularly for a guy who ran on a populist platform. The Stormy Daniels trial may be able to subpoena some of those records and possibly get Trump to take the stand to make statements about his finances under oath. This is all compounded by the fact he is already under investigation by the special counsel. Trump’s presidency is currently being held up by a strong economy bought, in part, with corporate tax cuts financed by future generations. That credit runs out at some point and wiser politicians use exhausting political correctness to build friends all around. Trump builds enemies everywhere and a little information leaked here and there will snowball to turn unrelated events into a cumulative avalanche. Government operates on a timeline of years, unlike the 24 hour news cycle that Trump dominates. Stormy Daniels, if you will pardon the pun, is a blizzard that's going to reveal just how bad things are even though Trump will survive the direct effects of the storm, it will give ammunition to build a more significant case against him being qualified to be President. At a time when Trump should be controlling the narrative, he is letting a porn star do it. That is the issue.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should I negotiate a higher sign-on bonus as an entry-level consultant if my start date got delayed by three months? They gave me $5k more ($7k to $12k), but I feel like a lot of my time is being wasted.
Answer: You should negotiate the highest signing bonus you can get regardless of your circumstances. As to whether you want to wait it out, my presumption is that there is no downside to you turning them down at a later time other then you won’t get paid and they probably won’t offer the job to you again. My advice would be to tell them that’s not a lot of money for 3 months of downtime, but leave the door open. Even if they offer you more, continue to look for a better gig while tentatively comitting to them . Signing the deal likely just commits you to working for that number, but has no penalties for walking so if you find a better gig you take it. Simple as that. It’s a no lose situation for you. If they firce an answer now, it’s a reluctant yes. You turning them down later is really no worse then them having you in for an interview for a job that doesn’t exist yet. Two wrongs don’t make a right, but this is just business.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is the best option for a software engineer internship between a good, established company and a Silicon Valley Start-up? (My concern is, how will a little known, but very good, startup stand on my resume when I apply for full-time next year?)
Answer: The point of an internship is to get experience at the place you want to work. Your goal should not be to pick the place that will pad your resume the best, the goal should be which place gives you the best opportunities to do the things you want to do and rewards you accordingly with the expectation that they will be so impressed after experiencing your skills they will hire you at a rate far exceeding what someone not familiar with your talents would offer. Assuming compensation is competitive between the two options now, the best option is the company you want to start your career at. That doesn’t always work out, but if right now, neither of those options seem appealing beyond an internship, you should maybe consider looking for a third option. If that’s not possible, pick the one that looks more enjoyable and the one you think is more conducive to building friendships. Being happy and building a career are one in the same until you get baggage in your personal life. Also realize, a successful company looks good on your resume and the more well known the company, the better it will be. However, good developers don’t get thier second job based on thier resume, they get it through thier network of professional relationships. More then half of new hires come from referrals. If you are taking a job, just as a stepping stone to get to your next one, the thing you want to maximize is the breadth and depth of your professional relationships. Bigger companies give you more options to do that, but smaller startups nessitates commitment and more comradre. Go with your gut and take the job that looks like more fun to you. Screw the resume, if you build great things and those you work with know it, the job will be a whole lot easier to get next go around.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How should I start a freelance career as a web designer & programmer? How do I not be cheated?
Answer: You need to build a network of customers. That’s hard to do by cold calling, particularly if your skills are in building amazing web applications that speak for themselves and less so in selling abstract ideas like your personal brand. The most common way to build a network is to work as a full time employee for several years and develop a reputation as an independent problem solver who can figure what needs to be done, then do it. You can have a specialty, but it should be a general specialty, like UI programmer or designer. Being the best jQuery or other framework developer ever is worse than just being known as a solid developer who always delivers. Build strong relationships with the people who make hiring decisions or those exemplary employees who seem like they are going places. Diversify and bounce around every couple of years either in company or outside of it. Make as many professional friends as possible. You will know you have succeeded when at any point in time, you can think of three past associates who you could call who would likely have a opportunity they could offer to you and would love to work with you again. You will almost never have to worry about being cheated if you do work for your friends who work as large, stable companies as long as you do good work. Getting paid on time, is a whole other can of worms, but large companies almost always pay up as long as you do your part and provide well documented invoices.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why doesn't WebAssembly support DOM access? What design challenges would the people making it possible to access the DOM face?
Answer: I think the first problem is that I don’t really think it’s a design challenge, it sounds more like a requirements problem that comes from a fundamental misunderstanding of the value that WebAssembly brings. The only reason to put yourself through the interop hell that is webassembly is for performance and DOM access is one of the slowest things you do in web development. It is the bottleneck that makes almost all other tasks you do in native JavaScript seen orders of magnitude faster. If you are manipulating the DOM you might as well just use JavaScript. It might add a few milliseconds to your runtime, but that is unnoticable to the hundreds of milliseconds your DOM access will require. You don’t want to make DOM access easy from WebAssembly as people may just start to use it for direct DOM manipulation instead of simply doing the simple thing and using JavaScript for that. If any computation heavy work needs to be done, you can send that off to WebAssembly, then do your DOM manipulation in JavaScript once you get your answer back and your sandbox is less restrictive and way more feature rich. Despite that, I am sure some genius will build some tools that do make it much easier to manipulate the DOM from WebAssembly. That doesn’t mean it’s a good idea though even if there are a handful of legitimate uses.
