Silicon Valley was formed around Stanford. It hosts NASA and several government contractors. A substantial amount of the population are either tech workers or medical workers. The population is very heavily college graduates, many with advanced degrees. Their trusted sources are the experts who have spent their lives devoted, in a rigorous scientific way, to studying and solving the problems of the world. You start spouting off extreme statements that the entire scientific community is wrong and referring to widely refuted theories from “alternate scientists” as your evidence and you are not going to make friends and rightfully so. Yes, rightwingers are definitely suppressed, but they have no one to blame, but themselves. Don’t confuse that for oppression though. Silicon Valley is very heavily economically conservative in practice. It may now be governed by a democratic super majority on the state level and locally dominated by the left, but in practice, offices are built at a level far exceeding residences and have been for a long time. If you are not high performing individual working in technology or another extraordinarily high paying sector, you will learn what true oppression is just trying to live here far quicker then you will with any right leaning statements. Finally, I will leave you with this. While the likes of Peter Thiel would have to piled in with the “oppressed” right wingers because he brings the crazy. Marc Andreessen, Larry Ellison, and countless other conservatives are both largely well respected and liked in Silicon Valley. Not only that, there is a yearning in Silicon Valley for more market based solutions that would be loosely, but smartly regulated. The housing crisis here is FUBAR and the local democratic government has only made it worse. If you want to see the real oppression in Silicon Valley, attend a local zoning meeting and see what the democratically elected officials are put through trying to solve the housing crisis when the most vocal tend to be existing homeowners violently arguing why they deserve for the view from their single story eichler house to not be blocked by the new high rise going up across the street.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would now be a good time to rename the current Republican Party (maybe the Authoritarian Party, or Extremist Party), and let the real Republicans start a new Republican Party?
Answer: What exactly would that look like? I get you can drop the social conservatism that plays to identity politics, but that leaves you with a party of pure economic conservatism. The one formed after Nixon where all pretense of caring directly about individuals was dropped in favor of Regans trickle down economics that says virtually all taxes are bad and the only good government actions are those that don't restrict existing corporations, no matter how much more egalitarian they are. Where only your friends and family can help and the government just gets in the way. Pull away from that extremism where you have a highly capitalist society, but one that recognizes regulation is still fundamental to keeping corporations in check and that taxes are what pay for the services that make people lives better and you arrive at a center right Party not unlike the mainstream democratic one that exists. I'm afraid that the only place open for a new party is that to the left of the Democrats. The republicans have gone so far right, they have brought the democrats with them and leave little room for a rational Republican Party that sits between the two we have now. You can be an extremist or you can go to the left of the democrats. Somehow it feels to me there really is only one option for the Republican Party and that's the self destructive path of extremism they are on now. I hope you like schadenfreude.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should I move to Orange County from the Bay Area?
Answer: People live in the Bay Area for a variety of reasons. Except in the case where you already own a home, that list does not include because it's simply easier to not move. Given the cost of living, you have to be actively engaged in the area to make it worth it. For most people that means family, friends, or a career tieing you to the area and really isn't a question for most people living here. They have to be here. Many of those leaving do so because they are forced out by costs, not by choice. If that list doesn't apply to you, or even more so, that list applies more in Orange County, yes get out. Orange County is by no means cheap, but places can be found for a fraction of the prices in the Bay Area, particularly those getting closer to the outskirts. It is much more viable to live a middle class lifestyle on a middle class income. If you can even ask the question does it make sense to move out and you aren't immediately confronted by the irreplaceable roots you have here, yes it makes sense. Oppurtunity can be found everywhere in this economy including Orange County.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Did Apple charge too little for the iPhone X, considering it sold out in 20 minutes?
Answer: I don't think Apple really knows the answer to that question. They added some truly innovative stuff to the iPhone X at the same time as expanding thier product line with the iPhone 8 which is a really solid competitor in the high end phone segment itself. Apple really could of charged a lot without worrying about losing customers. At worst anyone who decides the iPhone X is too much, just buys the 8. An iPhone X at $2k would certainly have far fewer customers, but still in the millions. Apple doubled what we were willing to pay for phones if it was truly a transcendent experience when the first iPhone came out. They could certainly do that again. It has to be worth it though beyond the marketing hype and that is a big question now at $1000. Apple consistently runs out of stock with hotly anticipated products regardless if they end up being worth the hype or not. There are lots of stories of design and production issues with the iPhoneX. They removed Touch ID and have a lot of brand spanking new tech that might not work out. Apple tends to be really good about quality control with just a few notable exceptions, however, it is much less apprehensive about forcing users away from thier comfort zone into sometimes compromised positions. The iPhone X is going to feel really expensive if FaceId doesn't work better then Touch ID in ALL of the common use cases. People will notice what's not as good even if everything else is better. Face ID needs to be flawless. The big ass screen better be very durable. There can be no wide ranging recalls and performance better meet or exceed expectations at all turns. Apple is the kind of company that can pull that off, but I'm waiting to see the reviews in a few weeks before deciding if it's a good value myself. It has some tech that has close competitors, but nothing that seems nearly as ambitious. It is an exciting phone with a lot to prove that presumably makes it the best of the best. If that holds true for a large number of consumers, it's price is not well contained by competitors. Yes, the iPhone X has potential to be underpriced even at $1000.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Donald Trump is a businessman. If everyone in the US donated $1 to be given to him on the condition he resigned from office by the end of 2017, we'd have 330 million to pay him off. Who's in?
Answer: That won't fix the Republican Party. The reason Trump exists is because a substantial number of Americans are complacent if not downright enthusiastic about the devisive rhetoric the President puts out on a daily basis rather then trying to fulfill his stated agenda. The president is but one man, the real fight is convincing half of America the subtlety of racism and that job creators might not spend thier tax breaks on thier businesses. Using tricks or aggressive tactics will only result in a more polarized constituency. Whenever the president puts out another cringeworthy and unpresidential statement, all that you can do is say “that's not cool” again and again and support the law and legislators holding authoritarianism at bay. It's working as well as it can right now. Trump has been more ineffective at any long term legislation then any democrat could of hoped for. The Republican Party has to break before it gets better. Dark times are upon us, but as long as the checks and balances still operate in some form, we have to let things run there course. There is no person better qualified then Trump right now to break the Republican Party and thus far he's doing a far better job then Hillary would have. If she were president, the republicans would be unified in opposition and have clear agenda, resistance at any cost, to rally around. Instead, they now have to govern to keep thier base excited and that's getting them to have to confront the profound absence of a workable policy agenda thier constituents will be happy with once it's implemented. Trump may have abandoned all standards and metrics by which a presidency is measured, but that won't change the fact he has to deliver to stay employed. I'll be saving my dollar for some popcorn. The schendenfreud show is just getting good. Trump’s presidency is an absolute disaster. Aside from passive resistance, there is little you can do, so sit back and enjoy the show.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: A soon-to-be employer (Bay Area startup) ruined my reputation. What can I do?
Answer: Your reputation sounds like it's just fine in all the areas that matter. Getting another job rarely relies on the recommendation of your past employer. You need references, but as long as you have other past relationships you can give, it shouldn't be a problem. Your resume isn't going to mention any of the unscrupulous things that happen and you will just talk about your accomplishments in any future interviews. It sounds like you still have a job lined up in the Bay Area which will both make your previous employment moot and be a place where there is tons of opportunity if you suddenly find yourself searching for greener pastures. Your reputation may be ruined at your past employer, but that is only of value if you planned on going back to that company. I can't imagine you would be worth the effort and expense to sue personally and sueing past clients is just bad business unless there is something more going on, but it sounds like an idle threat to me. In any case, jobs in tech are a dime a dozen right now. If you have the skills, your reputation at a single past employer isn't going to matter or likely come up. It sucks, but just put it in the past and move on. It sounds like there is little to be gained trying to prove you were the honest one. The best thing to do now is try to be successful in your future endeavors and apply whatever lessons you can from your past ones.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should I threaten my employer with offers from other companies when asking for a pay raise?
Answer: If you are at a well functioning company, your manager should be on your side. There should be no threatening. You want to give your manager the ammunition he needs to fight for you though. There will be metrics you have to meet to get to a certain payscale. Some may be BS, but either way, your manager should be the one who helps you check those boxes. He should not be the true impediment to your raise. You should be able to have a frank conversation with them about compensation and where you think you should be at and he should tell you exactly what it takes to get there or that you need to change your role to progress. Mentioning specifics like you know company X would offer you Y more should be enough to give him the hint that you are looking without being too explicit and provide some weight behind your ask. If you are truly under market and threatening is the only way that gets your manager on your side, you should leave regardless. However, letting your manager know your perceived market value periodically is good advice and something that should be welcomed all around as a measure of transparency. If he asks about whether you interviewed elsewhere, be honest and tell him why you want to stay with him anyway.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is Tesla really that innovative as it is depicted in the media?
Answer: Elon Musk simply did one thing. He looked at this chart. That's the cost of lithium ion batteries over time. What kind of idiot would you have to be in 2003 to see that and not say batteries, at some point in the near future, will make electric cars not only cost competitive, but will make them cheaper then ICE vehicles? Build an electric car that mitigates the other relatively benign issues with electrics which have clear maintenance, performance, and environmental advantages and you will have an industry killer. Still every other car company was laughing at electrics in 2003. The failure of the EV1 was in recent memory and well, change is hard. Innovative doesn't seem like the right word. I’m not saying Tesla doesn’t do innovative things, but Tesla is around today because it made an electric car normal people desire. The formula for which is well known and basically equates to performance, practicality, and range that exceeds the its price. That is hard, but not if you are a car builder. Building a car in the ultra low margin and super competitive automobile space takes an enormous amount of cash and technical know how. Musk did the painfully obvious, albeit extraordinarily difficult for a startup, thing to anyone considering what will work best in the future instead of only considering what works now. It was really risky to build an electric car given the enormous capital and logistical challenges involved, but he didn't let the current industry standards restrict him. That's innovative, of course, but I still feel that it's more of a reflection of just how incredibly conservative and mired in industry lock in the entire automobile industry is. GM could have continued evolving the EV1 without really affecting their overall profitability, even if the product line wouldn't deliver profit for several more years. Look at that chart again, how could you not at least let that play out until things level out. By all means they should have crushed Tesla. Musk had to build an entire manufacturing capability from scratch. Still, Musk managed to be innovative not so much by doing anything really creative. There is also a lot of crazy creative stuff in the Tesla, but he won the war with a car with phenomenal acceleration and decent range in a sizable sedan all of which come easily if you solve the battery problem. It really comes down to just acting logically with an eye to the future when all others stopped moving forward and simply rested on their laurels. That does seem to be Musk's trick. His success is not in completely novel concepts so much as he simply notices obvious trends that aren't being acted on and are likely to continue in the future. Then he does the hard work and takes the enormous risk to make those things happen. He then sprinkles a bunch of gee whiz tech things in like a large infotainment screen that people see as innovative, but really, he won the war simply producing an electric car that can compete toe to toe with its ICE competitors.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: My boss offered me a role with more responsibility with no increase in pay, implying it's "good for your career" and that my chances of a raise are higher, what would you think/do?
Answer: Take it. Make sure it comes with a better title. If you don't eventually get more pay commensurate with your new position, your boss has at least given you the ticket to getting more pay at your next employer. More responsibility is generally very good for your career regardless of pay. There is a question if you want to do that job that you will have to answer for yourself, but this is a good career move on all other accounts. Few companies will ever hire you into a higher position then the one you are leaving unless they are a startup and desperate. Other companies will almost certainly pay you more though if they want you. What you have been given is priceless in terms of career development. Worry about the money after you have delivered on your new title and find yourself undervalued and with new opportunity to get more pay elsewhere.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: It seems like, with iOS 11, Apple has introduced a new animation for how apps take over the entire screen when opened. Even though it’s happening so quickly, is it possible to define or deconstruct exactly what’s happening in mathematical terms?
Answer: I don't care enough to actually record and break down the timing of the animation. I'm too lazy to even look at my one iOS 11 device, however, my shot in the dark is they just chose a different easing function for the zoom, basically a different bezier curve. You can see programmatic models here: Simple Easing Functions in Javascript - see https://github.com/gre/bezier-easing. Browsers implement these natively these days. Easing in and out of a transition, like a zoom or a slide makes it seem much more natural than simply starting at full speed. Easing Functions Cheat Sheet has some visualizations of what these easing functions look like.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: In a large pile of similar "new CS grad" resumes, how are resumes noticed and selected for interviewing for a general "new grad" software engineer position at big tech companies like Google?
Answer: Your clearest path to getting hired is to get referred by someone already at the company. As a new grad that's likely hard as your professional network is likely limited to classmates who are in the same boat as you and looking for work. Your best path to Google though may be first taking a job at another silicon valley startup, particularly one close to the Google offices where you will have interactions with ex and current googlers that can facilitate your way in. The same holds true for any company, move close to the HQ and network locally. A competent engineer who has lived and worked in mountain view for at least 2 years should have a pretty easy time at least getting an interview at Google facilitated by one of several aquantences you will have who work there. That is the patient way. Simply having a well written resume and high quality background is also half your battle. Google is notorious not only for the high number of applicants, but for the high number of unqualified ones. You will stand out simply by being qualified for the position you are applying to and making sure your resume is simply up to professional standards. Crafting your resume to specifically speak to the position you are applying for will also do wonders.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What can the salary expectation be for a senior software engineering position with 10 years of experience in the Bay area for a Series A startup?
Answer: I’ve had a couple offers from $160k to $180k base. The equity is where it gets interesting, but with a pre-IPO startup you are really rolling the dice. I find most are overvaluing their equity and making an offer that only matches one of the famous Bay Area tech giants only if you assume rosy future growth. The last series A I interviewed at would of required a nearly 10x growth over 4 years from the price of their last private stock offering just to be competitive. That’s within the realm of possibility and the potential for more is even greater, but I’ve been burned before. Personally, I find you get a better deal joining a very early stage startup where you get points and the risk to go along with it, or joining something publicly traded where you have a real cash value for your compensation that you can rely on. Series A seems to be a not-insignificant amount of risk for a relatively meager upside. You really have to believe the company has a substantial chance of growing 100x to make it worth it.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If a corporation were to make its headquarters on an artificial island in international waters, could it avoid paying taxes altogether?
Answer: Taxes? Large corporations solved that problem already and you don't need to move your company physically. You just hire some creative accountants and do it virtually, maybe aquire a small company in an already tax friendly country and call it your “headquarters”, buy some stuff you already wanted and call it R&D expenses, maybe do real estate development. The really big companies make nice with the local politicians and get them to subsidize the new offices they were going to build anyway. Theres no clear single path, and I'm not saying it's easy, just way easier then making an island from scratch or even moving to an existing one. If arent afraid of restructuring your business in otherwise impractical ways and you can afford a team of tax attorneys, they can figure out the magic for your business that won't involve living amonst palm trees or turning your back on civilization. They can legally hide your malfeasance in layers of beauracracy and then say to blame the game not the player. You are a job creator, just look at our contrbution to economic growth as our taxes! The US tax code has no shortage of loopholes for those with enough money and means to make it happen. 18 of the 100 most profitable corporations not only pay no corporate tax, but the government pays them through rebates that make taxes a net gain for them. Maybe you could find a way around the political and logistical nightmare that would be building an artificial island, but that would be leaving money on the table. Why bother. Just hire a lobbyist and these days be sure to get a membership at Mar-a-lago to really smooth things over. Profitable Companies, No Taxes: Here’s How They Did It

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What were your impressions of the iPhone 8 and X?
Answer: Fuck. Did you see the animated poop emoji?! We have arrived. Seriously though the facial recognition thing and depth sense camera work better then anything else out there. I'm sure the several years integrating wireless charging was to make it work better then the current experiences. The new things the iPhone X does, on some level, may only be new to Apple, but it's going to do those new things better then everyone else. People will pay to have the best even if there are cheaper very similar options. Everyone keeps saying it wasn't innovative enough, but this is what apple does best. It takes technology others were first at and spends whatever it takes to make it into something people really love to use and turns a niche feature into something you can't live without. Touch screens and web browsers worked on phones well before the first iPhone came out, Apple just made it pleasurable to do on a phone. Android has had facial recognition and wireless charging for years, but it's hardly a mainstream feature that everyone has and uses and the experience is often poor. After today, my guess is that all phones a year from now, outside of the extreme value market, will need to have them and have them working solidly to compete. This is apple leading.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What are the chances that Amazon’s new headquarters will be in Silicon Valley?
Answer: Companies come to silicon valley for VC money and the connections to get VC money. You don't want to grow here unless you did something stupid like came here for VC money and hired all your principal staff from the area, which tends to happen a lot. Amazon having a satellite office here for R&D or M&A makes sense as lots of large companies do to keep an eye on the market and get ahead of any new competition, but not a second headquarters. I really can't see the value proposition. Hiring anyone out of thier twenties here is very difficult. Its a great place to found a company, but a terrible place to grow one. It takes a lot of money to get top talent from well vested companies like Google and unlike almost any other city, Amazon will be seen as a downgrade from many of the local large companies here. Few engineers will want to move thier families across the country to a place they won't be able to afford a house. Many silicon valley employers are already experiencing Amazon wants to avoid in Seattle and actively opening satellite offices just like Amazon wants to do to find a better place to grow. Amazon is presumably looking to move beyond Seattle as the NIMBYism there is limiting the growth potential, unfortunately silicon valley makes Seattle's inability to move away from single family homes and to more urban infrastructure look quaint. Moving from Seattle to Silicon Valley would be like moving from Florida to Hawaii to get away from the ocean. It makes no sense.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why does the technology industry receive a disproportionate amount of flack about diversity when other occupations, such as recruitment consultant and warehouse operative, are reportedly more inhospitable to women?
Answer: Why do people focus so much time on acts of terrorism when many more people die in automobile accidents? Why is Beyonce's pregnancy national news when having a child is commonplace? Whether you call it infamy or celebrity, the tech titans have a vaunted place in society. Everyone knows Google and Uber by name. They know what they do and interact with thier products on a daily basis. What's more, the engineering jobs are highly skilled creative pursuits that require motivation, dedication, and responsibility to create a working product and solve unique problems. If your workers are not motivated at a warehouse job, you can just hire some more workers and brute force it. It's a problem, but a more controllable one. If your software engineers make a bad product, it will be seen by customers and have a negative impact on more then just a few worker’s productivity. Culture is very important at tech companies where building a slightly better product can mean whether you survive or not. The perceived value of an engineer also comes from the success of the projects they work on and the visibility of them within the company. Performance is subjective and multiplied by the presence of the deliverables. You can't simply measure performance based on the the number of things you ship or the number of people who get hired from your recruitment activities. As an engineer, if you get put on a project that has a low potential upside, your career will see it's potential drop. Working on a tool to help a handful of administrative employees do thier job just doesn't have the reach of say working on search for Google. If you are made to feel uncomfortable on the project you are on, it may mean switching to a project with a less desirable career trajectory or even have to be down leveled. Switching divisions or jobs means not only a different evironment, but giving up a likely unique project that may hold outsized value to you. Diversity problems in tech companies have an exceptional effect on the company's bottom line, they have an exceptional effect on the employee’s career path, they have some exceptionally undiverse demographics, and the companies in question tend to be exceptionally famous. That doesnt mean diversity issues are unique to tech and if you are an individual experiencing them, it really doesn't matter which industry you are in to make it a problem. Tech is likely far from the most egregious industry. That being said, the tech industry does have a lot of reasons that make it a good place to evolve diversity in the workplace to the next level. Why not start a dialog there?

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do liberals not support Trump's wall? Do they not care about the risk our country faces from an economic and national security standpoint?
Answer: The risks we face from allowing more immigrants in from an economic standpoint is increased productivity, higher profit margins from more low wage workers, and cheaper goods. Employment in the US is near historic highs and has been for a while now. We need more workers. The laws of supply and demand dictate that a tight labor supply will increase cost as well as wages, that's held true for highly skilled labor that has seen increased competition, but lower skilled jobs get automated or simply disappear if the costs rise too much. The belabored point that immigrants are taking jobs and driving down wages simply hasn't proven true. We have seen a net decline in illegal immigration over the past few years and wages for low skilled work still remain low. Our economy, on the other hand, just can't seem to get past 2% growth and having a larger workforce to replace our aging baby boomers seems like it could only help. From a national security standpoint, Mexico may be the source of a lot of drugs, but the terrorists tend to come by planes from middle eastern countries or are home grown. The smuggling that happens also happens most in urban Mexican areas that already are protected by a wall. I'm not sure that building a wall in an area that is already a natural deterrent is the most productive use of resources.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Will open carry in TX curtail looting during Harvey, or is a gun-free zone being declared?
Answer: The majority of the city is underwater. Open carry will not have much of an effect. The opportunity for looting comes from the massive lack of people around in a flooded area and the lack of operating infrastructure that doesn’t allow security measures to operate effectively. Someone with a long gun standing at his front door is certainly going to deter looters, but so would someone without any gun at all. The looters are going to pick the stores and homes that are completely empty as they are easy to find. This is not the time of desperation where you go for the well guarded treasure trove, you simply find another store with the power off and the windows blown out, take what you want and get out without anyone being around to stop you. Poorly guarded property is pretty much everywhere. The opportunity of robbing a completely empty place is the same whether other places have people practicing open carry or not. You rob the evacuated places, it's like taking candy from a baby. Houston had to impose a curfew and upped the penalties for looting because widespread looting is already taking place. The chaos must be palpable. Everyone everywhere is trying to save their lives and their things and figure out what to do and the looters are able to thrive in that chaos. The looters have taken advantage of that by impersonating officers and FEMA representatives and telling people to evacuate while they rob them blind. Houston Reeling Amid Outbreak Of Looting, Armed Robberies; Vigilantes Emerge Open carry doesn’t help with that. You are not going to shoot someone who you appears to be trying to help you. The looters will stop when the people come back, with or without weapons, and order is restored. The police and heroic armed citizens are out there, but from what I've seen they seem to have more than enough to do on their hands saving people from drowning and starving.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: A job offer came in at about 25k less than my current job. They know my current salary. Is this a negotiating tactic for them to not pay me over my current salary? Do they really expect I take a pay cut?
Answer: That is not a negotiating tactic and they really expect you to take the offer, but likely know it's a long shot. You may be able to get them to raise it a little bit, but my guess is that it's already near the upper range for the position. You are just a bad fit for it based on your seniority. They will likely try to sell you on the opportunity or the potential equity upside, though it's almost certainly a bad deal for you and they know it, but it's likely their only option. Bad deals happen all the time. Employees accept them, sometimes they work out. This is just lipstick on a pig though. Move on. Your bottom line should be somewhere slightly north of your current salary. Give them that as an ultimatum, you don't need to negotiate or explain your position any more than that, then move on if they can't find a way to meet it.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it legal in the USA to create a non-profit with the sole purpose of providing for yourself and avoid (some) taxes?
Answer: Sure, as long as you aren't so transparent about it. The highest paid nonprofit CEOs were paid several million dollars. Nonprofit CEO salaries keep getting higher. See the region’s 50 highest-paid. They of course put on a nice dog and pony show about how thier compensation is required simply to make it baseline competitve, but about the only people they are fooling with that line is the IRS.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If the Night King didn’t get his hands on a dragon, how was the army of the dead going to get past the wall?
Answer: The wall is a shadow of the force it once was. The wildlings were recently able to get past the wall on many occasions. It was made to stop an invasion and fully manned, it's virtually impenetrable without a dragon, but in its current undermanned state, smaller forces can easily get past it at it's many weak points. Only 3 of the 19 castles along the wall are currently manned. The night's watch is not at full force. If Jon Snow didn’t go beyond the wall or if he did and died not using the Dragons, Snow would not have brought back a wight walker, in either case, the southern forces presumably wouldn't have been united and the wall would remain well undermanned. An unmanned wall is as good as no wall at all with a force like the wight walkers. They could initially use a smaller force at a weakpoint to control that immediate territory, then open up the wall unabated and take their time to get the entire force through. If they can raise a dragon from the bottom of a lake, they can certainly dig through 20 feet of earth and ice with an undead army if there’s no one actively stopping them. Jon had to go past the wall to get the army to man it. It’s easy to now think the army was being raised just for when the wight walkers breached the wall, but it was really needed to prevent that scenario from ever happening and truly make the wall into the impenetrable barrier it should be. We already saw how the wall can be penetrated when the wildlings got through. They were ultimately defeated / assimilated. The path for the wight walkers without a dragon would of looked similar, but without the happy ending of joining forces.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: I just received my annual raise. I want to ask for more, and I have supporting data to do so. How should I go about it?
Answer: If you are working for a company with an HR organization, the data your HR department has on what people of your caliber should be making will make yours look quaint. They don't need a lesson on pay scales. Simply say you like the work, but are not happy with your raise and say you feel the opportunities elsewhere feel like they will be much more rewarding. Your manager should know you intimately and what you bring to the organization already. You can mention your data now to let them know your expectations, but the data likely isn't going to change many minds, so keep it terse. It will warrant an explanation from your manager on why your expectations are mismatched. Which may be in itself satisfying. Your data is not negotiating power, it simply shows what you think your worth is and possibly explains why you think that. Your past work and the cost of losing you will be what really matters and hopefully won't be something you have to detail for your manager. If your manager is not already familiar with what value you bring, you need to work on having more visible impact prior to asking for a raise. Unless you are ready to leave immediately, tread lightly. Your subtle suggestion will either be enough to convince them to give you a bump or it won't. If not, don't push it, take the hint, graciously accept your manager's explaination for your pay level as enlightening and silently start interviewing elsewhere. You will either get a better offer and can leave to pursue greener pastures or will not and will have a new found appreciation for your current employer. This advice is, of course, predicated on the fact you work for a nominally functional organization and your manager is at least nominally competent. If either of those things don't apply to your situation, consider my advice null and void.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What should be considered when deciding whether to buy or rent in the Bay Area?
Answer: Renting is relatively cheap here. Ha! I know, but the place I'm in now rents for $5k ($60k a year) and the same model of the same town home just sold for $1.45 million. I would further say, that's typical of the market for the inventory of 3 bedroom homes in the Bay Area. Let's break down the numbers. Let's say you get 3.5% mortgage on the remaining $1.15 million after your down payment. That costs $40k a year, but it's largely tax free. So call it $28k in after tax dollars. Property taxes are only good for your neighbors who have lived in the Bay Area for a while and with a new home purchase, you are going to have to cover them. That's another $17k, tax free again so let's call it $12k. HOA fees are $3k a year. Buying that place is going to take putting down $300k. Instead, let's take that and put it in Reality Shares and put it to work financing other people's debt. That will typically return 8.5% on loans where the borrower has a great credit score and is putting at least 20% down. You can further spread that investment out among 50 different borrowers. That nets you around $25k a year on the same principal that would be tied up in your house with a substantially lower risk profile. After taxes let's say it's $18k. 28+12+3+18=$61k a year to buy. That also ignores the cost of maintenance and upgrades that could be substantial on older homes around the area and the $60k plus it will cost to sell the place with an agent. The AMT and other tax implications can substantially up those numbers for many upper income buyers here. Also the rate you get on your mortgage will really effect things too. In any case, buying right now costs you more then renting per year, but potentially not much more. The thing you are looking at is the past several years and seeing double digits appreciation on leveraged money. Buying in 2010 was the better path by a long shot, although still not as good as dumping your down payment in Google stock at that time. This is not 2010 though. The market is at an all time high, both in stocks and real estate. Still companies are planning to hire more and build offices for significantly more people then new homes are scheduled to be built for. The economy also appears stable at this point, but past performance tells us it's inherently cyclical and in the Bay Area, the last down cycle halved home prices in many areas. In other words, real estate here is extremely risky. If a recession hits the Bay Area I can't see the prices for houses in suburbs that are only remarkable for thier proximity to work holding thier value. Past history has shown this to be true. We may not be able to predict the market, but I can tell you if a recession hits it will be reflected with a dramatic down swing in real estate prices. That brings us back to pure real estate investing. It's certainly not without it's risks. Debt investment properties can typically lose at least 20% of thier value before you should feel it though and have a time frames that can be a year or less so you can tune things as the market turns. They also are typically adding value to properties by redeveloping them. Not just speculating and hoping for a rise in real estate to beat the costs over time. Unlike your primary residence where any depreciation hits you directly and is not usually liquidatable without significant changes to your life goals. Lose your job in that recession and your house may soon follow at a major loss. Also, if you want more risk in outside investments to parity the Bay Area apperciation of past years, you can double your return by putting it in more risky second lien debt or equity investments while still mitigating some of it by spreading it across the country and multiple investments. You can construct an investment that has nearly all the potential upsides of buying in the Bay Area while maintaining much greater control over the risks. Unlike buying a house near your affordability range, you can decide how much or how lillte exposure you want. My point is, buying a house in the Bay Area as a primary residence is a bad investment at this point in time. Still, there is potentially tremendous value to quality of life to owning a house beyond monetary returns to many people. There are things you simply can't get from renting. That also means when buying here, you are competing against very high earners with kids already in school that don't want to have to move to another district because thier landlord decides it's a good time to sell or investors from China who want to hide thier money from thier government. If things like that don't have value to you, you are overpaying. By pure numbers, it's a really bad investment unless you assume there is no top. Don't buy a house here because you think you are going to lose more money renting. Investments that outperform Bay Area housing are easy to find.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: To retain grandfathered Prop. 13 property tax benefit, can you trade houses with your friend in a different state (both of you occupying the other's house) without changing prospective ownerships of said houses?
Answer: California is the only state stupid enough to have a property tax tied to the purchase price of a house and not the true market price so only one of you will get the benefit. It's a giveaway to property owners no matter how rich, which nation you are a citizen of, whether you are a multi billion dollar corporation, or where you actually live. No worries, as long as you don't sell the property, you will get to take advantage.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What can I do if I’m in my current contract job and I get a new job offer from another company that will pay more?
Answer: Most contracts I've worked under simply estabilsh an hourly rate and an expectation of how long they will need you for. They can generally terminate you early for any reason without notice as well as you can leave at any time. There are few limitations on what the contract can and cannot do though so you will have to consult the contract you signed as to any termination clauses or penalties which should be spelled out.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Since a software developer in my team always misses deadlines and spends 3 to 4 times more than other developers, should I fire him?
Answer: Estimating software development tasks becomes exponentially harder as the tasks become larger. Never have I worked at a software company where there wasn’t some deadline given based on how long it takes to write some software that has never been done before based on some estimate with more unknowns than trivial implementations. In all those cases, the deadline was pure BS from a technical perspective. At best, it was a target that allowed features to be scaled back as difficulties became reality and to deliver some form of product by that deadline. Dysfunctional software development happens when you demand fixed features on a fixed deadline and tends to be the rule more than the exception. Solving large problems in 3 to 4 times what you initially thought it would take to solve sounds pretty normal to me. There are ways to deliver something on time that makes the stakeholders happy even with that assumption. In any case, a developer who doesn’t hit estimates isn’t necessarily bad, particularly if the culture around him is dysfunctional and doesn’t have realistic explanations even if those around them have found a way to ignore the issues and deliver in dysfunction for better or worse. Still, the only thing you mentioned is what this developer doesn’t do well, not what his redeeming qualities are, like code maintainability, cost, flexibility, etc. Based on that he is only a negative to you, yeah, sounds like he should go, but you should be basing that on way more details then just not consistently meeting deadlines. The why matters more than the what in this case.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What if I brought a 2017 car to 1960?
Answer: The Jetsons was made in 1962 as a representation of 2062 during the time when most older adults could still remember the era of horse and buggies and yet during that generation they managed to progress to the point of putting a man on the moon. It's still a bit early, but no matter what example of 21st century automobile tech you bring back, it won't fly, it won't fold up into a suitcase, it will have a recognizable power source. Instead of George Jetson's two hour work week, our men work longer hours for less relative pay and we put our women to work for just as long. Our best robots vacuum the floor, but expect you to clean up for them and the ones with a sense of humor are reperitious at best. Our dogs don't talk. The nav system would be nifty, but 50 years to put what seems a step above a TV in the car? You'd get a better reception if you gave a spoiled child coal for Christmas.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should Democrats start holding rallies as a counterpoint to Trump's rallies?
Answer: Nah. Rallies are too easy to organize these days. Simply put up a viral post on Facebook and you have a following with hardly leaving your house or doing any real work. If you want real power to change you need to do things that are hard. Before computers that was rallies as developing phone lists of like minded individuals was hard. Calling them up and organizing them all took massive effort and leadership to get everyone to show up. If you did that with enough followers, it would be pretty clear you could do the same to rally the vote and any politician would fear and court you. Trump crushes it because he knows how to relate to an audience. It doesn't matter if lots of people show up to his rallies or not, his messaging is what matters and he is a master at getting extreme support and condemnation at the same time. He will turn your counterpoint into more support to show how democratic elites are trying to hold the common man down. You want to win against Trump, the way isn't to show his followers are racist or out of touch with the rest of the world with a massive counter rally and greater numbers isn't going to scare the politicians like it use to. You need a better economic message that resonates with Trump's followers. That means ignoring the social conservative values and focusing on the economy.. Answer the question, how can a Democratic agenda boost the lives of everyday Anericans in a way that works with thier values using a catchy one-liner and you will win with or without a rally.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How difficult would it be to study computer engineering MS program with nearly none related knowledge but with experiences in programming?
Answer: Colleges have these things called prereqs. Without them, you will not be accepted into any accredited master's program. For engineering, that means a but load of credits for courses that themselves have prereqs. The short of it is, you will need an undergraduate degree to start and if say that degree is in something like philosophy, you are looking at three years of completing classes for credits before you can even apply. Software engineering is also not computer engineering. If you are good at algorithms, patterns, and architecture though, you will likely not find computer engineering outside of your wheelhouse. It's still a different thing so most of your knowledge will not be directly transferable, but will make learning the amount of new stuff a little easier

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: You just got elected President. What's your first tweet?
Answer: Now that I am president, my words carry more weight then ever. The economy of the United States and the world can rise and fall based on decisions made about future policy directions which will be directed by what I say my intentions are. My statements must always be well thought out and complete. As much as I like fostering a personal connection with my followers, professionalism demands a level of trust and thoughtfulness that just can't be found in a stream of consciousness on Twitter. I will still be in frequent contact, that's why I have an entire communications team who will make sure my words always reflect my well considered intentions. Goodbye forever Twitter.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do you found a startup company and manage it when all your co-founders are in different parts of the world or country?
Answer: Startup founders should all be self starters who should have the ability to take responsibility of getting a project done no matter where it takes them and fill in for whomever to make it work. There should be no special sauce to making a remote startup work other then working with committed people. There are a multitude of tools to help you, pick some and get started. I know that's kind of a non answer, but the difficult part when a company is largely remote comes when you start hiring people who you have to delegate work too and expect them to deliver a very specific thing that meets detailed needs you define rather then a simple direction and having them figure out the details. Growing past 10 employees is when the challenges will start. For now, all you need is trust and committed cofounders.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do people live in the Bay Area when there are so many other places which are more affordable?
Answer: The Bay Area is a land of disparity. After adding in cost of living, California has the highest poverty rate in the nation. It's dead last in student to teacher ratio. That being said, some schools in the Bay Area are the highest ranked in the state. Taxes may be high and the high cost of living means people living a lower class lifestyle are paying upper class rates. However, if you bought property in a downturn, you pay some of the lowest property taxes in the nation for an urban area. Most people are rich here from equity in large companies and a good portion of your income may come from long term capital gains. Despite a highly progressive current legislature, the tax regime is a reflection of decades old policy and is very friendly to certain special interests that is not reflective of the socially liberal values that dominate the areas politics. For someone without kids who is living in the city center. There is little difference between San Francisco and London, in terms of cost of living, or pretty much any other US growing city. What makes the Bay Area special is that you dont have a choice to move to cheaper suburbs and commute in like you would in London. Revealed: London's most affordable commuter towns The problem with San Francisco is that it is not the central hub for jobs as cities typically are. There are no commuter towns. Most of the big companies are dispersed throughout the South Bay and means even with an hour commute, you are still looking at needing a million dollars plus for a starter home as the suburbs are also tech centers themselves. That doesn't matter if you don't have kids or are otherwise a city dweller who lives and works in the city center. San Francisco is hardly less affordable then living in most other trendy cities. A few roommates make your big paycheck go really far. San Francisco has less under 18 residents then any other US city for a reason. The Bay Area is a profoundly unfair place to live, but that also means it's both profoundly beneficial and profoundly disparaging to different groups depending on which special class you fall into. The reasons to live here are as extreme as the reasons to move out.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Which companies prefer to hire software developers who value quality and creativity over speed-to-market concerns?
Answer: The bad ones. Seriously. You want to to create great software, you need analytics to tell you what your users appreciate and want to use. No designer or developer can tell you what will work better then observing your users can. Quality can be quick, just scale back to the minimum viable product, done well, but limited. Be creative, but do it quickly. Don't waste time finding the best idea. Figure out ways to test them all till you are confident you have the right one. You want to try 20 ideas out with a limited audience then iterate, find the problems while they are small. You can't do that if it takes you months just to build a protype that tries to do everything perfectly. Don't see this as an endorsement of companies that rush a broken product out the door because the developers are asked to build too much. That's quick done poorly. Be agile my friend. Drop the ego, embrace the unknown, and work around it. Promise quick and consistent turn around and that things will always get better with time. You can not promise perfection, but you can promise you are always on a journey to the perfect product. A market is not something you get to, it's discovered.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What percentage of software written by software development companies is ever used (included in a stable release for example)?
Answer: I can tell you 99% of the software I have written for large companies has been released. Thats not true of some of the early stage startups I have worked for, which don't ship for a combination of lack of funds, pivoting, overly ambitious technical challenges, lack of business acumen, etc. I’m also excluding prototypes, proof of concepts, and internal tools not meant to be released. I have also been called in at otherwise successful companies as a consultant many times to fix projects. That has sometimes meant throwing out entire code bases. I still don’t think your question has a good answer though. The amount of dysfunction that is acceptable in a nominally functioning company that rises to the level of not shipping products is none. Well functioning companies should always be able to implement and ship the products they design. A failure to do that sometimes happens, but is very significant and is a massive failure when it happens. It should not happen and does not happen regularly at most companies and not something you quantify like number of bugs that make it to production. Don’t start coding on something you don’t know is achievable and do your homework first and you should never be put in a position of having spent lots of time writing code and never seeing it ship save for non-technical decisions made for business reasons.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does James Damore have a case for suing Google?
Answer: Of course. Google is a huge corporation with billions upon billions of dollars. It has an image to protect that some would consider left leaning, but the marketing leadership would surely like to portray the company as totally non-partisan and would like as little detail of it's dirty laundry aired in public one way or another. The case for Damore sueing Google is the 7 or 8 figures that it will likely pay to not have to prove themselves in court and keep thier name from being in the headlines for next few years as the company that has fucked up diversity for it's workforce. In this case, the merits of the case are largely immaterial. There's enough questions that it likely won't be dismissed outright and the win here for Google is to settle in secret ASAP. That's what I would call Rock solid.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should I encourage my son who is graduating from a top CS program to pursue a PhD? He likes all his summer internships but I worry that in the long term, he would miss out on the opportunities to pursue a higher degree.
Answer: Absolutely not. A doctorate has negative value in computer science. Gifted computer scientists will do just as well without one and pursuing a path in private business will likely be much more lucrative then staying in academia. That doesn't mean your son shouldn't pursue a PhD, the degree can open up a very small number of jobs and research positions, but those are only worth pursuing if research and publishing is your true passion. That does mean you should not force him to do it. It's a harder path and less rewarding unless the work itself is your reward and something your son should be very passionate about on his own before going down that path. If you want your son to maximize his earning potential a CS PhD is not the way. Encourage your son to start working for a place that respects him, offers him advancement opportunities, and allows him to work on projects he is passionate about. There should be lots of potential opportunities, particularly if he's open to moving to a tech center. Don't worry about picking the wrong one too much, if it doesn't work out, it's pretty common to jump to another position every couple of years and is usually beneficial to a career in software engineering.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Where or how can conservatives in Silicon Valley safely express themselves to the public?
Answer: First don't confuse being conservative with being an alt right, gun toting, anti-abortion, global warming denying Republican. Second go to literally anywhere in Silicon Valley. Conservatism is the holding of political views that favor free enterprise, private ownership, and socially conservative ideas. Double check on those first two without caveats in Silicon Valley. There are few places that will be more accepting of leaving your highly regimented, stable 9 to 5 to go off and form your own startup. Even the company you are leaving will likely applaud your effort and welcome you back with open arms after you fail or have no qualms about trying to acquire your new company if you succeed. The area may talk about lots of protected classes, but none are more protected than homeowners without regard to income and offices here are built 2 to 1 over private residences. Talking about economics, particularly with respect to who deserves to live here may be divisive conversation, but not shunned. More than anything, actions speak louder than words and Silicon Valley's actions says it absolutely loves economic conservatism. As to social conservatism California has always been a free loving and special place all to its own. It's socially conservative values may be vastly different from those in say rural Arizona, but all the same it is a place that does not like change. NIMBYism has been enshrined in California’s Constitution that gives individuals the public power to stop change at abnormally high rates. Prop 13 locks in property taxes and protects homeowners against the most progressive instruments of change and if you ever go around looking at silicon valley, you will not notice a modern city adapting to the economic prosperity with rapid change to accommodate its new found economic status, but widespread resistance to building up and reducing green spaces so the unwashed masses have a place to live. It is sink or swim here. If you adjust for cost of living, California has the highest poverty rate. The only way you make it here is by overcoming adversity on your own. The median six figure salary will not even come close to allowing you to buy into the area. For that you need to bring another level of free enterprise and disruption to earn your place. Buying in also means owning a single story home built 50 years ago where half your neighbors will be new tech people, the other half will older residents who don’t want to move out. Despite a massive influx of new college graduates every year, the older residents already bought in here are incentivized to stay to such a massive degree that California, which for all of existence has always been a draw and a state that skews young, is now aging rapidly. It is still a huge attraction for younger generations who would love to live here, but are eventually forced out by the lack of affordable options as they get to child rearing age unless they can make a multiple or two more then what the average salary will deliver. If that’s not economic conservatism at its most extreme, I don’t know what is! I get it, you are spouting off the favored talking points of the right like building a wall, misogyny as a good thing, and how global warming is a hoax and not finding an audience in Silicon Valley. That's not conservative. That's just illogical and dumb. The surprise should be that kind of anti-science idiocy is accepted in large numbers anywhere and has been adopted as formal policy positions by mainline Republicans. As to actually being a free enterprise person who believes that motivation to do your best should be ever present and those who can't cut it don't deserve to be here, you will find no place else that better represents that mantra in practice then Silicon Valley.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do most software developers suck at algorithm-type interview questions?
Answer: Most experienced developers don't suck at interview questions. Your interview skills suck if what you want from a programmer in an interview is an exact discrete solution to a non-obvious problem though. The path you took to solve a problem and why you took it is what's important. Actually solving a problem in the confines of an interview is a little less so. I don't want to know that you know that 2+2 is 4. I want to know that given adequate time and resources, you can add any two numbers together and know the limitations of your abilities and how to get around them. Coming up with the optimal solution to really tricky algorithm questions in record time is not the defining quality for a 10x programmer. I want the guy who gets shit done consistently and deals well with explaining the risks when there are unknowns. That almost always involves compromise and implementing solutions in suboptimal ways that are simply quicker to code and more importantly, easier to debug and maintain. The code should always be good enough, but only optimal if it delivers enough value to justify the cost. I want the guy who can eloquently explain that in an interview. The guy I want to hire is the one that gives me multiple possible answers, not necessarily complete solutions, but states the easiest way he knows to solve the problem then details it's limitations and whether he believes other solutions exist, the unknowns, LOE required to solve it better, and the confidence that he thinks it's right regardless of whether it actually is. We then have a discussion on the path with the right amount of risk that brings the most value. You ask hard algorithm questions to get that kind of response. An interview question should find me a problem solver who can break down the costs of solving the problem in different ways, revealing just the solution doesn't do that and tells me little about who answered the question other then he is may be good at memorizing random trivia. Although, I do have to admit, I am a little bit impressed by the guy who immediately spouts out the text book answer to a really exotic question, I am going to have to ask him another question though to see if I really want to hire him.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is an associates in graphic design valuable when trying to become a front end web developer?
Answer: I've looked over hundreds of resumes and made hiring decisions on lots of developers. What I look for is past experience. Assuming you have that and it's relevant, you have likely already earned yourself an interview already in 90% of the cases. Relevance is not a discreet thing though and usually you find people that come close. If you are in that iffy case, you'll get tossed in the proceed pile if your education or academic background is strong. A graphic design degree would likely not qualify unless you got it from an Ivy league or someplace that really stood out. Then I might give you a chance or if for some reason your relevance was low, but still better then any other candidates you'd also get through. The degree may actually make your interview harder though as I would press you more on coding questions that designers are not likely to encounter when doing some light coding to make sure you have fully committed to being an engineer. In any case, your associates isn't worthless. It's better then no degree or something like a philosophy degree, but I'm going to be impressed more by a project, no matter how simple, implemented using the technology we are looking to hire for. That being said I'm not HR and havimg a degree can be more of a gate and the associates may be the difference of whether it makes it to me or not, but in general with development, you are going to be judged way more on your experience and specific akills then your academic record. Frontend development also crosses over into design quite often and having design skills and demonstrating they are compatible with whatever design process we have would be a real win. The associates will speak to that, but not much more then a portfolio would. Some positions at smaller companies explicitly look for candidates who can both design and code and your degree would be a real boon in those rare cases, but again in the majority of cases, your tech skills are going to be sole thing that gets you hired as a developer.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How hard is it to get an interview as a software engineer or a software developer at Google, Facebook, etc.? What degree of education is required (bachelor, master, etc.)?
Answer: It's more about who you know then what you know. Of course having a stellar resume helps a lot, but even an Ivy League graduate with lots of relevant experience can get lost in the millions of resumes those companies receive. What really helps is knowing someone already at Google or Facebook who can recommend you. That gets you bumped to the front of the line. No one is going to recommend you if you are incompetent, but if you are friends with or at least an aquaintence who hasn't screwed your champion over before, you have your in. You still need enough in your resume that they can point to and say you can do the job, but that should be a pretty low bar. That's obviously not hard academically speaking if you are already an engineer. It takes a bit of luck, but more so it helps being social and always expanding your network. That may be out of the comfort zone for many engineers, but my advice to you if you are trying to separate yourself from the rest of the pack, would not be to obtain more or better schooling, or even to pursue more interesting work (although the latter may be critically helpful during and after the interview stage). It would be to make friends, go out to conferences, talk to people there and follow up electronically, and job hop often to expand your network. If you really want the garunteed path to getting an interview, assuming you are a baseline engineer who can hold your own in geeky tech banter, move to silicon valley. You won't be able to go outside for long without seeing someone who works for Google or Facebook. When I moved to mountain view, in the apartment complex I moved into, of the 4 guys living below me, one worked at Facebook, another at Google. About half the households in the complex I live now probably have a Google employee. Getting an interview would be no problem, getting hired would be a different challenge though. However, given the cost of living here, moving to Silicon Valley may be the hardest thing you could do.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Do I want to base my startup in Silicon Valley or Austin? The technical skillsets are about 75% computer software, 25% hardware. My market is global.
Answer: Austin has more then enough qualified individuals. You will get much better talent paying average silicon valley wages in Austin. Silicon valley is where the money is though so if you haven't gotten your series A yet or don't have a clear path to it, Silicon Valley may be better. I don't see the talent options much better for the price you are paying. There's definitely more of it and we'll credentialed, but a lot is tied up working for options as good as cash worth double what you are likely able to offer. You will definitely be able to find the exact guy who does just what you need here, but will likely not be able to hire him. It's easier to find cofounders in silicon valley, but for building out your team, I haven't found much of an advantage here and given the $1.5 million it takes to buy a livable place in the valley, your talent just simply won't be able to weather the hard times when your equity doesn't look like it will deliver. I've personally passed up a couple really great opportunities in silicon valley that were a perfect fit just because I couldn't make the numbers work out. An offer that needs a 10x in the strike price just to break even isnt much of an offer at all. Top talent can be extremely picky in silicon valley. Silicon Valley is a great place to found a startup, since the housing market went back to bonkers 5 years ago its a really terrible one to try to grow one into a profitable company. Good luck.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What should I specialize in to find a good remote software engineer job with an expected salary of $140K+?
Answer: Very few jobs paying that much will be offered as fully remote. However, several of the places that I have worked at were quite willing to let proven existing employees go fully remote and keep thier salaries some of which were in excess of that. Unless the job is coming from someone in your network who can be your champion, don't expect to find many places willing to hire an unknown asset remotely. In either case, you need to spend several years building your network working in person at a couple of places or work for a place for several months then request to go remote. Don't expect to simply find such a job browsing monster. The opportunity is out there though, you just can't do it very easily through the classifieds model.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Which things about Silicon Valley were most unbelievable when you talked to people back home?
Answer: That you can be making $500k a year and still questioning if you can afford a starter home.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How hard is it to get into Virginia Tech?
Answer: 73% of applicants are accepted. The average GPA is around 3.5 depending on the year you look at. Compared to Harvard which has a 6% acceptance rate and a 4.01 average GPA, Virginia Tech seems a relatively easy target. However, also consider it has a graduation rate in the low 80s vs 97% for Harvard. The college of engineering that VA tech is known for is even worse with a 4 year graduation rate of about 50% and only 70% do it after 6 years. I went there for computer science which was easier to graduate in 4 years then other engineering majors as the prereqs don't stack as much, but they really like to weed you out early. If you didn't have a passion for computers coming in and some idea of programming, you were in for a rude awakening. I saw several previously 4.0 students on scholarship see grades failing or at least fall well below thier scholarship requirements during thier first semester. Some recovered and after you figure out the transition things get more predictable and often feel easier despite taking on exponentially more difficult coursework. My senior year, I took an algorithms course where the highest grade on the tests was typically in the 60s before the curve was applied. For in major courses, academic performance in high school was less of a predictor of success then how much of a computer geek you were. I was a graduate teaching assistant for the Intro to C++ course which welcomed students to the computer science major. Unlike many tutorials on the web that teach you to program by copying practical examples, the intro course was focused on teaching you abstract theory concepts that required not just writing some code to achieve a practical goal, but using binary math, pointers, and things that have few everyday analogies to perform a real world task in what was a completely foreign way to many students. I would say VA Tech is easy to get into, but hard to graduate from, exceptionally so if you are pursuing engineering for the career prospects and potential it offers rather then an intrinsic love for logical problem solving. It's likely not unlike many other good engineering schools, but a word to the wise, unlike the Ivyies where the acceptance process does a good job of making sure only those prepared for the challenges make it in, getting in is merely warming you up for the real challenges ahead.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How will Snap come back from where it is now? Can they win against Facebook/Instagram? Is there anything they can do to become a tech giant like FB?
Answer: It's going to be a content war. The question is can snapchat get thier followers to create more engaging content or if that fails can snap pay celebrities to create content that users will flock to in great numbers. Snap has enough daily active users in the US to be dangerous though. It will never post the numbers that Facebook has though. Creating videos is both bandwidth and CPU intensive and many nations just don't have users with those capabilities and that may be a decade or more away in some countries. Snapchat also dominates the younger demographics and unlike Facebook, the older generations haven't made the leap to video. Unfortunately, for snapchat, the younger demographics are also less loyal, but if Snapchat can develop a compelling case for parents to check in and more importantly communicate with thier kids through video, there is enormous potential to grow thier numbers. That being said, if Snapchat can simply instill loyalty somehow and continue to appeal to the youngest generation, it will continue to grow slowly as the young users it has now become older and continue to use it as thier defacto social network. They can win simply by sticking around long enough as they are the young people's social network of choice. Of course they will have to become profitable to do this and resign themselves to slow growth over a decade or more rather then trying to return to and sustain triple digit growth numbers. Losing half a billion dollars a year is not a very good start to that though and being trendy and appealing to the next generation is a very finicky business, but they are much better positioned then Facebook to do exactly that.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How do you decide where to live when moving to the San Francisco Bay Area with school-aged children?
Answer: Decide? That presumes you have real choices. When we moved here 2 years ago, we stayed in temporary housing for 3 months, during that time, we literally found 1 place with 3 bedrooms, a not terrible commute to work, and in a good school district. Commutes of more then 10 miles can exceed an hour in some places at rush hour which really limits options. California has the worst student to teacher ratio in the nation and schools in the Bay area range between excellent to terrible often within the same town. No place accepted dogs with our minimum criteria so we had to leave our dog behind. A month to month lease was $7k a month vs $5k for yearly so waiting for better places to show up was also a non starter. Places would only be on the market for about 2 weeks so if you didn't immediately fill out an application and put down a deposit ASAP you were SOL. Expect bottom of the line appliances and things that should be trivial fixes for $5k a month to mind bogglingly persist. There seems to be a few more places on the market now then when we moved here and prices are about the same so you might have a bit more selection. The good news is, your decision will likely be easy once you resign yourself to the level of compromise you will have to make to live here as your real choices will be very few and far between. This place was designed for allowing the affluent families already living here to continue to do so without compromise, but the opposite holds true for new families trying to move here who are locked out of the decent suburban houses and must compete for places optimized for 20 something new college grads. Good luck.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it a good idea to buy homes in cities where monthly rents match up (or are more) to mortgage payments?
Answer: It's risky. Whether it's good or bad will be a function of how long you stay in the house and how much it appreciates. Rents typically tail home prices so a city with a mortgage payment less then rent is likely one on the decline. In the short term, you may see a double digit percent of loss in your homes value immediately after buying that locks you in and could be precipitously bad if the decline comes from a recession in which you experience a job loss. On the converse you may double your investment in a short period. It's impossible to tell what will happen especially looking at just rent vs housing prices for metrics. If this is your primary household, don't look at it as an investment. It's a good idea to buy a house regardless of the rent vs buy metrics, if you can afford it and can see yourself living in it for a decade or more. Full stop. Don't over think it, assuming your following the standard advice of a 20% down mortgage and the house appraised, that's all you need to consider. Anything else may not prove to be a bad idea, but you aren't going to know that just by looking at the relative mortgage to rent costs. In other words, whether it's a good idea or not should be a function of how much you will like the house long term, not whether the investment will deliver.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Are there too many future programmers?
Answer: Programming is problem solving. Sure, you need to learn the language which anyone can do with perserveramce, but not everyone will be drawn to the detail oriented work that it takes to think through every aspect of the problem. That type of commitment and patience is learned over longer then a few classes. The difficulty of software development will always make it self limiting. Still your question was how many is too many. I struggle to think of a time when all problems with solutions that have enough economic return to make them viable will be solved no matter how many programmers you have. You are essentially asking when will people stop wanting more and the answer is never. Once you create a product that solves a problem, it tends to create five more that suddenly have more relevance. For example, the internet was created by engineers and suddenly the number of programmers needed was exponentially more. Microsoft Windows made computers easy enough to use for the masses and suddenly you again needed more programmers. Facebook created demand for Instagram and countless games, etc. As it turns out, programmers are far more prolific at revealing new problems then they are at solving existing ones. There is rarely any project I work on where I don't find several unrelated things that I wish there was a better way to do. No, there will never be too many programmers.
