Question: If I found lots of cash buried under my property, say $10 million, would I legally be allowed to keep it?
Answer: In the US it's generally finders keepers if it's on your property. There are exceptions for things that are misplaced and the seeker can prove they were looking for it and haven't abandoned it. I.e. if you lose a diamond ring on someone's property, if the property owners know this and find it, they have an obligation to return it to you and keep it safe until you return. In this case, $10 million in cash would take up close to a cubic yard of space using $100 bills. I would like to hear the circumstances under which the previous owner lost track of that!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do public sector workers pay income tax?
Answer: If they weren't taxed, they couldn't get deductions. That means buying a house would be more expensive as well as saving for retirement, college, medical expenses, etc. It would be harder to compare compensation for public sector workers to private ones and would likely make hireing harder. It would also skew the cost of government programs. Services like the postal service wouldn't see nearly as much savings per worker as postal workers wages are relatively low and taxed at lower levels. Someplace like NASA that employs lots of engineers and high earning individuals would see greater savings as they could pay those employees less who would see a greater tax windfall. It would also have a negative effect on contracting as contractors would likely need to be paid far more to cover the taxes they wouldn't have to pay for government employees. That being said you could overcome all these issue, but if you were hoping to save on administrative costs by not having to deal with taxes, you would likely find the opposite to be true as you would have to constantly monitor and fix the alternative system to keep it fair and sustainable.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is there a death tax when taxes were already paid on that $? Should we not fight to end it?
Answer: We need to pay for our government somehow and there is literally no one who could complain less then a dead person. The Republican opposition to the estate tax seems a bit oxymoronic to me. You have to get revenue from somewhere and a large estate tax should allow you to reduce taxes elsewhere like taxes on corporations or taxes on income for job creators. Inherited money really seems tantamount to welfare by another name. Take some personal responsibility to earn your own wealth. Kids of highly successful people rarely live up to those expectations. Isn't it better to tax the money a person hasn't earned then to tax the money earned through hard work and demonstrable success? Still, I get it, it's a tax so everyone hates it on some level, doubly so when it hits you, but as the lesser of evils, no matter whether you are conservative or liberal there's lots to like about the estate tax relative to other options.

Question: Is it socially acceptable to be a conservative in Silicon Valley?
Answer: It is socially acceptable to be Conservative in silicon valley. They are in the minority for sure, but I know a couple. Openly Republican is a bit harder to pull off though. Silicon valley has a lot of serious problems that liberals put at the top of thier priority list to address. California has statutory tax rates that are highly progressive on paper, but given the extreme cost of living in silicon valley, combined with the tax deferrals that prop 13 creates overwhelming go to rich property owners and corporations, there is a lot to not like about the liberal government that oversees an effectively regressive tax regime while claiming the opposite. Also, after adjusting for the cost of living, California has the highest poverty rate in the nation and the highest student to teacher ratio in the nation. Don't get me started about the mass transportation that fails anyplace outside of the heart of San Francisco. There is no more universal complaint then the cost of living in Silicon Valley and a conservative free market path in place of the one that has allowed older individual property owners to lock out future generations has a lot of appeal to many here, particularly to younger tech workers struggling to buy a house where the jobs are and who consider themselves die hard liberals. There is no place better on earth where you can see the effects of liberal policies that don't have adequate checks and balances in place then Silicon Valley. Conservative ideas without Republican spin can actually go far if presented with a plan to fix those problems and not simply stop at saying give more money to job creators and less to government and all will be corrected. You mention trickle down economics as a realistic policy position or start referring to the 1% simply as job creators who deserve a tax break for thier hard work without qualifying your statements, you aren't going to find an ear. The nuclear option is really adopting any of the bat shit crazy ideas that seem to be the top priorities of the Republican platform these days though. You claim that global warming isn't happening or isn't one of the defining issues our government needs to address and you will be avoided. Everyone has something to hate about Obamacare, even here, but talking about repeal rather then reform isn't going to earn you many friends and trying to say the free market is a solution for heathcare will find almost universal derision. Most people here don't actually care much for guns either way and you can feel free to own them as long as you jump through the many hoops to do it legally, just don't try to make the point that good guys with guns are a solution to bad guys with guns. Immigrants also make up a significant amount of the population and many are in high profile positions and a significant source of money and jobs here. The recent citizens also have family that like to visit from Muslim countries. Talk of a wall, immigrants as terrorists, or that immigrants are murderers and rapists will get you shunned virtually instantly. Talking of reforming immigration, including getting rid of garunteed citizenship for anchor babies and kicking out violent criminals is acceptable, particularly with a slant towards letting all those in who can easily pay thier own way and accepting those already here with well established roots. As long as your ideas will stand up to critical thinking, you can be safely conservative, even if never completely related to. Those kind of ideas seem few and far between in the modern Republican party, so claiming that affliation will give you a real uphill battle. Talking about how some liberal policies failed to achieve liberal goals, well that's a gold mine and you can let your conservatism shine a light on that issue.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do computer manufacturers purposely complicate the process of adding new components? Why not just add convenient "RAM" slots on the exterior?
Answer: Ram use to be expensive and a real bottleneck. If you didn't have enough ram you couldn't run a particular program and many times you didn't realize that until after you bought the computer and had it for several months when a new application comes out. That is no longer the case. Today, you get at least 4 Gbs in even bottom of the line machines and that amount does what most people want just fine. Even 8 Gb of value ram will cost manufacturers less than $20. In fact, adding more ram by default can be cheaper then adding the ability to add more ram in the future. We know how much ram the vast majority of even power users use on modern operating systems and it tends to max out at 8 Gb. More solves problems for exceedingly few users doing a few very specific tasks. Manufacturers don’t add convenient RAM slots today because people would expect their computers to get faster or more capable when they used them. Today if you add more ram to a slow PC, you will still just end up with a slow PC with more ram.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What happens if a founder, holding minority share, is fired in the first year of a 3-year vesting and 1 year cliff with a double trigger acceleration?
Answer: The founder should consider himself lucky to get out of an obviously abrasive relationship after wasting so little time at the company. As to the double trigger clause those are generally messy. It's not a formal legal term, just one that's spelled out specifically in your employment contract and can really have any terms. It might not be applicable if you were fired preacquisition or have a small timeline in which it applies, like 3 months prior to the acquisition. It may or may not have special terms prior to the cliff. You would have to consult your employment contract knowing specifically what happened to know your rights for sure. In any case, they are meant to be mutually beneficial. The new company knows a specific amount it will take to keep the old employees and the employees have a large payout to keep them at a company they never directly agreed to work for. They work when all parties want to move forward and both make it clear of the cost of the acquisition and to protect you if things go south after it. That being said, prior to the acquisition, if the acquiring company doesn’t actually want the employees or they only care about a scant few of the remaining founders who hold all the voting power, there are seven ways from sunday to get around it. They can simply dissolve all common stock and make an all cash offer for the company or simply devalue the common stock. If there is no stock left, there’s nothing to vest… Basically if the new company has a lawyer on retainer and both the other founders and the new company are intent on not paying you, a double trigger clause, probably isn’t going to save you.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Should I consider a move to a tech start up from being a software engineer in an investment bank?
Answer: I don't get why you are saying the new place pays you the same and then say they give you RSUs on top of that. RSUs have value. Figure out what that is, if it's 10% or more of your salary, it's a no brainer. It should be the better career move unless you are regarded as a rising star at your current location and are on a quick promotion track. You'll have to decide if there is a work life balance upside or not too, but software engineering isn't a career that rewards you for sticking around, just the opposite. Strike while the iron is hot. Also, unless you are an early founding member, working for a startup shouldn't be much different then working for an established company. The culture may be different, but no more so then difference s between companies of similar size. In my experience the day to day for a software engineer isn't dictated by startup status, but more by the processes the company adopts. That being said, startups do tend to have less beauracracy, but that may not be true for your specific role.
